Abū Jaʿfar said: The more correct of the two readings is the reading of those who recite "shanaʾāni qawmin" with the "nūn" vowelled with fatḥa, because the widespread interpretation of the people of interpretation is that it means "the hatred of a people," and they directed it to the sense of the verbal noun rather than the noun.

Since it is directed to the sense of the verbal noun, the eloquent Arabic usage for verbal nouns in the form "faʿlān" with a fatḥa on the "fāʾ" is to vowel the second letter, not to make it sukūn, as I described from their saying "al-darajān" and "al-ramalān," from "daraja" and "ramala." Likewise "al-shanaʾān" from "shanaʾtuhu, ashnaʾuhu, shanaʾānan." Some Arabs say "shanānun" on the pattern "faʿāl," though I know of no reader who recited it so. Among this is the verse of the poet: [[He is al-Aḥwaṣ ibn Muḥammad al-Anṣārī.]]

"Life is nothing but what you enjoy and desire,
even if he who has hatred (dhū al-shanān) and arrogance blames it."

[[Ṭabaqāt Fuḥūl al-Shuʿarāʾ: 539; al-Aghānī 13:151-153; Maṣāriʿ al-ʿUshshāq: 62, 75; al-Shiʿr wa al-Shuʿarāʾ: 501; Lisān (shnʾ); there is hardly a book that does not contain it.]]

This is in the dialect of one who dropped the hamza from "shanaʾān," so it became on the pattern "faʿāl," though originally it is "faʿalān."
* *

Mention of those among the people of interpretation who said "shanaʾāna qawmin" means the hatred of a people.

[10993] Muthannā narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiya narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying, "And let not the hatred of a people incite you," he said: let not the hatred of a people impel you.

[10994] Muthannā narrated to me again with his chain, from Ibn ʿAbbās, and he said: let not the enmity of a people impel you to transgress.

[10995] Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah: "And let not the hatred of a people incite you," he said: let not the hatred of a people incite you.

[10996] Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying, "And let not the hatred of a people incite you," he said: their hatred, that you transgress.
* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿that they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, that you transgress﴾
Abū Jaʿfar said: The readers differed in its recitation.

Some of the people of Medina and the majority of the Kufan readers recited: ﴿an ṣaddūkum﴾ with a fatḥa on the "alif" of "an", meaning: let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, impel you to transgress against them.
* *

Some readers of the Ḥijāz and Basra recited it: ﴿wa lā yajrimannakum shanaʾānu qawmin in ṣaddūkum﴾, with a kasra on the "alif" of "in", meaning: let not the hatred of a people incite you if they inflict a bar upon you from the Sacred Mosque, that you transgress. They claimed that in the reading of Ibn Masʿūd it is ﴿in yaṣaddūkum﴾, and they read it so, following his reading. [[See al-Farrāʾ's Maʿānī al-Qurʾān 1:300.]]
* *

Abū Jaʿfar said: The correct view in this matter, in my judgment, is that both are well-known, widely transmitted readings among the readers of the cities, and the meaning of each is sound.

This is because the Prophet ﷺ was barred from the House, he and his companions, on the day of al-Ḥudaybiyya, and Sūrat al-Māʾida was revealed to him after that. Whoever reads ﴿an ṣaddūkum﴾ with a fatḥa on the "alif" of "an", its meaning is: let not the hatred of a people, O people, impel you, because they barred you on the day of al-Ḥudaybiyya from the Sacred Mosque, that you transgress against them.

Whoever reads ﴿in ṣaddūkum﴾ with a kasra on the "alif," its meaning is: let not the hatred of a people incite you if they bar you from the Sacred Mosque when you wish to enter it. For those who fought the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions from Quraysh on the day of the conquest of Mecca had attempted to bar them from the Sacred Mosque. So God forewarned the believers, according to the view of the one who reads with kasra on "in," against transgressing against them if they bar them from the Sacred Mosque, before that could come from the barrers.

Nevertheless, even if the matter is as you have described, the reading with the fatḥa on the "alif" is clearer in meaning, because there is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that this sūrah was revealed after the day of al-Ḥudaybiyya.

Given that this is so, the barring had already occurred from the polytheists, so God forbade the believers from transgressing against the barrers because of their barring them from the Sacred Mosque. [[See the explanation of "al-ṣadd" above, p. 410, note 1, and the references there.]]
* *

As for His saying, "that you transgress," it means: that you exceed the limit God has set for you concerning them. [[See the explanation of "al-iʿtidāʾ" above in the indices of language.]]
* *

So the interpretation of the verse is: "And let not the hatred of a people incite you, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, O believers, to transgress God's judgment concerning them, so that you exceed it to what He has forbidden you. Rather, hold fast to obedience to God in what you love and what you dislike."
* *

It is mentioned that it was revealed concerning the prohibition of pursuing the vendettas of the Jāhiliyya. [["Dhuḥūl" is the plural of "dhaḥl" (with fatḥa then sukūn): the blood-revenge.]]

Mention of those who said this:

[10997] Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid regarding God's saying, "that you transgress": a believing man, one of the allies of Muḥammad, killed an ally of Abū Sufyān from Hudhayl on the day of the Conquest at ʿArafa, because he used to kill the allies of Muḥammad. So Muḥammad ﷺ said: May God curse whoever kills over a vendetta of the Jāhiliyya.

[10998] al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abū Ḥudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the like of it.
* *

Others said: this is abrogated.

Mention of those who said this:

[10999] Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying, "And let not the hatred of a people incite you that you transgress," he said: their hatred, until you commit what is not lawful for you. And he recited: "that they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, that you transgress and help one another," and said: all of this has been abrogated; jihād abrogated it.
* *

Abū Jaʿfar said: The more correct of the two views is the view of Mujāhid, that it is not abrogated, because it allows the meaning: "that you transgress the truth in what I have commanded you." When that is possible, it is not permissible to say it is abrogated except with a proof that must be accepted.
* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾
Abū Jaʿfar said: By His saying, "And cooperate in righteousness and piety," He, may His praise be exalted, means: "let some of you, O believers, help others" in "righteousness," which is acting upon what God has commanded to be acted upon [[See the explanation of "al-birr" above, 2:8/3:336-338, 556/4:425/6:587.]], and "piety," which is guarding against what God has commanded to be guarded against and avoiding His disobedience. [[See the explanation of "al-taqwā" above in the indices of language, root (wqy).]]
* *

And His saying, "and do not cooperate in sin and aggression," means: "let none of you help another in sin," i.e., in abandoning what God commanded you to do, "and in aggression," i.e., "nor in exceeding what God has set as limits for you in your religion, and has obligated for yourselves and for others." [[See the explanation of "al-ithm" and "al-ʿudwān" above in the indices of language (ʾthm) (ʿdw).]]

The meaning of the speech is: "And let not the hatred of a people, that they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, incite you to transgress. Rather, let some of you help others by commanding one another to stop at what God has set as limits for you concerning the people who barred you from the Sacred Mosque and concerning others, and to refrain from what God has forbidden you to commit against them and against others, and in all that He has forbidden you. Let none of you help another in opposition to this."
* *

The people of interpretation said likewise regarding "righteousness and piety."

Mention of those who said this:

[11000] Muthannā narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiya narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying, "And cooperate in righteousness and piety": "righteousness" is what you were commanded, and "piety" is what you were forbidden.

[11001] Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ, from Abū al-ʿĀliya regarding His saying, "And cooperate in righteousness and piety," he said: "righteousness" is what you were commanded, and "piety" is what you were forbidden.
* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And fear God; indeed God is severe in penalty﴾ (2)
Abū Jaʿfar said: This is a warning from God, may His praise be exalted, and a threat to whoever transgresses His limit and exceeds His command. He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "And fear God," i.e., beware of God, O believers, lest you meet Him in your return having transgressed His limit concerning what He set as limits for you, and opposed His command in what He commanded you, or His prohibition in what He forbade you, so that you deserve His punishment and merit His painful torment. Then He described His punishment as severe, saying, may His remembrance be exalted: indeed God is severe in punishing whoever He punishes from among His creatures, for it is a Fire whose heat is not extinguished, whose embers are not quenched, and whose flame does not subside. We seek refuge with God from it and from any deed that brings us near to it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 1 of 7):

The Explanation of His Words: ﴿Forbidden to you are dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than God⟩

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: God has forbidden you, O believers, dead animals.

*   *   *

"Dead animals" (al-maytah) means every creature with a flowing soul (nafs sa'ilah) among the land animals and birds, of those whose eating God has permitted, whether domesticated or wild, whose soul has departed from it without slaughter ("tadhkiyah"—the ritual slaughter).

Some have said: "Dead animals" is whatever life has departed from among the land animals and birds without ritual slaughter, of those whose eating God has made lawful. [See the explanation of "dead animals" above, 3:318, 319.]

We have already explained the reason that makes our saying correct on this matter in our book ﴿The Book of Subtle Discourse on Rulings⟩. [The name of this book has been mentioned several times, and in some places it appears as "al-Latif fi Ahkam Shara'i' al-Islam," 1:109. Here in the manuscript and the printed edition it read: "Kitab al-Latif al-Qawl fi al-Ahkam," which is not correct.]

*   *   *

As for "blood," it refers to flowing blood, not what is not flowing, because God, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be dead animals, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 145]. As for what has become part of the flesh, such as the liver and the spleen, and what in the flesh is not flowing, that is not forbidden, by the consensus of all on this.

*   *   *

As for His words "and the flesh of swine," it means: the flesh of swine has been forbidden to you, both domestic and wild.

The "dead animal" and "blood" are, in their outward form, general in expression, while what is meant by them is particular. As for the flesh of swine, its outward and inner parts are alike, and its inner parts are like its outer parts; all of it is forbidden, and nothing of it has been exempted.

*   *   *

As for His words "and that which has been dedicated to other than God," it means: that over which the name of other than God has been invoked.

*   *   *

Its origin is from "the crying out of a newborn" (istihlal al-sabi), which is when it cries out as it falls from its mother's womb. From it comes "the iḥlal of the pilgrim (muhrim) for the Hajj," when he utters the talbiyah. [See the explanation of "al-ihlal" above, 3:319, 320.] From it is the saying of Ibn Ahmar:

They cry out by the Farqad, their riders, as the rider performing 'umrah cries out... [Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah 1:150; al-Jamharah 2:387; Lisan (ʿ-m-r) (h-l-l). He describes a desert in which they cannot find their way. "Al-mu'tamir" is one who wraps himself in a turban. "Al-Farqad" intends "al-Farqadan," which are two stars of the Lesser Bear, or two stars in the sky that never set, but circle around the Pole Star.
There are two explanations of the verse. Al-Asma'i said: "When the clouds clear from the Farqad for them, they cry out, that is, they raise their voices with takbir, as the rider who intends 'umrah cries out, because they were guided by the Farqad."
Another said: "He means that they are in a remote desert far from water, and when they see a farqad—which is a young wild cow—they cry out, that is, they say takbir, because they knew they had come near water."
I say: The Arabs take the "two Farqads" as a guide for finding their way by them, because they are never sought at any time of the night without being found. Al-Ra'i said: They take nothing as a guide when they climb a desert, except the whiteness of the two Farqads.]

*   *   *

He only meant by His words "that which has been dedicated to other than God" that which was slaughtered for idols and images, over which the name of other than God is invoked. [See above, 3:321.]

*   *   *

The people of interpretation have said what we have said on this, and we have already mentioned the narrations from those who said it earlier, so we dislike repeating them. [See the earlier reports, numbers 2468–2477.]

*   *   *

The Explanation of His Words: ﴿And the strangled﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed about the manner of "strangling" (al-inkhinaq) that God, may His praise be exalted, meant by His words "and the strangled."

Some of them said:

11002 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn told us, Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal told us, Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "And the strangled," he said: that which puts its head between two branches of a tree, so it is strangled and dies.

11002a – Ibn Waki' told us, Abu Khalid al-Ahmar told us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak regarding "the strangled," he said: that which is strangled and dies.

11003 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, Ma'mar told us, from Qatadah regarding His words "and the strangled," that which dies in its khinaq. [Al-khinaq (with a kasra on the kha'): the rope with which it is strangled; he means the rope tied at its neck.]

*   *   *

Others said: It is the one that is bound, so its bond strangles it and kills it.

Those who said this:

11004 – It was reported to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say, 'Ubayd informed us, I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words "and the strangled": a sheep is bound, and its tether strangles it, so it is forbidden.

*   *   *

Others said: Rather, it is a beast of the cattle, which the polytheists used to strangle until it died, so God forbade eating it.

Those who said this:

11005 – al-Muthanna told me, 'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, Mu'awiyah told me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And the strangled," which is strangled and dies. [In the printed edition: "tukhtaniq fa-tamut" (it is strangled and dies), which is a plain error that corrupts Tabari's argument; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]

11006 – Bishr told us, Yazid told us, Sa'id told us, from Qatadah: "And the strangled": the people of the Jahiliyyah used to strangle the sheep until it died, then they ate it. [Report 11006: "Bishr ibn Mu'adh," which has passed, and its chain has passed hundreds of times, the nearest being no. 10995. But in the manuscript and the printed edition here it read: "Anas told us, Yazid told us," which is a plain error.]

*   *   *

The most correct of these sayings is the saying of those who said: "It is the one that is strangled, either in its bond, or by putting its head into a place from which it cannot free itself, so it is strangled until it dies."

We only said that this is more correct in interpreting it than others, because "al-munkhaniqah" is the one described as being strangled, not one who is strangled by another; if it were intended that it was the object of the action, it would have been said "al-makhnuqah," so that the meaning of the sentence would be what they said.

*   *   *

The Explanation of His Words: ﴿And the beaten to death﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "al-mawquzah," may He be exalted, He means the dead animal being "waqidh" (beaten to near death).

*   *   *

It is said of it: "waqadahu yaqiduhu waqdan," when he struck it until it was near to death. From it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

A she-camel that kicks the weaned calf with her leg, a striker of the udders of the virgin she-camels [Diwan: 452; Naqa'id: 332; from his satire of Jarir, before it: "How many a maternal aunt and paternal aunt of yours, O Jarir, a broad-hipped woman who has milked my camels..." 
...]

*   *   *

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

11007 – al-Muthanna told me, 'Abd Allah told us, Mu'awiyah told me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And the beaten to death," he said: the beaten to death is that which is struck with wood until it is beaten to death by it. [In the printed edition: "hatta taqdhaha fa-tamut," and in the manuscript: "hatta tuwqidhaha fa-tamut"; the correct reading is what I have set down. "By it" means by the piece of wood; see the following reports, which show the correctness of this reading.]

11008 – Bishr told us, Yazid told us, Sa'id told us, from Qatadah: "And the beaten to death": the people of the Jahiliyyah used to strike it with sticks until it died, then they ate it.

11009 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar told us, Rawh told us, Shu'bah told us, from Qatadah regarding His words "and the beaten to death," he said: they used to strike it until they beat it to death, then they ate it.

11010 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His words "and the beaten to death," which is beaten until it dies.

11011 – Ibn Waki' told us, Abu Khalid al-Ahmar told us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak who said: "al-Mawquzah," that which is struck until it dies.

11012 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn told us, Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal told us, Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "And the beaten to death," he said: it is that which is struck and dies.

11013 – It was reported to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say, 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words "and the beaten to death": a sheep or another of the cattle was struck with wood for their idols, until they killed it and ate it.

11014 – al-'Abbas ibn al-Walid told us, 'Uqbah ibn 'Alqamah informed me, Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah told me, Nu'aym ibn Salamah told me, from Abu 'Abd Allah al-Sunabihi who said: "al-Mawquzah" is only in the case of livestock, and there is no "waqidh" in game. [Report 11014: "al-'Abbas ibn al-Walid ibn Mazid al-Amali," Tabari's teacher, mentioned earlier as no. 891. "'Uqbah ibn 'Alqamah ibn Hudayj al-Ma'afiri," one of the companions of al-Awza'i, was a good and trustworthy man; he is biographed in the Tahdhib. "Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah ibn Shamr ibn Yaqzan al-Ramli," transmitted from by Malik, al-Layth, and Ibn al-Mubarak; trustworthy. Damrah ibn Rabi'ah said: "I have not seen anyone more eloquent than him," and he used to recite fine poetry. He is biographed in the Tahdhib and al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 1/1/310. "Nu'aym ibn Salamah al-Azdi," also said to be "Nu'aym ibn Salaman." He held the seal of Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz. They did not mention any criticism of him; he is biographed in al-Kabir 4/2/98, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/462, and Ta'jil al-Manfa'ah: 423. "Abu 'Abd Allah al-Sunabihi" is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Usaylah ibn 'Asal ibn 'Assal al-Muradi. He travelled to the Prophet ﷺ but found that he had died five or six nights before. He was trustworthy and transmitted little hadith. Al-Tabarani related through Ibn Muhayriz who said: "We visited 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, and Abu 'Abd Allah al-Sunabihi came, and 'Ubadah said: Whoever would be pleased to look at a man who was taken up to the heavens and saw the people of Paradise and the people of Hell, and returned acting according to what he saw, let him look at this one.]

*   *   *

[1]1028. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "and that which the beast of prey has eaten," he said: that which the beast of prey has taken.

1029. Ibn Wakiʿ narrated to us, saying: Abu Khalid al-Ahmar narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak regarding "and that which the beast of prey has eaten," he said: that which the beast of prey has taken.

1030. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada regarding "and that which the beast of prey has eaten," he said: When the beast of prey killed any of these or ate from it, the people of the Jahiliyya would eat what remained.

1031. Ibn Wakiʿ narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, from Qays, from ʿAta' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Abu al-Rabiʿ, from Ibn ʿAbbas that he recited: ﴿And that which the beast of prey has eaten (wa-akil al-sab')﴾.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿except what you slaughter (illa ma dhakkaytum)﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "except what you slaughter," He means: except what you have purified by the slaughter which God has made a means of purification.

* *

Then the people of interpretation differed concerning what God excepted by His saying, "except what you slaughter."

Some of them said: He excepted from the whole of what God named as forbidden in His saying: "and that which has been dedicated to other than God, and the strangled, and the beaten to death, and the fallen, and the gored, and that which the beast of prey has eaten."

Those who said this:

1032. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "except what you slaughter," he says: whatever you reach its slaughter from all of this, while its tail is still moving or its eye still blinking, then slaughter it and mention the name of God over it, and it is lawful.

1033. Ibn Wakiʿ narrated to us, saying: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Ashʿath, from al-Hasan regarding "Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than God, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and that which the beast of prey has eaten, except what you slaughter." Al-Hasan said: Whichever of these you reach its slaughter, slaughter it and eat. I said: O Abu Saʿid, how do I know? He said: When it blinks its eye or strikes with its tail.

1034. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada regarding "except what you slaughter," he said: all of this which God, mighty and majestic, named here, except the flesh of swine, when you reach from it an eye that blinks, or a tail that moves, or a leg that kicks [[al-rakd: the movement and agitation of a leg, or striking with it. "irtakada al-shay'": when a thing became agitated.]] and you slaughter it, God has made that lawful for you.

1035. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada regarding "except what you slaughter," from all of this. If you find it blinking its eye, or moving its ear, from all of this, it is lawful for you.

1036. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym and ʿAbbad narrated to me, both saying: Hajjaj informed us, from Husayn, from al-Shaʿbi, from al-Harith, from ʿAli who said: If you reach the slaughter of the beaten, the fallen, or the gored while it moves a hand or a foot, then eat it.

1037. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Ibrahim who said: If the beast of prey eats from the game, or the beaten, or the gored, or the fallen, and you reach its slaughter, then eat.

1038. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Musʿab ibn Sallam al-Tamimi narrated to us, saying: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from his father, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib who said: If it kicks with its leg, or blinks its eye, and moves its tail, then it suffices. [[The report: 1038 — Musʿab ibn Sallam al-Tamimi, whose biography passed under no. 5382. Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib is Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, whose biography passed under no. 2003. His father, Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, is Muhammad al-Baqir, who passed under nos. 5123, 5463.]]

1039. Ibn al-Muthanna and Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, both saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj informed us, saying: Ibn Tawus informed me, from his father who said: When you slaughter it and it wags its tail or moves, it is lawful for you — or he said: that is sufficient for him. [["Masaʿat bi-dhanabiha": it moved and struck with its tail. In the printed edition it read "aw qala: fa-hasbuhu," the correct reading from the manuscript being "fa-hasbuhu," meaning that suffices him and makes it permissible for him, i.e., for one who wishes to eat it.]]

1040. Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Humayd, from al-Hasan who said: If the beaten one blinks its eye, or kicks its leg, or wags its tail, then slaughter it and eat.

1041. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Qatada, similarly.

1042. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Abu al-Zubayr, that he heard ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr say: If it blinks its eye, or wags its tail, or moves, it is lawful for you.

1043. I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say: The people of the Jahiliyya used to eat this, so God forbade it in Islam except what is slaughtered of it. Whatever of it is reached while a man or a tail or an eye moves, and it is slaughtered, it is lawful.

1044. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine," and His saying: "and the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored," through the verse: "and that which the beast of prey has eaten, except what you slaughter," he said: all of this is forbidden, except what is slaughtered of it.

* *

So the interpretation of the verse according to these people is: The beaten and the fallen are forbidden if they die from falling, beating, goring, or the mauling of the beast of prey, except that you reach their slaughter before they die, in which case their eating is then lawful.

* *

Others said: It is an exception from the prohibition, but not an exception from the prohibited items God mentioned in His saying: "Forbidden to you is carrion," because carrion has no slaughter, nor does swine. They said: The meaning of the verse is: Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and the rest of what we have mentioned along with that, except what you slaughter of the animals which God has made lawful for you through slaughter; that is lawful for you. Among those who said this was a group from the people of Medina.

Some of those who said this:

1045. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Malik said, when asked about the sheep whose belly the beast of prey has torn open until its intestines come out: I do not think it should be slaughtered, nor should any part of it that is slaughtered be eaten.

1046. Yunus narrated to me, from Ashhab, saying: Malik was asked about a beast of prey that attacks a ram and breaks its back: Do you think it should be slaughtered before it dies and then eaten? He said: If it has reached the sahr [["al-sahr" (with fatha then sukun): the lung, or what clings to the throat and gullet from the upper belly.]], I do not think it should be eaten. If it has only struck its limbs, I see no harm in it. It was said to him: It leapt upon it and broke its back? He said: It does not please me that it be eaten; this one does not survive. It was said to him: What about the wolf that attacks a sheep and tears its belly but does not tear the intestines? He said: If it has torn its belly, I do not think it should be eaten.

* *

According to this view, His saying "except what you slaughter" must be a disjunctive (munqati') exception.

= So the interpretation of the verse is: Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and the rest of what we have mentioned, but what you slaughter of the animals which I have made lawful for you through slaughter is lawful.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The more correct of the two views in our opinion is the first, namely that His saying "except what you slaughter" is an exception from His saying "and that which has been dedicated to other than God, and the strangled, and the beaten to death, and the fallen, and the gored, and that which the beast of prey has eaten," because all of that is characterized by the attribute it bears before the moment of its death [[In the manuscript: "mawtiha" (its death), and both are the same.]]. It is said of what the polytheists offered to their idols and named for them: "It is that which has been dedicated to other than God," meaning named as an offering to other than God. Likewise "the strangled," when it is strangled even if it does not die, it is still strangled. Likewise all that God, mighty and majestic, forbade after His saying "that which has been dedicated to other than God," except by slaughter; it is characterized by the attribute it bears before its death, and God has forbidden it to His servants except by the permitted slaughter, not by death through the cause by which it was characterized. Since that is so, the interpretation of the verse is: Forbidden to you is that which has been dedicated to other than God, and the strangled, and so-and-so, and so-and-so, except what you slaughter of those.

Here "mā" = since that is its interpretation = is in the accusative position as an exception from what precedes it. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative.

Since the matter is as we have described, then whatever of a bird or beast is reached for slaughter before its soul leaves and its spirit departs from its body, its eating is lawful, if it is among what God has made lawful for His servants.

* *

If someone says to us: If that is its meaning in your view, then what is the purpose of repeating what was repeated in His saying "that which has been dedicated to other than God, and the strangled, and the beaten to death, and the fallen," and the rest of what was enumerated as forbidden in this verse, when He opened the verse with His saying: "Forbidden to you is carrion"? You know that His saying "Forbidden to you is carrion" encompasses every carrion, whether it died of illness from a natural cause without anyone's offense against it, or died from someone's striking it, or strangling, or goring, or the mauling of a beast of prey? Would not His saying — if the matter is as you describe, that it refers to the prohibition in all of those: carrion by strangling, goring, beating, or the beast's eating, or otherwise, not that its prohibition refers only to when it falls, is strangled, or is mauled by a beast so that it is known it will not live from what befell it except with a little life — would not "Forbidden to you is carrion" have been sufficient, dispensing with the repetition of what He repeated in His saying "that which has been dedicated to other than God, and the strangled," and what else was mentioned with it, and its enumeration of what it enumerated?

It was said: The purpose of its repetition — though the prohibition of those things applies when they die by the causes by which they are characterized, and that was already stated in His saying "Forbidden to you is carrion" — is that the people addressed by this verse did not count as "carrion" among animals anything that died from an acquired illness other than strangling, falling, goring, and the mauling of a beast of prey. So God informed them that the ruling on those is the ruling on what dies from acquired illnesses, and that the cause which makes carrion forbidden is not its death from a sickness or harm it had before its destruction, but the reason is that it was not slaughtered by one who made it a slaughter for himself, in the sense by which it becomes lawful, as in what follows:

1047. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi regarding His saying: "and the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and that which the beast of prey has eaten, except what you slaughter," he says: This is forbidden, because some of the Arabs used to eat it and did not count it as carrion; they only counted as carrion the one that dies from pain. So God forbade it to them, except what they mentioned God's name over, reached its slaughter, and while the spirit was still in it. [[The report: 1047 is the completion of the report passed earlier as no. 1024.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿and what is sacrificed on the stone altars (wa-ma dhubiha ʿala al-nusub)﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "and what is sacrificed on the stone altars," and forbidden to you also is that which is slaughtered on the nusub.

"Mā" in His saying "and what is sacrificed" is in the nominative, conjoined to the "mā" in His saying "and that which the beast of prey has eaten."

"Al-nusub" are idols of stone, the plural of anṣāb, which were gathered in a place on the earth, and the polytheists would offer sacrifices to them, and they were not idols.

Ibn Jurayj used to say concerning its description:

1048. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: "Al-nusub" are not idols; "the idol" is shaped and carved, whereas these are stones set upright, three hundred and sixty stones [[His saying "three hundred and sixty stones" refers to the number of anṣāb that were around the Ka'ba. See Ibn Saʿd 2/1/98: "The Messenger of God ﷺ circumambulated, and around the Ka'ba were three hundred and sixty idols," but these are idols, not anṣāb, as you see.]], some of whom say three hundred of them belonged to Khuzaʿa [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "bi-Khuzaʿa" with a bāʾ; the correct reading is what is given here.]]. So when they slaughtered, they sprinkled the blood on whatever faced the House, and cut the meat into thin slices and placed them on the stones. The Muslims said: O Messenger of God, the people of the Jahiliyya used to honor the House with blood, so we have more right to honor it! It seemed that the Prophet ﷺ did not dislike that, so God revealed: ﴿Their flesh does not reach God, nor their blood﴾ [Sura al-Hajj: 37].

* *

What confirms Ibn Jurayj's view that the "anṣāb" are other than the "aṣnām" is what follows:

1049. Ibn Wakiʿ narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿUyayna narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "and what is sacrificed on the nusub," he said: stones upon which the people of the Jahiliyya would slaughter.

1050. Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning God's saying "the nusub," he said: stones around the Ka'ba, upon which the people of the Jahiliyya would slaughter, and they would replace them when they wished with stones more pleasing to them.

1051. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

1052. Bishr ibn Muʿadh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada regarding "and what is sacrificed on the nusub," and "the nusub": stones which the people of the Jahiliyya worshipped and slaughtered for, so God forbade that.

1053. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada concerning His saying "and what is sacrificed on the nusub," meaning the anṣāb of the Jahiliyya.

1054. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding "and what is sacrificed on the nusub," and "the nusub" are anṣāb upon which they would slaughter and invoke (the names of their idols).

1055. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from ʿAnbasa, from Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza, from Mujahid regarding His saying "and what is sacrificed on the nusub," he said: Around the Ka'ba were stones upon which the people of the Jahiliyya would slaughter, and they would replace them when they wished with a stone more beloved to them.

1056. I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim say: "The anṣāb" are stones over which they would invoke and upon which they would slaughter.

1057. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying "and what is sacrificed on the nusub," he said: "What is sacrificed on the nusub" and "what has been dedicated to other than God" are one and the same. [[In the printed edition: "huwa wahid" without a wāw; the manuscript reading is better.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows (wa-an tastaqsimu bi-l-azlam)﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: By His saying, "and that you seek decision by the arrows," He means: and that you seek knowledge of what has been apportioned to you or not apportioned, by means of the arrows.

* *

It is the form "istaf'alta" from "al-qasm," the apportioning of provision and needs. That was because one of the people of the Jahiliyya, when he wanted a journey or a raid or something similar, would shuffle the arrows — and these are the "azlam," arrows on some of which was written "My Lord has forbidden me," and on others "My Lord has commanded me." If the arrow on which was written "My Lord has commanded me" came out, he would proceed with what he intended of journey, raid, marriage, or other things. If the one on which was written "My Lord has forbidden me" came out, he would refrain from proceeding and hold back. So it was said: "and that you seek decision by the arrows," because by their action they were as if asking their arrows to apportion for them. From this is the poet's saying, boasting of abandoning seeking decision by them: [[I could not identify the speaker; it resembles the words of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, though it is not in his diwan.]]

"And I did not seek decision, so the lots' portions did not trouble me."

[[Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu ʿUbayda 1:152. The phrase "lam aqsim" comes from "qasamtu amri aqsimuhu qasman," meaning I weighed it, considered, and inclined to do it or not do it. They said: "I left so-and-so deliberating, I left him seeking decision": that is, he thinks and wavers between two matters. So too does one who seeks decision by the arrows, so "aqsama" is used in this verse in the sense of seeking decision by arrows. "Al-qusum" is the plural of "qism" (with kasra on the qaf and sukun on the sin), meaning share or lot; its plural is "aqsam," but it was pluralized as "qusum," like the plural of "ḥilm" as "ḥulum" and "aḥlām."]]

* *

As for "al-azlam," its singular is "zalam," and it is also said "zulam," and they are the arrows whose matter we have described. [["zalam" (with two fathas) and "zulam" (with damma on the zay and fatha on the lam).]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 3 of 7):

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

11058 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar and Ibn Wakî' narrated to us, both saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī narrated to us, from Sufyān, from Abū Ḥuṣayn, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "The qidāḥ (arrow-shafts used for divination). When they wished to set out on a journey, they would make qidāḥ for 'sit' and 'go out'. If the 'go out' one came up, they went out; if the 'sit' one came up, they sat."

11059 – Ibn Wakî' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sharīk, from Abū Ḥuṣayn, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "White pebbles with which they would cast lots."
Abū Jaʿfar said: Sufyān ibn Wakî' said to us: "It is chess (al-shiṭranj)." [This is a statement of extreme strangeness!! It is as if he was ignorant of what chess is, or as if he thought they did this with chess pieces, without this act being playing chess.]

11060 – Yaʿqūb narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: ʿUbbād ibn Rāshid al-Bazzār informed us, from al-Ḥasan regarding His saying ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "They would, when they wanted a matter or a journey, resort to three arrow-shafts, on one of which was written 'Command me', on another 'Forbid me', and they left the third unmarked between them with nothing on it. Then they would shuffle them. If the one with 'Command me' came out, they proceeded with their affair. If the one with 'Forbid me' came out, they refrained. If the blank one came out, they repeated it." [Report 11060: ʿUbbād ibn Rāshid al-Tamīmī al-Bazzār, the nephew of Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind. He narrated from Thābit al-Bunānī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, and Qatādah. Narrated from him Hushaym, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Abū ʿĀmir al-ʿAqadī, and others. Al-Bukhārī mentioned him among the weak narrators, and narrated from him only in conjunction with others; he is spoken of critically. Biography in al-Tahdhīb.]

11061 – Ibn Wakî' narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿUyaynah narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid regarding ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "Stones on which they would write; they called them al-qidāḥ."

11062 – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid regarding the saying of God ﴿by the arrows﴾: "The qidāḥ, which they cast for every journey, raid, and trade."

11063 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abū Ḥudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the same.

11064 – Ibn Wakî' narrated to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Ādam narrated to us, from Zuhayr, from Ibrāhīm ibn Muhājir, from Mujāhid regarding ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "The knucklebones (kiʿāb) of Persia with which they gamble, and the arrows of the Arabs."

11065 – Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim al-Ghifārī narrated to me, saying: Abū Nuʿaym narrated to us, saying: Zuhayr narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm ibn Muhājir, from Mujāhid regarding ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "The arrows of the Arabs and the knucklebones of Persia and Rome, with which they gambled."

11066 – al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatādah regarding His saying ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "When a man wanted to set out travelling, he would write on an arrow-shaft: 'This commands me to stay,' and 'This commands me to go out,' and he would place with them a munīḥah [a blank arrow-shaft with nothing written on it]. Then he sought decision by them when he wished to go out. If the one commanding to stay came out, he stayed; if the one commanding to go out came out, he went out; and if the other came out, he shuffled them again until one of the two arrow-shafts came out." [In the printed edition and the manuscript: "maʿahā" (with them), and the correct reading is the dual. In the printed edition: "munīḥan," which is correct in meaning. However, I retain what is in the manuscript, because "al-munīḥ," as in the printed edition, is the arrow-shaft borrowed from the arrows of gambling, the blank one with no share unless its owner grants something, so it is borrowed and sought for blessing; while "al-munīḥah" is the borrowed she-camel or sheep, so they looked to the meaning of the borrowed and named this thing which has no command in the seeking of decision "munīḥah," just as they named its like in gambling "munīḥ," which means borrowed.]

11067 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah: "and that you seek decision by the arrows." The people of the Jahiliyyah, when one of them wanted to go out, would take an arrow-shaft and say: "This commands going out." If it came out, he would be successful in his journey with good. He would take another arrow-shaft and say: "This commands remaining," and he would not succeed in his journey with good; and the munīḥ was between them. God forbade that and gave precedence to its prohibition.

11068 – I was told, from al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say regarding His saying ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "They would seek decision by them in matters."

11069 – Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "al-azlām" are arrow-shafts they had. Whenever one of them wanted something from those matters, he wrote what he wanted on those arrow-shafts and cast them. Whichever arrow-shaft came out – even if it was the most hateful of them – he committed to it and acted upon it.

11070 – Muhammad ibn al-Ḥusayn narrated to me, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī regarding ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "al-azlām are arrow-shafts that existed in the Jahiliyyah with the soothsayers. When a man wanted to travel, or marry, or undertake a matter, he came to the soothsayer, gave him something, and he cast them for him. If something came out that pleased him, he commanded him and he did it; if something came out that he disliked, he forbade him and he desisted, just as ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib cast lots over Zamzam, and over ʿAbd Allāh and the camels." [See the account of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and ʿAbd Allāh in Ibn Hishām's Sīrah 1: 160–164.]

11071 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr, who said: We have heard that the people of the Jahiliyyah would cast arrow-shafts regarding travel (ẓaʿn) and remaining (iqāmah), or regarding a thing they wanted; the arrow of travel would come out and they would travel, and the arrow of remaining, and they would remain.

* *

Ibn Isḥāq said regarding "al-azlām":
11072 – Ibn Ḥumayd narrated this to me, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said: Hubal was the greatest of the idols of Quraysh in Mecca, and it was over a well inside the Kaʿbah, and that well was where what was offered to the Kaʿbah was collected. Beside Hubal were seven arrow-shafts [in the printed edition: "aqdāḥ"; I retain what is in the manuscript; the plural of qidḥ is aqdāḥ, qidāḥ, and aqdah, all correct], each arrow-shaft of which had a writing. One arrow-shaft had "al-ʿaql" [the blood-money] written on it: when they disagreed about the blood-money, who among them should bear it, they cast the seven arrow-shafts, [and whoever the blood-money came out for, bore it]. [This addition in parentheses is from Ibn Hishām, and it is necessary for the sentence to be complete.] Another had "Yes" for a matter when they wished to do it; they cast it, and if the "Yes" arrow-shaft came out, they acted upon it. Another had "No"; when they wished a matter they cast with it, and if that arrow-shaft came out, they did not do that matter. Another had "from among you." Another had "attached" [in the manuscript: "yalṣaq," with above it "thus," meaning it is so in the copy from which it was copied; the correct reading is that of the printed edition and Ibn Hishām's Sīrah]. Another had "from other than you." Another had "waters": when they wished to dig for water they cast the arrow-shafts, and that arrow-shaft was among them, and wherever it came out, they acted upon it. When they wanted to circumcise a boy [in the printed edition: "yajtabūa", which has no meaning; the manuscript is unpointed, and the correct reading, in Ibn Hishām's Sīrah, is as I have given it], or to marry a bride, or to bury a dead person, or doubted the lineage of one of them, they took him to Hubal with a hundred dirhams and a camel, and gave them to the keeper of the arrow-shafts who cast them, then they brought near the one they wanted to do something to, and said: "O our god, this is so-and-so son of so-and-so; we want to do such-and-such with him, so bring forth the truth concerning him." Then they say to the keeper of the arrow-shafts: "Cast," and he casts. If "from among you" came out for him, he was a mediator [wasīṭ]. And if "from other than you" came out for him, he was an ally (ḥalīf). [The words between the brackets are an addition from Ibn Hishām, and it is without doubt the context. "Wasīṭ" means one of pure lineage, noble among his people.] If "attached" came out, he was in his rank among them, with no lineage and no alliance. If anything other than these came out, among what they act upon, "Yes," they acted upon it. And if "No" came out, they postponed it that year until they came to it again. They terminate their affairs at what the arrow-shafts bring out.

11073 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abū Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾: "meaning the qidāḥ; they sought decision by them in matters."

* *

On the interpretation of His saying ﴿That is a transgression (fisq)﴾
Abū Jaʿfar said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "That," He means these matters He mentioned: eating carrion, blood, pork, and everything else mentioned in this verse as forbidden to eat, and seeking decision by the arrows. "Transgression (fisq)" means departure from the command of God, may His mention be honoured, and obedience to Him, toward what He forbade and prohibited, toward disobedience to Him. [See the explanation of "fisq" in what has passed: 1: 409, 410 / 2: 118, 399 / 4: 135–137 / 6: 91, 92 / 7: 107. In the printed edition: "wa-zajara, wa-ilā maʿṣiyatihi," with an added wāw; both are correct.] As:
11074 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "That is a transgression," meaning: whoever eats any of all that is a transgressor.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾
Abū Jaʿfar said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion," the meaning is: now the hope of the factions and the people of disbelief and denial has been cut off, O believers, ("of your religion") meaning: of your religion, that you would abandon it and turn back to polytheism, as:
11075 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: "Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion," meaning: that you would return to their religion forever.
11076 – Muhammad ibn al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī regarding His saying: "Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion," he said: I think they despaired that you would turn back from your religion. [I am in doubt about his saying "I think" here, and it is unpointed in the manuscript.]

* *

If someone says: Which day is this day on which God informed that those who disbelieved despaired of the religion of the believers?
It is said: It is mentioned that it was the Day of ʿArafah, in the year the Prophet ﷺ performed the Farewell Pilgrimage, and that was after the Arabs had entered Islam.
Mention of those who said that:
11077 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, Mujāhid said: "Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion" and "Today I have perfected your religion for you": this was when it was done. Ibn Jurayj said: Others said that it was the Day of ʿArafah, on a Friday, when the Prophet ﷺ looked and saw none but monotheists, and saw no polytheist; he praised God, and Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended to him: "Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion," that they would return as they were. [His saying "others said" is, in my estimation, from Ibn Jurayj's own words, and therefore I have included it in the report.]
11078 – Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion," he said: This is the Day of ʿArafah.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying ﴿So do not fear them﴾
Abū Jaʿfar said: By this is meant: So do not fear them, O believers, those disbelievers who have despaired of your religion, that you would turn back from it, and do not be afraid of them that they would prevail over you, overpower you, and turn you back from your religion. ("And fear Me") means: but fear Me, if you oppose My command and dare to disobey Me, and transgress My limits, that I will bring down My punishment upon you and send down My torment upon you. [See the explanation of "khashyah" in what has passed: 1: 559, 560 / 2: 239, 243 / 8: 548.] As:
11079 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "So do not fear them and fear Me": so do not fear them that they would prevail over you.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾
Abū Jaʿfar said: The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of this.
Some of them said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "Today I have perfected for you your religion," the meaning is: Today I have perfected for you, O believers, My obligations upon you and My limits, and My command to you and My prohibition, and My lawful and My unlawful, and My revelation of what I have revealed of it in My Book, and My clarification of what I have made clear to you of it through My revelation upon the tongue of My messenger, and the proofs I have set up for you concerning everything you need in the matter of your religion; so I have completed for you all of that, and there is no addition to it after this day. They said: This was on the Day of ʿArafah, in the year the Prophet ﷺ performed the Farewell Pilgrimage. And they said: After this verse, nothing of the obligations was revealed upon the Prophet ﷺ, nor the making lawful of anything or its making unlawful, and the Prophet ﷺ did not live after the revelation of this verse except eighty-one nights.

Mention of those who said that:
11080 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: "Today I have perfected for you your religion," and it is Islam. He said: God informed His Prophet ﷺ and the believers that He had perfected faith for them, so they have no need of addition ever, and God, may His mention be exalted, has completed it, so He never diminishes it, and God is pleased with it, so He never becomes displeased with it.
11081 – Muhammad ibn al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī regarding His saying: "Today I have perfected for you your religion": this was revealed on the Day of ʿArafah, and after it nothing lawful or unlawful was revealed. The Messenger of God ﷺ returned and died. Asmāʾ bint ʿUmays said: I performed the pilgrimage with the Messenger of God ﷺ that pilgrimage; while we were travelling, Gabriel ﷺ appeared to him upon the riding-beast, and the riding-beast could not bear the weight of what was upon it of the Qur'an, so it knelt down, and I came to him and covered him with a cloak that was mine. [Sajjāhu bi-l-thawb tasjiyah: he covered him with it.]
11082 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: The Prophet ﷺ remained, after this verse was revealed, eighty-one nights: "Today I have perfected for you your religion."
11083 – Sufyān narrated to us, saying: Ibn Fuḍayl narrated to us, from Hārūn ibn ʿAntarah, from his father, who said: When "Today I have perfected for you your religion" was revealed, and that was the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage, ʿUmar wept. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "What made me weep is that we were in increase in our religion; now that it is complete, nothing is completed except that it diminishes!" He said: "You have spoken truthfully." [By "the diminishing of religion" he meant the people of religion: when time lengthens over them, their hearts harden and some of them become less steadfast in what they were commanded. God forbid that ʿUmar meant the diminishing of religion itself. Similar to it is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Islam began as a stranger and will return as a stranger as it began, so blessed are the strangers."]
11084 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Bashīr narrated to us, from Hārūn ibn Abī Wakī', from his father, who mentioned something similar. [Report 11084: Aḥmad ibn Bashīr al-Kūfī, passed as no. 7819. Hārūn ibn Abī Wakī' is Hārūn ibn ʿAntarah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, whose biography passed in the report before it, and passed as no. 405. His father: ʿAntarah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, whose kunyah is Abū Wakī', also passed as no. 405.]

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: "Today I have perfected for you your religion" – your pilgrimage, that you, O believers, were singled out to perform the pilgrimage to the Sacred Land, to the exclusion of the polytheists, and no polytheist mixes with you in your pilgrimage.
Mention of those who said that:
11085 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Abī Ghaniyyah narrated to us, from his father, from al-Ḥakam: "Today I have perfected for you your religion": He said: He perfected their religion for them: that they performed the pilgrimage and no polytheist performed it with them. [Report 11085: "Yaḥyā ibn Abī Ghaniyyah" is Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Ḥumayd ibn Abī Ghaniyyah, passed as no. 10597, and this is the same chain. His father ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Ḥumayd ibn Abī Ghaniyyah passed as nos. 8535 and 10597. "Al-Ḥakam" is al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUtaybah, who has passed many times. In the manuscript and printed edition it read "Yaḥyā ibn Abī ʿUtaybah," which is a copyist's error.]
11086 – al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatādah: "Today I have perfected for you your religion": He said: God made their religion pure for them, and removed the polytheists from the House.
11087 – Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to us, saying: Abū Nuʿaym narrated to us, saying: Qays narrated to us, from Abū Ḥuṣayn, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: "Today I have perfected for you your religion": He said: the completion of the pilgrimage, and the removal of the polytheists from the House.

* *

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 4 of 7):

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the statements on this matter is that it should be said: Almighty God informed His Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers in him that on the day this verse was revealed to His Prophet, He had perfected for them their religion (dinahum), by singling them out with the Sacred House (al-balad al-haram) [[In the printed edition: "bi-ifradihim bi-l-balad al-haram" with the letter ba', which is what the lexicons say. As for what is in the manuscript, which is what I have recorded, it has a valid basis in Arabic, in my view, so I left it as it is. My impression is that he read it this way, transitively, in some of Abu Ja'far's books or others. If I find it, I will record it, God willing.]] and by expelling the polytheists from it, so that the Muslims performed the pilgrimage without the polytheists, and no polytheist mixed with them.

As for the obligatory duties and rulings (al-fara'id wa-l-ahkam), there is disagreement over whether they were completed on that day or not. It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi what we mentioned earlier about them. [[That is, what has passed, numbers 11080 and 11081.]]

It has been related from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that the last verse to be revealed of the Qur'an was: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah﴾ [Surah al-Nisa': 176]. [[See what has passed, numbers 10870–10873.]]

No person of knowledge denies that revelation did not cease to come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) until he died; rather, revelation was at its most frequent just before his death. Since that is so, and since His saying, ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: God gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah﴾ was the last of it in revelation, and that was among the rulings and obligatory duties, it is known that the meaning of His saying, "Today I have perfected for you your religion," is contrary to the aspect that those who interpreted it have interpreted, namely the perfection of the acts of worship, rulings and obligatory duties.

If someone says: What makes the statement of the one who said, "Obligations were revealed after that," preferable to the statement of the one who said, "Nothing was revealed"?

It is said: Because the one who said, "Nothing was revealed," is reporting that he does not know of the revelation of an obligation, and negation does not constitute testimony, whereas testimony is the statement of the one who said, "It was revealed." It is not permissible to reject the report of the truthful person in what it is possible for him to be truthful about.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And I have completed My favour upon you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: And I have completed My favour, O believers, by making you victorious over My enemies and your enemies among the polytheists, by expelling them from your lands, and by cutting off their hope of your returning to and reverting to what you were upon of polytheism.

* *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said things similar to what we have said on this. Those who said so:

11088. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Abd Allah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The polytheists and the Muslims used to perform the pilgrimage together. Then when Bara'ah (surah al-Tawbah) was revealed, He expelled the polytheists from the House, and the Muslims performed the pilgrimage, with none of the polytheists sharing with them in the Sacred House. So that was part of the completion of the favour: "And I have completed My favour upon you."

11089. Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: "Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you," the verse. It was mentioned to us that this verse was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the Day of 'Arafah, a Friday, when God expelled the polytheists from the Sacred Mosque and made the pilgrimage of the Muslims sincere.

11090. Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, saying: Dawud related to us, from al-Sha'bi, who said: This verse was revealed at 'Arafat, when the landmark (manar) of the Jahiliyyah was demolished and polytheism was wiped out, and no polytheist performed the pilgrimage with them that year. [["Al-manar": the sign of the road and the boundaries of the land. He meant by it the laws of the people of the Jahiliyyah.]]

11091. Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Dawud related to us, from 'Amir concerning this verse: "Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you." He said: It was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while he was standing at 'Arafat, with people encircling him, and the landmarks and rites of the Jahiliyyah had been demolished, polytheism had been wiped out, and no naked person circumambulated the House. So God revealed: "Today I have perfected for you your religion."

11092. Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, similarly.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: And I have approved for you submission to My command and compliance with My obedience, in accordance with what I have prescribed for you of its limits, obligations and markers ["Islam" — see the explanation of "Islam" earlier in the indices of language, root (s-l-m)]. "As a religion" — by which He means: obedience from you to Me. [[See the explanation of "religion" (al-din) earlier, 1:155, 221; 3:571, 572; 6:273–275, 564, 570.]]

* *

If someone says: Was God not approving Islam for His servants until the day this verse was revealed?

It is said: God has never ceased to approve Islam as a religion for His creation. But He, may His praise be exalted, has never ceased to turn His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions through the degrees and stations of Islam, degree after degree, station after station, state after state, until He completed its laws and markers for them and brought them to its farthest degrees and stations. Then, when He revealed this verse to them, He said: "And I have approved for you Islam" in the description it has today, and the state you are in today from it, "as a religion," so hold fast to it and do not part from it.

* *

Qatadah used to say concerning this, what follows:

11093. Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that on the Day of Resurrection each people's religion will be presented to them in the form of an image. As for faith (al-iman), it will give good news to its adherents and people and promise them good, until Islam comes and says: "My Lord, You are al-Salam and I am Islam." He will say: "Today I accept only from you, and today I recompense only through you." [[Report 11093: Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related in his Musnad (324) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "'Abbad ibn Rashid related to us, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abu Hurayrah related to us, and we were then in Medina, saying: Islam will come on the Day of Resurrection, and God, the Mighty and Majestic, will say: 'You are Islam and I am al-Salam; today I give through you and take through you.'"]]

* *

= I think that Qatadah directed the meaning of "faith" in this report to the meaning of affirmation and acknowledgment by the tongue, because that is the meaning of "faith" among the Arabs [[See the explanation of "faith" earlier in the indices of language, root (a-m-n).]] = and he directed the meaning of "Islam" to the submission and humility of the heart before God through monotheism, and the compliance of the body with Him through obedience in what He commanded and forbade. That is why it is said to Islam: "Today I accept only from you, and today I recompense only through you."

* *

Those who said: This verse was revealed at 'Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage (hajjat al-wada') upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

11094. Muhammad ibn Bashshar and Ibn Wakī' related to us, both saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: The Jews said to 'Umar: "You recite a verse which, had it been revealed concerning us, we would have taken as a festival!" 'Umar said: "I know well when it was revealed, and where it was revealed, and where the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was when it was revealed: it was revealed on the Day of 'Arafah, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was standing at 'Arafah." Sufyan said: "And I am uncertain whether it was a Friday or not." [The verse:] "Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and approved for you Islam as a religion." [[Report 11094: Ahmad recorded it in al-Musnad (272) from 'Abd al-Rahman, from Sufyan, in like manner. Al-Bukhari (al-Fath 8:203) recorded it from Muhammad ibn Bashshar, from 'Abd al-Rahman, by the same chain as Abu Ja'far. Muslim (18:152) recorded it from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Zuhayr ibn Harb, from 'Abd al-Rahman. In all of them is "I know where it was revealed" and "where the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was when it was revealed," and al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) pointed this out in al-Fath. Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his Tafsir (2:67) and attributed it further to al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i. Then he said: "Sufyan, may God have mercy on him, was in doubt. If it was in the narration, then it is scrupulousness, since he doubted whether his shaykh had told him that or not. If it was doubt about whether the standing at the Farewell Pilgrimage was on a Friday, then that is something I cannot believe would issue from al-Thawri, may God have mercy on him, for this is a known matter, decided upon, about which none of the scholars of the campaigns and biographies (al-maghazi wa-l-siyar) or the jurists disagreed. Numerous reports have come concerning it whose authenticity is beyond doubt, and God knows best."]]

11095. Abu Kurayb and Ibn Wakī' related to us, both saying: Ibn Idris related to us, saying: I heard my father, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: A Jew said to 'Umar: "If we, the group of Jews, had known on the day this verse was revealed, 'Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and approved for you Islam as a religion,' we would have taken that day as a festival!" 'Umar said: "I know the day on which it was revealed, and the hour, and where the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was when it was revealed: it was revealed on the night of Friday, and we were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at 'Arafat." The wording of the report is that of Abu Kurayb, and the report of Ibn Wakī' is similar to it. [[Report 11095: Muslim recorded it in his Sahih (18:153) by this chain, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu Kurayb, from 'Abd Allah ibn Idris. In it: "It was revealed on the night of Jam'" (laylat Jam'). Al-Nawawi said in his commentary: "So it is in the copies. The narration: 'laylat Jam',' and in the copy of Ibn Mahan: 'laylat Jumu'ah' (Friday night). Both are correct. Whoever narrates 'laylat Jam'' means the night of Muzdalifah, and that is what is meant by his saying 'and we were at 'Arafat' on a Friday, because the night of Jam' is the evening of the Day of 'Arafat. And what is meant by his saying 'laylat Jumu'ah' is Friday. 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, meant: we have taken that day as a festival in two respects, for it is the Day of 'Arafah and a Friday, and each of them is a festival for the people of Islam."]]

11096. Ibn Wakī' related to us, saying: Ja'far ibn 'Awn related to us, from Abu al-'Umays, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq, from 'Umar, similarly. [[Report 11096: This hadith was recorded by al-Bukhari (al-Fath 1:97) by way of al-Hasan ibn al-Sabah, from Ja'far ibn 'Awn, from Abu al-'Umays. Ahmad recorded it in al-Musnad (188) by way of Ja'far ibn 'Awn, from Abu 'Umays. Muslim recorded it in his Sahih (18:154) by way of 'Abd ibn Humayd, from Ja'far ibn 'Awn, and al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan (8:114). Furthermore, al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar in al-Fath (1:97) made clear that this man among the Jews was Ka'b al-Ahbar (Ka'b al-Ahbar), as shown by Musaddad in his Musnad, al-Tabari in his Tafsir, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, all by way of Raja' ibn Abi Salamah, from 'Ubadah ibn Nasi (with a dammah on the nun and a fathah on the sin), from Ishaq ibn Kharashah, from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, from Ka'b. This is the following report, number 11100 (see the comment on it and the error in it). In another place (al-Fath 8:203) he pointed to the possibility that Ka'b's question occurred before his conversion, because his conversion was in the caliphate of 'Umar according to the well-known account, and he was referred to thus in view of what had passed.]]

11097. Ibn Wakī' related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ammar, mawla of the Banu Hashim, who said: Ibn 'Abbas recited: "Today I have perfected for you your religion," and there was with him a man from the People of the Book, who said: "If we had known which day this verse was revealed, we would have taken it as a festival!" Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was revealed on the Day of 'Arafah, a Friday." [[Report 11097: Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi recorded it in his Musnad (353), from Hammad, from 'Ammar ibn Abi 'Ammar. It will come by another route in the next report.]]

11098. Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Qabisah related to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah related to us, from 'Ammar, that Ibn 'Abbas recited: "Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and approved for you Islam as a religion." A Jew said: "If this verse had been revealed upon us, we would have taken its day as a festival!" Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was revealed on a day of two festivals: a festival day and a Friday." [[Report 11098: Al-Tirmidhi recorded it in the Book of Tafsir, by way of 'Abd ibn Humayd, from Yazid ibn Harun, from Hammad, and in it: "It was revealed on a day of two festivals, on Friday and the Day of 'Arafah." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a good, strange hadith from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas." Al-Suyuti pointed to it in al-Durr al-Manthur (2:258) and attributed it further to 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il.]]

11099. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal related to us, saying: Hammad related to us, from 'Ammar ibn Abi 'Ammar, from Ibn 'Abbas, similarly.

11100. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, saying: Raja' ibn Abi Salamah related to us, saying: 'Ubadah ibn Nasi informed us, saying: Our amir Ishaq related to us = Abu Ja'far said: Ishaq is Ibn Kharashah = from Qabisah, who said: Ka'b said: "If any other community than this one had had this verse revealed to them, they would have looked to the day on which it was revealed to them and taken it as a festival in which they gather!" 'Umar said: "Which verse, O Ka'b?" He said: "'Today I have perfected for you your religion.'" 'Umar said: "I know the day on which it was revealed and the place where it was revealed: a Friday and the Day of 'Arafah, and both of them, praise be to God, are festivals for us." [[Report 11100: "Raja' ibn Abi Salamah Mihran," Abu al-Miqdam, the Palestinian. He related from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, al-Zuhri and others. Related from him Ibn 'Awn, who was among his shaykhs, the two Hammads, and Ibn 'Ulayyah. Trustworthy (thiqah), he was among the most excellent people of his time. His biography is in al-Tahdhib.

"'Ubadah ibn Nasi al-Kindi," the Shami Jordanian, judge of Tiberias. He related from Aws ibn Aws al-Thaqafi, Shaddad ibn Aws, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah and others. Related from him Raja' ibn Abi Salamah and others. Ibn Sa'd, among the Tabi'un of the people of Syria, said: "Trustworthy." Al-Bukhari said: "'Ubadah ibn Nasi al-Kindi" was their chief. Maslamah ibn 'Abd al-Malik said: "In Kindah there are three men, through whom God sends down rain and by whom He grants victory over enemies: 'Ubadah ibn Nasi, Raja' ibn Haywah, and 'Adi ibn 'Adi." He died in the year 118. His biography is in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim (3/1/96). "Nasi" is with a dammah on the nun, a fathah on the sin, and a shaddah on the ya'.

As for "Ishaq," Abu Ja'far claimed that he is Ibn Kharashah, but I have not found "Ishaq ibn Kharashah" among the narrators or among the amirs. As for "Ibn Kharashah," he is "'Uthman ibn Ishaq ibn Kharashah" (with a fathah on the kha' and the ra') al-Qurashi, from whom al-Zuhri related. 'Ubadah ibn Nasi is not recorded as relating from him, nor was he an amir. His lineage, as related by Ibn Sa'd (5:180), is: "'Uthman ibn Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Kharashah ibn 'Amr ibn Rabi'ah ibn al-Harith ibn Habib ibn Judaymah ibn Malik ibn Hasl ibn 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy." His lineage is also given by al-Mus'ab in Nasab Quraysh (432), who said: "Ibn Shihab related from him, from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, the hadith of the grandmother," which is the hadith related by the authors of the four Sunan (Sunan Abi Dawud 3:167, no. 2894), by way of Malik in al-Muwatta' (513) in his narration from "Ibn Shihab, from 'Uthman ibn Ishaq ibn Kharashah, from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb."

I have no doubt that Abu Ja'far erred. He intended to identify "Ishaq" in this chain, and "Ibn Kharashah" came to his mind, meaning "'Uthman ibn Ishaq ibn Kharashah," not "Ishaq ibn Kharashah."

As for "Ishaq" in this report, I have no doubt that he is "Ishaq ibn Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb," who relates from his father, "Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb." This is for the following reasons: first, because "Ishaq ibn Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb al-Khuza'i" relates from his father and from Ka'b al-Ahbar. Second, 'Ubadah ibn Nasi of Jordan, judge of Tiberias, is mentioned in his biography, and it is said that he relates from Ishaq ibn Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb. Third, Ishaq ibn Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb is the one who was an amir and an official of Hisham over Jordan, as Abu Zur'ah al-Dimashqi said. Ibn Sumay' said: "He was in charge of the diwan of the disabled in the days of al-Walid." 'Ubadah ibn Nasi was a judge among the judges of Jordan, as I have mentioned.

So what is beyond doubt to me is that "Ishaq" in this chain is Ishaq ibn Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, who relates from his father, and that Abu Ja'far erred and confused it in identifying him.

I have pointed out, in the comment on report number 11096, what al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar transmitted in Fath al-Bari (1:97), quoting from this place in al-Tabari, but he also attributed it to Musaddad in his Musnad and to al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and those two are not with me. But if it is in one of them, then the error in it is older than Abu Ja'far. Written by Mahmud Muhammad Shakir.

In the printed edition here: "wa-kilahuma bi-hamdi Allah," and in the manuscript: "wa-kilayhuma." It has a valid basis in Arabic.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 5 of 7):

11101.
