Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from ʿAnbasa, from ʿIsa ibn Jariya al-Ansari, who said: "We were sitting in the diwan (the register office), when a Christian said to us: 'O people of Islam, there has been revealed to you a verse which, if it had been revealed to us, we would have taken that day and that hour as a festival for as long as two of us remained: "Today I have perfected for you your religion."' None of us answered him. So I met Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi and asked him about that. He said: 'Why did you not reply to him?' They said: 'What did ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab say?' He said: 'It was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was standing on the mountain on the Day of ʿArafa, so that day remains a festival for the Muslims for as long as any of them remains.'"

[[Report 11101: "Hakkam" is Hakkam ibn Salm al-Kinani, a trustworthy narrator from whom al-Tabari transmitted often in what has passed. "ʿAnbasa" is ʿAnbasa ibn Saʿid ibn al-Durais al-Asadi, who has also passed several times; he is biographed under nos. 224, 3356 and 5385.
"ʿIsa ibn Jariya al-Ansari" narrated from Jarir al-Bajali, Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, Ibn al-Musayyab and others. Yaʿqub al-Qummi and ʿAnbasa ibn Saʿid narrated from him. Hamid ibn Masʿada narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from ʿAmir, who said: "The verse 'Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and approved for you Islam as a religion' was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the evening of ʿArafa while he was at the station."

[[The report: "Muhammad ibn Harb al-Khawlani" al-Abrash. Ahmad said: "There is no harm in him," and Ibn Maʿin said: "Trustworthy."  He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.
"Ibn Lahiʿa" is ʿAbd Allah ibn Lahiʿa, who has passed under nos. 160, 2941, 5355 and 5518, and my brother al-Sayyid Ahmad's authentication of him has passed.
"Khalid ibn Abi ʿImran al-Tujibi," judge of Ifriqiya. Trustworthy; Ibn Saʿd and al-ʿIjli and others deemed him trustworthy.

Al-Tabari adopted this report, as will come at the end of his discussion, because of what they said about the weakness of Ibn Lahiʿa, and because some abstained from relying on him.
Ahmad narrated this report in his Musnad under no. 2506, through Musa ibn Dawud, from Ibn Lahiʿa, and its text is: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was born on a Monday, was given prophethood (istunbiʾa) on a Monday, died on a Monday, left Mecca for Medina as an emigrant on a Monday, arrived in Medina on a Monday, and the Black Stone was raised on a Monday."
My brother al-Sayyid Ahmad commented on it: "Its chain is sound. Ibn Kathir mentioned this hadith in al-Tarikh 2:259, 260, from this same place, and said: 'Ahmad alone narrated it.' It is in Majmaʿ al-Zawaʾid 1:196, attributed to Ahmad and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and al-Haythami said: 'In it is Ibn Lahiʿa, who is weak, but the rest of its narrators are trustworthy, from the people of the Sahih.'"
There is nothing in Ahmad's report about "and Surat al-Ma'ida was revealed..." For this reason, when Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his Tafsir, 2:68, from this place in Tabari's Tafsir, he attributed it to al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh, then said: "A strange report, and its chain is weak, and Imam Ahmad narrated it..." Then he cited the hadith of Ahmad, and then said: "This is the wording of Ahmad, and it does not mention the revelation of al-Ma'ida on Monday. God knows best. His saying "the Remembrance was raised on a Monday" means the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), may my father and mother be sacrificed for him, and the cessation of revelation after his passing and his joining the Highest Companion.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿So whoever is compelled in severe hunger﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: By His saying "so whoever is compelled," may His remembrance be exalted, He means: whoever is afflicted by harm, ["idtarra": see its explanation earlier at 3:56, 321] "in severe hunger," meaning: in famine.

* *

"Makhmasa" is of the pattern "mafʿala," like "majbana," "mabkhala," and "manjaba," from "khamas al-batn," which is the contraction of the belly. I think that in this place it means the contraction of the belly from hunger and severe exhaustion. It may in other places mean contraction not from hunger and exhaustion, but from natural build, as the Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan said describing a woman with a contracted belly:

"The belly has folds, slender and smooth, and the chest is raised by a firm breast."

[["Khamas" (with fatha on the kha and the mim). This is a fine explanation of the meanings of "khamas" and "makhmasa," which you will not find in this way in lexicographical dictionaries.]]

["Diwan": 66; al-Lisan (q-ʿ-d). Its version: "lataif tayyuhu" (delicate its folding), and there is no evidence in it then. It is from his qasida in which he praised the description of the woman who was unaffected (al-mutajarrida), the companion of al-Nuʿman ibn al-Mundhir, which led to what was between them of separation.
"Al-ʿukan": the folds of the belly, not from fat alone as the lexicographers say, for this verse is evidence against that. Rather "al-ʿukan" here is what is folded in the folds of the belly from the thinness of its skin and its smoothness and the delicacy of her body and its softness, which is why it folds. Had it been from "fat," as the people of the language say, he would not have said after it "khamis layyin," describing her with slenderness and thinness (in the version of Abu Jaʿfar), nor "latif tayyuhu," which is also a metaphor for slenderness and thinness, which is the opposite of fat. Whoever explains "al-ʿukan" in this verse and its like as fat has erred and turned the meanings of the poetry away from their proper aspects.
His saying "wa-l-nahr tanfajuhu": "al-nahr" is the upper part of the chest, the place of her necklace. Everything that rises is "nafaja, intafaja, tanaffaja," and "nafajahu al-rajul yanfajuhu nafjan." One says: "the woman's breast nafaja her shirt" when it raises it. He attributed to her that she raises her chest with her breasts, even though that is natural and she has no action in it, because he looked at what comes over a woman when she struts to tempt onlookers, adopting a manner and bearing that makes the forbearing man lose his composure. The Nabigha hit the mark completely in pointing to the secret of woman in her movement and her qualities.
But those who undertook to explain such poetry harmed it from the very direction they intended to benefit it. The minister Abu Bakr said in his commentary on the Diwan of al-Nabigha: "It is narrated: 'wa-l-itb tanfajuhu,' 'al-itb' being a garment you wear, and it is more suitable to the meaning, because the breast inflates the garment, that is, raises it and magnifies it." Then he also said: "It is narrated: 'wa-l-nahr tanfajuhu,' meaning she raises it above the garment." This is an example of confusion in understanding poetry and corrupting its meanings. What the minister preferred is a washed-out, feeble meaning in such a place in the poetry of al-Nabigha, by which he wasted the poet's labour in his verse.
"Thadyun muqʿad": protruding over the chest, when it is full-breasted and has not yet sagged.]]

So it is known that he did not intend to describe her by "khamis" with thinness and harm from hunger, but rather he meant to describe her by the delicacy of the folding of what is on the hips and thighs of her body, because that is praised in women. But what has the meaning of description by contraction and thinness from harm of that kind is the saying of the A'sha of Banu Thaʿlaba:

"You spend the winter nights with full bellies, while your neighbour women spend the night hungry, contracted (khamaʾis)."

[["Diwan": 109; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu ʿUbayda 1:153, from one of his qasidas which he composed concerning the story of the dispute between ʿAlqama ibn ʿUlatha and ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl (al-Aghani 15:50). After the verse: "They watch from hunger, through the fear, the stars of winter, the murky, the hidden ones." "Ghurthā": hungry; it is also narrated as "jawʿā" (hungry). His describing the stars with the word "al-ʿatimat" means that they are darkened by the dust that is in the sky, and that is in the time of barrenness (which is winter), because the winter stars are more brilliant because of the clearness of the sky, so they seek the time of their concealment. "Al-ghawamis" means: those whose light is weak from the dust. Its commentator said: "They spend the night hungry, frightened, awaiting the rising of the dawn stars, so that they may go out seeking something, so that they are not recognised." His saying "khilal makhafa" is among the finest expressions in this verse.]]

meaning by that: they spend the night with bellies contracted from hunger, exhaustion and harm. From this meaning is His saying "in severe hunger."

* *

Some of the grammarians of Basra used to say: "al-makhmasa" is the verbal noun (masdar) from "khamasahu al-juʿ" (hunger contracted him).

* *

Others among the scholars of Arabic held that it is a noun for the verbal noun, not a verbal noun itself, and for that reason the pattern "mafʿala" occurs as a noun in verbal nouns, for the feminine and masculine.

* *

Those of the people of interpretation (ahl al-taʾwil) said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿without being inclined toward sin﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: whoever is compelled in severe hunger to eat what I have forbidden to you, O believers, from carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and all else that I have forbidden in this verse, "without being inclined toward sin," that is, not inclining toward sin.

[[In the printed edition: "illa mutajanifan" (except inclining), which corrupts the meaning greatly; the correct reading is from the manuscript, where it reads: "lā mutajānifa" (not inclining), and the correct reading is what I have recorded.]]

So "ghayr" was put in the accusative for its exclusion from the noun in His saying "so whoever is compelled," and it means "lā" (not), and so "mutajānif" is put in the accusative in the sense in which it would be accusative if the sentence had come as "lā mutajānifan" (not inclining).

[["Al-khurūj" (exception) is the ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), as has passed in the index of terms.]]

[[In these two places also, in the printed edition: "wa-hiya bi-maʿnā: illā" (and it means: except), and then "law jāʾa al-kalām: illā mutajānifan" (if the speech had come: except inclining), which is a pure error; the correct reading is what I have recorded from the manuscript.]]

See the commentary on the meaning of "ghayr" as "not" in what has preceded, 3:322, in the commentary on His words in Surah al-Baqarah 2:173, "neither desiring nor transgressing," meaning: neither desiring nor transgressing, in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).]]

* *

As for "mutajānif li-ithm" (inclining toward sin), it means one who inclines toward it and deviates to it. In this place it means the one who intends it deliberately and aims at it, from "janafa al-qawm ʿalayya" (the people deviated against me) when they turned aside. Every crooked thing is called "ajnaf" according to the Arabs.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "janaf" (deviation) with its evidence in His words: ﴿Then whoever fears deviation (janafan) or wrongdoing from a testator﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah 2:182], in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "janaf" in what has preceded, 3:405–408, and the explanation of "ithm" (sin) in the lexical indices earlier, under the root (a-th-m).]]

* *

As for the deviation of one who eats carrion, in eating it and in other things that God has forbidden to the believers by this verse, for sin in the state of his eating it, [[The context: "As for the deviation of one who eats carrion ... for sin in the state of his eating it ..."]] it is: his deliberately eating that for other than averting the necessity that has befallen him, but rather out of disobedience to God and opposition to His command in what He commanded him, namely abstaining from eating that. [[In the printed edition: "it is his deliberately eating for other than averting the necessity," which differs from the manuscript and has no meaning.]]

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ (3)

Abū Jaʿfar (al-Ṭabarī) said: In this statement something is omitted, the sense being understood from what was mentioned. The meaning of the statement is: So whoever is compelled by hunger toward that which is forbidden to him, of what was mentioned in this verse, not inclining toward sin in eating it, then indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful. So the mention of "in eating it" was omitted, and the mention of "to him" [[He means by "and the mention of 'to him'": it is conjoined with his statement "and the omission of 'in eating it'," and the meaning is: "and the omission of 'toward that which is forbidden to him, eating it'." In my view it would have been better to make that clear and mention it as I have mentioned it.

As for his statement "and the mention of 'to him'," it means in His words "indeed God is Forgiving to him ..."]] was retained, because the rest of what was mentioned in the statement indicates both.

* *

As for His words, "indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful," its meaning is: indeed God, to the one who eats what is forbidden to him by this verse, in hunger, not inclining toward sin, is "Forgiving, Merciful." It means: He covers over for him his eating of what he ate of that, by His pardon for holding him accountable for it, His overlooking it, and His not punishing him for it. "Merciful" means: He is gentle with him. And from His mercy and gentleness toward him [[In the printed edition: "from His mercy," without the waw; I have restored it from the manuscript.]] He permitted him to eat what He permitted him to eat of carrion and the rest of what is mentioned with it in this verse, in a state where he fears for his own self from the ravening of hunger and the harm of the pressing need that afflicts his body.

* *

If someone says: What is the eating for which God promised forgiveness to the one compelled toward carrion and the other forbidden things along with it in this verse, if he eats of them?

It is said: It is what:

11125. Ibn Wāṣil al-Asadī narrated to me, saying: Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim al-Asadī narrated to us, from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah, from Abū Wāqid al-Laythī, who said: We said: O Messenger of God, we are in a land where we are afflicted with hunger, so what is permissible for us of carrion? He said: "If you do not have a morning drink, or an evening drink, or do not gather green herbs, then it is yours to take." [[The report: 11125 – the report of al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah, which al-Ṭabarī narrates later under number 11132, from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān, as a mursal (broken) report. Then he narrates it under number 11133, from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān, from a man who was named to him. They are one report.

"ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ibn Wāṣil ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ibn Hilāl al-Asadī," the teacher of al-Ṭabarī, from whom al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Abū Ḥātim narrated. Abū Ḥātim said: "ṣadūq" (truthful), and al-Nasāʾī said: "thiqah" (trustworthy). He is biographically treated in al-Tahdhīb.

"Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim al-Asadī" was accused of lying and fabrication. Abū Dāwūd said: "not trustworthy and not reliable, his reports are fabricated." Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal also criticized him and declared him weak. Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim narrated from al-Awzāʿī. He is biographically treated in al-Tahdhīb.

"Al-Awzāʿī" is the well-known Imam.

"Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah al-Muḥāribī" was among the most excellent people of his time. Aḥmad, Ibn Maʿīn and al-ʿIjlī declared him trustworthy. He narrated from Abū Umāmah, ʿAnbasah ibn Abī Sufyān, and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab. They stated explicitly that he transmitted from Abū Wāqid al-Laythī as a mursal, and apparently they meant this very report.

"Abū Wāqid al-Laythī," it is said his name was "al-Ḥārith ibn Mālik," and it is said "al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAwf," and it is said "ʿAwf ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Asad," from the Banū Layth ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manāt, of Kinānah. He was a Companion. He narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), and from Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. His two sons ʿAbd al-Malik and Wāqid narrated from him, along with ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtbah, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, and others.

The chain of Abū Jaʿfar here is a weak chain, because of the weakness of Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim, but the report has been transmitted through a sound route, as you will see in the takhrīj (the tracing of sources).

Aḥmad transmitted it in his Musnad, 5:218 (Ḥalabī edition), from Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim, from al-Awzāʿī, which is the very chain of al-Ṭabarī, so it is weak.

Then he transmitted it again on the same page, from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from al-Awzāʿī. (I say: in the Musnad it reads: "Ḥaddathanā al-Walīd, ḥaddathanā Muslim, ḥaddathanā al-Awzāʿī," which is an undoubted error; the correct form is al-Walīd ibn Muslim, as Ibn Kathīr quoted it from this place in the Musnad in his tafsīr, 2:69.)

Ibn Kathīr said after quoting this second report of Aḥmad's: "Aḥmad alone transmitted it by this route, and it is a sound chain according to the conditions of the two Ṣaḥīḥs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)."

But al-Haythamī traced it in Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid, 4:165, and said: "Aḥmad transmitted it by two chains, the narrators of one of them are narrators of the Ṣaḥīḥ [meaning the second of Aḥmad's two reports], except that al-Mizzī said: Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah did not hear it from Abū Wāqid, and God knows best."

Then al-Haythamī also traced it in Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid, 5:165, and said: "al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it, and its narrators are trustworthy." He did not mention al-Mizzī's statement, nor the break in the chain.

Al-Ḥākim transmitted it in al-Mustadrak, 4:125, by way of Abū Qilābah al-Raqqāshī, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah, from Abū Wāqid, with the like of it. He said: "This is a sound ḥadīth according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim), though they did not transmit it." al-Dhahabī criticized him, saying: "There is a break (inqiṭāʿ) in it," alluding to what al-Mizzī said, as reported by the author of Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid.

Al-Bayhaqī transmitted it in al-Sunan, 9:356, by three routes: Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim al-Asadī, from al-Awzāʿī, like the report of Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarī.

And by a route through Abū ʿUbayd, from Muḥammad ibn Kathīr, from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān, from Abū Wāqid.

Then he transmitted it through al-Walīd ibn Muslim (this is the second route of Aḥmad), but with an addition: he transmitted it from Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Ḥanẓalī, from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah, from Ibn Murthad, or Abū Murthad, from Abū Wāqid al-Laythī.

Ibn Kathīr pointed to this route in his tafsīr, 3:69, after he had quoted the report of Aḥmad in the Musnad, saying: "But some transmitted it from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah, from Muslim ibn Yazīd, from Abū Wāqid, with it; and some transmitted it from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān, from Murthad, or Abū Murthad, from Abū Wāqid, with it." He thus differed from what is in the Sunan of al-Bayhaqī, where he said "Murthad," whereas it there reads "Ibn Murthad."

I have found no mention in the books of biography of Muslim ibn Yazīd, or Murthad, or Ibn Murthad. So the chain of this report, as you see, is, even if sound, broken (munqaṭiʿ).

Al-Suyūṭī traced it in al-Durr al-Manthūr, 2:259, and did not attribute it to anyone other than Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim.

* *

As for His words, "if you do not have a morning drink": that is, if you do not find ṣabūḥ (a morning drink). And "al-ṣabūḥ" (with a fatḥah on the ṣād) is what is milked from the milk in the early morning and drunk then. "Iṣṭabaḥa al-qawm" means: they drank the morning drink. "Ṣabbaḥa al-rajul ḍayfahu" means: he gave his guest the morning drink at dawn.

As for His words, "or an evening drink": that is, if you do not find ghabūq (an evening drink). And "al-ghabūq" (with a fatḥah on the ghayn) is what is milked from the milk in the evening and drunk then. "Ghabaqa al-rajul ḍayfahu" means: he gave his guest an evening drink. "Ightabaqa al-qawm" means: they drank the evening drink.

As for "tataḥtafiʾū" (gather green herbs), its explanation will come after report number 11133, p. 542, note 2.]]

11126. Abū Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from al-Khaṣīb ibn Zayd al-Tamīmī, who said: al-Ḥasan narrated to us: that a man asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saying: "Until when is the forbidden lawful for me?" He said: "Until your family has enough of milk, or their provision (mīrah) comes." [[The report: 11126 – "al-Khaṣīb ibn Zayd al-Tamīmī," who heard from al-Ḥasan; his report is mursal. Hushaym narrated from him, as al-Bukhārī said in al-Kabīr 2/1/201. In al-Tahdhīb it is said: "Aḥmad declared him trustworthy," and Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him among the trustworthy. In Ibn Abī Ḥātim 1/2/396 it is written "Khaṣīb ibn Badr al-Tamīmī," but the correct form is "Khaṣīb ibn Zayd," as al-Bukhārī said.

"Al-mīrah" (with a kasra on the mīm) is the bringing in of provisions. In the manuscript it reads "wa-tajī'" with a waw; I have adopted what is in the printed edition, and Ibn Kathīr 3:69.]]

11127. Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Khaṣīb ibn Zayd al-Tamīmī informed us, saying: al-Ḥasan narrated to us: that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and he mentioned the like of it, except that he said: "or their provision is gathered (tujbā)." [[In the printed edition it reads "or their provision lives (taḥyā)," from "ḥayāh" (life), while in the manuscript it reads "tujbā" without dots. I thought it best to read it so, from "jabā al-māʾ fī al-ḥawḍ yajbīhi" (he gathered water in the basin) and "jabā al-kharāj" (he collected the tax). If it were read "yujnā" from "janā yajnī," as one gathers fruit, it would be a metaphor. The printed "yuḥyā" has some justification, but I preferred what I have adopted. I have not found this report elsewhere with this transmission.]]

11128. Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUrwah narrated to me, from his grandfather ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, from someone who narrated to him: that a man of the Bedouins came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him for a ruling concerning what God had forbidden him and what He had made lawful for him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Good things are lawful for you, and foul things are forbidden for you, except that if you become needy of food [that is not lawful for you], [[The words in brackets are necessary for the sentence to be complete, from Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid.]] then eat of it until you become independent of it." The man said: "What is the need that makes it lawful for me? And what is the independence that would suffice me from that?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If you hope for offspring, then sustain yourself on the meat of your livestock until your offspring come, or if you hope for a wealth you seek, then sustain yourself on some of that, [[To "sustain oneself with some food or other": to be satisfied with it. His statement "some," meaning a little, without excess in it. Compare the explanation of "shay'" meaning "little" in what has preceded, 6:448, note 2/8:403, note 1.]] then feed your family whatever appears to you, until you are independent of it." The Bedouin said: "What is the independence that I leave when I find it?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you have given your family an evening drink from the night." [[In Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid: "an evening drink of milk." What is in al-Ṭabarī is better.]] "Then avoid what God has forbidden you of food. [And as for] your property [[The words in brackets are added, from Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid and al-Durr al-Manthūr. His later statement "all of it easy" means: it is made expansive for you in it.]] then it is all easy (maysūr), there is nothing forbidden in it."" [[The report: 11128 – al-Haythamī traced it in Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid at length, from "the ḥadīth of Samurah ibn Jundub, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that a man of the Bedouins came to him," then he said: "al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it in al-Kabīr, and al-Bazzār in summary. In the chain of al-Ṭabarānī are obscure narrators (mastūrūn), and the chain of al-Bazzār is weak."

Ibn Kathīr mentioned it from this place of the tafsīr, 3:70, and in it: "ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, from his grandmother," but the correct reading is what is in al-Ṭabarī and al-Durr al-Manthūr, and by what has become clear that the report is from the ḥadīth of Samurah ibn Jundub. He traced it in al-Durr al-Manthūr 2:260, and did not attribute it to anyone other than al-Ṭabarī.]]

11129. Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, from Ibn ʿAwn, who said: I found with al-Ḥasan the book of Samurah, and I read it to him, and in it was: "What suffices in necessity is an evening drink or a morning drink." [[The report: 11129 – "Samurah" is Samurah ibn Jundub ibn Hilāl al-Fazārī, the companion of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This book of his was his letter to his sons. Ibn Sīrīn said: "In the letter of Samurah to his sons there is much knowledge." See the following report.]]

11130. Hannād and Abū Hishām al-Rifāʿī narrated to us, both saying: Yaḥyā ibn Abī Zāʾidah narrated to us, from Ibn ʿAwn, who said: I read in the book of Samurah ibn Jundub: "An evening drink or a morning drink suffices from necessity = or: from need (ḍarūrah) = ." [[The report: 11130 – al-Bayhaqī narrated this report in al-Sunan from Abū ʿUbayd, from Muʿādh, from Ibn ʿAwn, who said: "I saw with al-Ḥasan the books of Samurah to his sons: that it suffices of necessity – or of need –..." "Ḍarūrah" and "ḍārūrah" are the same, and both are the name of the verbal noun "iḍṭirār" (necessity).]]

11131. ʿAlī ibn Saʿīd al-Kindī and Abū Kurayb narrated to me, both saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Idrīs narrated to us, from Hishām ibn Ḥassān, from al-Ḥasan, who said: When a man is compelled to carrion, he eats from it his sufficiency (qūt) = that is: his maskah (what keeps him going). [["Al-maskah" (with a ḍammah on the mīm and sukūn on the sīn) is what keeps the bodies going of food and drink. Likewise "al-qūt" is what sustains the human body of food, and what keeps the life-breath from failing of provision.]]

11132. Hannād ibn al-Sarī narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubārak narrated to us, from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah, who said: A man said: "O Messenger of God, we are in a land of makhmaṣah (hunger), so what is lawful for us of carrion? And when is carrion lawful for us?" He said: "If you do not have a morning drink, or an evening drink, and do not gather green herbs, then it is yours to take." [[The two reports: 11132, 11133 – these are the report of Abū Wāqid al-Laythī that passed as number 11125, and see the note on it there.]]

11133. Hannād ibn al-Sarī narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus narrated to us, from al-Awzāʿī, from Ḥassān ibn ʿAṭiyyah, from a man who was named to us: that a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are in a land of hunger, so when is carrion lawful for us?" He said: "If you do not have an evening drink, and do not have a morning drink, and do not gather green herbs, then it is yours to take." [[The two reports: 11132, 11133 – these are the report of Abū Wāqid al-Laythī that passed as number 11125, and see the note on it there.]]

* *

Abū Jaʿfar said: This is narrated in four ways: "tataḥtafiʾū" with a hamzah; "tataḥtafiyū," with the ṭāʾ and the yāʾ lightened; "tataḥaffū," with the fāʾ doubled; and "tataḥtafū" with the ḥāʾ and light pronunciation, which admits the hamzah. [[What Abū Jaʿfar mentioned are the narrations of this letter with the ḥāʾ. But it is also narrated with the jīm, hamzated: "tajtafiʾū," from their saying "jafaʾa al-baql yajfaʾuhu jafʾan, wa-ijtafaʾa" (the herb was uprooted), when he tore it out from its root.

It is also narrated with the jīm not hamzated, "tajtafū," with the same meaning as the hamzated form: "jafaytu al-baql wa-ijtafaytuhu" (I plucked the herb).

It is narrated with the unpointed khāʾ: "takhtafū," from "akhfā al-shayʾ," when he made it appear after its concealment, as if he had removed its concealment.

As for what al-Ṭabarī narrated with the ḥāʾ, the explanation of "tataḥtafiʾū" is from "al-ḥafaʾ," which is papyrus. It is said: "iḥtafa al-ḥafaʾ": he uprooted it from its place.

As for "tataḥtafiyū" (with a kasra on the fāʾ and a ḍammah on the yāʾ), from their saying "iḥtafā al-ḥafaʾ, al-baql" when he uprooted it from the surface of the earth with the fingernails; its root is the hamzah.]]

As for "تحتفوا" with the fa' doubled (tashdid), it comes from their saying "احتف الطعام" when one eats everything that is in the pot, and from their saying "احتفت المرأة" when a woman removes the hair of her face by plucking it with two threads. It is as if they pluck the greens (al-baql) from the surface of the earth because they are small.

As for "تحتفوا," it comes from "احتفى البقل" when one uproots it, and it is unhamzated (ghayr mahmuz).

Moreover, al-Azhari said: "Abu Sa'id said: the correct form is 'تحتفوا,' with the fa' lightened and without hamza. Everything that is completely uprooted has been ihtafa (احتفى), and from this comes 'ihfa' al-sha'r' (the removal of hair). He said: 'Ihtafa al-baql' means taking it from the surface of the earth with the tips of the fingers, because it is short and scanty." He said: "Whoever says 'تحتفئوا' with hamza, from al-hafa' (al-hafa', the papyrus), is wrong, because papyrus is not among the baql. The baql is what grows of herbage on the surface of the earth that has no root-stalk. He said: there is no papyrus in the lands of the Arabs." It is also related as "ما لم تجتفئوا" with the jim. He said: "Ijtifa' with the jim is also wrong, because ijtifa' means overturning the vessels when one tips them over (jaffa'tuha)." It is also related as "ما لم تحتفوا," with the fa' doubled, from "احتففت الشيء," when one takes all of a thing, just as a woman removes the hair of her face.

**The discussion of the interpretation of His saying: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: "The good things have been made lawful for you, and [the game caught by] what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained."﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His majesty be exalted, means: They ask you, O Muhammad, your Companions: what is it that has been made lawful for them to eat of foods and provisions? So say to them: "Made lawful for you from them are *al-tayyibat* (the good things, i.e., the lawful things), which your Lord has permitted you to eat from the slaughtered animals.[[See the explanation of *al-tayyibat* in what has preceded: 3:301 / 5:555 / 6:361 / 8:409 / 9:391.]] Also made lawful for you, in addition to that, is the game of what you have trained of *al-jawarih* (the hunting beasts and birds), which are the predators among the animals that catch [prey]."

* *

Birds were called *jawarih* because they wound their masters' prey and earn their livelihood for them from the game. It is said of this: "Fulan *jaraha* (earned) good for his family" if he earned them good; and "Fulan is the *jarihah* of his family," meaning: their earner; and "There is no *jarihah* for so-and-so (a woman)" if she has no earner. [[See Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubaydah 1:154.]] From this is the saying of al-A'sha of Bani Tha'labah:

*Dhāta ḥaddin munḍijin mīsamuhā... tudhkiru al-jāriḥa mā kāna ijtaraḥ*

[*Possessor of a sharp edge, its branding iron ripening, it reminds the wounder of what he had committed.*]

[[From his Diwan, p. 164. It is from a long poem of his in which he praises Iyas ibn Qabisah al-Ta'i, king of al-Hirah. Then he concluded the poem by mentioning wine and his youth, what he had of amusement, manliness and valour, and he said, describing the sharpness of his speech against one who opposes him (according to the version of the Diwan):

*Wa-laqad amnaḥu man 'ādaytuhu... kalaman yaḥsimna min dā'i al-kashaḥ*
*Wa-qaṭa'tu nāẓirayhi ẓāhiran... lā yakūnu mithla laṭmin wa-kamaḥ*
*Dhā ḥabārin munḍijin mīsamuhu... yudhkiru al-jārima mā kāna ijtaraḥ*

"Kalaman" is the plural of "kalimah," meaning: his satire and his poetry. In the Diwan, "kalamā" is vocalised with a damma on the kaf and a shadda on the lam, and it is reported from the Diwan as "kulla mā," which in my judgement is an error. "Ḥasama al-dā'a yaḥsimuhu" means: he cut it with medicine. "Ḥasama al-'irq" means: he cut it, then cauterised it so its blood would not flow. "Al-kashḥ" (with a fatha on the kaf and the shin) is a disease that afflicts a person in his flank, which is then cauterised. "Al-kashḥ" (with a fatha then a sukun) is what lies between the waist and the rib at the back; a person has two flanks. "Ṭawā fulān kashḥahu" means: he turned away and showed his flank, out of hatred and enmity. He meant by his saying "the disease of the flank" enmity and hatred. He says: I satirise him with a satire that cures him of the disease of hatred!

His saying "wa-qaṭa'tu nāẓirayhi" means: I cauterised him with a visible cautery in the middle of his forehead, between his eyes down to his nose. His saying "ẓāhiran" is an adjective of an omitted noun, i.e., a visible branding whose mark is evident. Its mark is not like the mark of a slap or of a horse's bit. "Al-kamḥ" (with two fathas) is the mark left by a horse's bit, i.e., the pulling and jerking of the horse with the bridle to make it stop, leaving a mark where the bit sits. This is a word that the lexicographical books have not mentioned, and I explained it from the context of the poem's meaning. He says: the mark of a slap is not clear, for it disappears; the mark of the bit is light, coming in succession and so not harmful; but this visible one is a branding by fire (as the third verse makes clear). I am in doubt about the transmission of this verse.

His saying "dhā ḥabār" means: possessing a mark; it is a second adjective of his saying "ẓāhiran." "Al-ḥabār" (with a fatha on the ḥa) is a mark on the skin from a blow or a branding or otherwise. Similar is "al-ḥibr" (with a kasra then a sukun). In the Diwan it is "dhā jubār" (with a damma on the jim), which has no meaning; the correct recitation is what I have established. "Al-mīsam" is the iron with which one brands. He likens his satire to a hot branding iron which ripens the skin and leaves in it a mark that does not disappear, and it never ceases to remind him of what he committed.

As for the version of Abu Ja'far, it is in the manuscript as "dhāt ḥadd" (with an open ḥa). If it is correct thus, it is an adjective of his saying "kalaman yaḥsimna," and "al-ḥadd" means the hardness, intensity and penetration of a thing, as one says "ḥadd al-ẓahīrah," meaning: its intense heat. And if his version is correct as it was in the printed edition, "dhāt khadd" (with an unpointed/aspirated kha), from "al-khadd" and "al-ukhdūd," which is a cut; "khaddat al-ḍarbah jildahu" means when the blow cut his skin and left a trench in it; and "akhādīd al-siyāṭ" are the marks of whips on the skin. Both are good in meaning.]]

Notice: the Diwan of al-A'sha printed in Europe is a Diwan with much error, distortion and misreading. For this reason I strove to correct this poetry and much else of al-A'sha's poetry that has preceded.

That is, "he earned" [*ijtaraḥa*].

And the words "and what you have taught" and "game" were omitted from His saying "and what you have trained of," being sufficient by the indication of what was mentioned in the speech over what was left out.

* *

This is because the people, as has reached us, had asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he ordered them to kill dogs, about what was lawful for them to keep of them and to hunt with them. So Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, revealed this verse concerning what they asked about. He made an exception from what He had forbidden keeping of them, and commanded the keeping of hunting dogs, guard dogs of livestock, and dogs of cultivated fields, and permitted them to keep such dogs.

Mention of the report concerning that:

11134. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Zayd ibn Hubab al-'Ukli narrated to us, saying: Musa ibn 'Ubaydah narrated to us, saying: Aban ibn Salih informed us, from al-Qa'qa' ibn Hakim, from Salma Umm Rafi', from Abu Rafi', who said: Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) seeking permission to enter, and he was given permission. He said: "We have indeed given you permission, O Messenger of Allah!" [[By his saying "Messenger of Allah," he means Jibril, the messenger of Allah with His revelation to the Prophet, may Allah bless them both.]] He said: "Indeed, but we do not enter a house in which there is a dog!" Abu Rafi' said: So he commanded me to kill every dog in Madinah, and I killed them until I came to a woman who had a dog barking over her, so I left it out of mercy for her. Then I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and he commanded me, so I returned to the dog and killed it. Then they came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for us of this community that you have commanded to be killed?" He said: So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was silent, and Allah revealed: "They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: The good things have been made lawful for you, and [the game caught by] what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained." [[The report: 11134. "Zayd ibn al-Hubab al-'Ukli," previously mentioned under nos. 2185, 5350, 8165; he is trustworthy, one of the teachers of Ahmad.
"Musa ibn 'Ubaydah ibn Nashit al-Rabadhi," previously mentioned under nos. 1875, 1876, 3291, 8361; he is extremely weak. Ahmad said: "Munkar al-hadith (a narrator of rejected reports), it is not permitted to narrate from him." In the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir it is "Yunus ibn 'Ubaydah," which is an error that must be corrected.
"Aban ibn Salih ibn 'Umayr ibn 'Ubayd," trustworthy; previously mentioned under nos. 4337, 4338. In the printed edition here it was: "narrated to us Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, he said: informed us Salih," and in the manuscript: "he said: Ana Salih," and both are errors, and the correct form is what I have established, from al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Kathir.
"Al-Qa'qa' ibn Hakim al-Kinani," a trustworthy Successor; previously mentioned under no. 304.
"Salma Umm Rafi'," the freedwoman of the Prophet (ﷺ), she was the wife of Abu Rafi', and she narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) and from Fatimah al-Zahra.
"Abu Rafi'," the freedman of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).
The chain of this report is weak, due to the weakness of Musa ibn 'Ubaydah al-Rabadhi. Ibn Abi Hatim also related it through the route of Hajjaj ibn Hamzah, from Zayd ibn Hubab, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, as Ibn Kathir reported it in his Tafsir 3:72, 73. Al-Haythami mentioned it in Majma' al-Zawa'id 4:42, 43, and said: "al-Tabarani related it in al-Kabir, and in it is Musa ibn 'Ubaydah al-Rabadhi, who is weak."
As for al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan 9:235, and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:311, they related it in abridged form through the route of Mu'alla ibn Mansur, from Ibn Abi Za'idah, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Aban ibn Salih, and this is more sound than the chain of Abu Ja'far and Ibn Abi Hatim. Al-Hakim said: "This is a hadith with a sound chain, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed with him.
The hadith of Abu Rafi' has been related with other than this wording through several routes. See al-Haythami in Majma' al-Zawa'id 4:42, 43, and Musnad Ahmad 6:8-10, 391.
His saying "a dog barking over her" means: it repels by its barking what she fears from a predator, and warns her of the arrival of a guest if it senses his scent. Its explanation came in the report narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad 6:391: "She said: 'I am a neglected woman, and this dog drives away the predator from me, and alerts me to the one who comes.'"]]

11135. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ikrimah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent Abu Rafi' to kill dogs, and he killed until he reached al-'Awali [[Al-'Awali: places at the upper lands of Madinah; the nearest of them to Madinah is four miles away, and the farthest in the direction of Najd is eight miles.]]. Then 'Asim ibn 'Adi, Sa'd ibn Khaythamah and 'Uwaym ibn Sa'idah entered, and they said: "What has been made lawful for us, O Messenger of Allah?" So this was revealed: "They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: The good things have been made lawful for you, and [the game caught by] what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained."

11136. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr narrated to us, saying: they related to us from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the killing of dogs, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for us of this community?" So this was revealed: "They ask you what has been made lawful for them," the verse.

* *

Then the people of interpretation differed regarding *al-jawarih* (the hunting beasts and birds) which Allah meant by His saying: "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds."

Some of them said: It is every creature that is taught to hunt and learns it, whether a quadruped or a bird.

Mention of those who said that:

11137. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Muslim, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained," he said: Everything that is taught and then hunts, whether a dog, a falcon, a leopard or other.

11138. Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Muslim, from al-Hasan: "training them," he said: Everything that is taught and then hunts, from a dog or a leopard or other.

11139. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the game of the leopard, he said: It is of the hunting beasts.

11140. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Anbasah, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained," he said: The birds and the dogs.

11141. Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Abu Khalid al-Ahmar narrated to us, from al-Hajjaj, from 'Ata', from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid, the like of it.

11142. Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from Humayd, from Mujahid: "mukallibīn," he said: From the dogs and the birds.

11143. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding the saying of Allah: "from the hunting beasts, training them," he said: From the birds and the dogs.

11144. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

11145. Yaqub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us = and [another chain]: Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Shu'bah =, from al-Haytham, from Talhah ibn Musarrif, who said: Khaythamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said: "This is what I have made clear to you: that the falcon and the hawk are of the hunting birds." [[The reports 11145, 11146: "al-Haytham" is "al-Haytham ibn Habib," that is "al-Haytham ibn Abi al-Haytham" al-Sayrafi al-Kufi. Ahmad praised him and said: "How good are his narrations and how firm their correctness." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.
"Talhah ibn Musarrif al-Iyami," previously mentioned under no. 5431.
"Khaythamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Sabrah al-Ju'fi," a trustworthy Successor; previously mentioned under no. 8267.]]

11146. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Haytham relate, from Talhah al-Iyami, from Khaythamah, who said: "I have made clear to you: [[In the printed edition: "I was informed that the falcon," and in the manuscript: "I came to you that the falcon," and it seems the correct form is what I have established, by inference from the preceding report.]] that the falcon, the hawk and the dog are of the hunting beasts." [[The reports 11145, 11146: see the note above.]]

11147. Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar narrated to us, from Nafi', from 'Ali ibn Husayn, who said: The hawk and the falcon are of the hunting birds.

11148. Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Shurayk, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far, who said: The hawk and the falcon are of "the hunting beasts that train." [[In the printed edition: "of the hunting beasts that train," and I have established what is in the manuscript, which is correct.]].

11149. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained": by "the hunting beasts" he means the fierce dogs, the leopards, the falcons and their likes.

11150. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, regarding His saying: "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained," he said: From the dogs, and from the falcons and the *bizan* [[*Al-bizan* (with a kasra on the ba') is the plural of *baz*, without a ya' at its end, and it is also pluralised as *abwaz*. And their saying *baz* is a dialectal form of *bazi*, and the plural of *bazi* is *bazah* and *bawaz*.]] and their likes, of what is taught.

11151. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained": the hunting beasts are the dogs and the trained falcons.

11152. Sa'id ibn al-Rabi' al-Razi related to me, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, that he heard 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr say regarding His saying: "from the hunting beasts, training them," he said: The dogs and the birds.

* *

Others said: Allah, may His majesty be exalted, meant by His saying "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained" only the dogs, to the exclusion of other predators.

Mention of those who said that:

11153. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, saying: 'Ubayd narrated to us, from al-Dahhak: "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts [al-jawar] training them," he said: They are the dogs.

11154. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi regarding His saying: "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained," he says: "He has made lawful for you the game of the dogs which you have taught."

11155. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'idah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj informed us, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: As for what the birds catch = and the hawks among the birds = whatever you reach [alive] is yours, and otherwise do not feed it [to yourself]. [[In the printed edition: "fa-la tutmi'hu," and this is a printing error.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two sayings concerning the interpretation of the verse is the saying of the one who said: "Every creature that hunts, whether of the birds or of the beasts of prey, is among the hunting animals, and the game of all of them is lawful when it hunts after being trained," because Allah, may His majesty be exalted, by His saying "and what you have trained of the hunting beasts and birds, training them as hunting dogs are trained," encompassed every hunting creature and did not specify any of them. So every "hunting creature," whatever it is, of every bird and predator, provided it has the attribute that Allah described, its game is lawful to eat.

* *

There has also been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) a report similar to what we have said about this, together with what the verse indicates of the evidence we mentioned for the soundness of what we have said about it, and it is this:

11156. Hannad narrated this to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Yunus narrated to us, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the game of the falcon, and he said: "What it holds for you, eat." [[The report: 11156. "Hannad" is "Hannad ibn al-Sari ibn Mus'ab al-Darimi," trustworthy; previously mentioned under nos. 2058, 2758, 2998, 3960.
"'Isa ibn Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq al-Sabi'i," the jurist, son of a jurist, son of a jurist, trustworthy, a firm and reliable Hafiz, who died in 187 AH. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.
"Mujalid": he is "Mujalid ibn Sa'id ibn 'Umayr al-Hamdani," previously mentioned under nos. 1614, 2987, 2988, and it has already been stated that he is trustworthy, though some imams weakened him, and that the sound judgement regarding him is the correction of the reports of the early scholars from him, and that the most balanced thing said about him is the saying of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi: "The hadith of Mujalid among the young ones, Yahya ibn Sa'id and Abu Usamah, is worth nothing. But the hadith of Shu'bah and Hammad ibn Zayd and Hushaym, and those early scholars," and the saying of Ibn Abi Hatim: "That is, his memory changed in the last part of his life. He died in 144 AH."
The report of al-Sha'bi from 'Adi ibn Hatim was related by Muslim and al-Bukhari through the route of Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'idah, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adi ibn Hatim, that 'Adi asked the Messenger of Allah about the game of the dog. He said: "It holds for you, eat," the hadith [see al-Bayhaqi's al-Sunan 9:235, 236].]]

Also narrated by the Imams through the chain of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Safar from al-Sha'bi, and through the chain of 'Asim al-Ahwal from al-Sha'bi, and through the chain of Bayan from al-Sha'bi. They also narrated it through several chains from 'Adi ibn Hatim, but none of them contains the mention of "al-Baz" (the falcon). (See al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra 9: 235-238.) And see what will come, no. 11210.

Then al-Bayhaqi narrated with his chain from 'Abd Allah ibn Numayr, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adi ibn Hatim: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "What you have taught of a dog or a falcon, and then released, having mentioned the name of God, eat of what it has caught for you," and the hadith continues. Then al-Bayhaqi said: "...However, the mention of the falcon in this narration was not reported by the memorizers whom we have mentioned from al-Sha'bi; it was reported only by Mujalid, and God knows best."

The narration of 'Isa ibn Yunus from Mujalid is counted among the narrations of the early transmitters from Mujalid, before his memory changed. 'Isa ibn Yunus is trustworthy and firm, so it seems that Abu Ja'far considered this hadith sound and relied on it, since it is a narration of a trustworthy transmitter from a trustworthy transmitter before his change.]]
* *
= So the Prophet ﷺ permitted the hunting of the falcon and counted it among the hunting animals (al-jawarih). In this there is clear evidence of the error of the one who said: "God by His saying 'and what you have taught of the hunting animals' meant only what we have taught of dogs specifically, to the exclusion of the other hunting animals."
* *
If someone supposes that in His saying "trained (mukallibin)" there is an indication that the hunting animals mentioned in His saying "and what you have taught of the hunting animals" are dogs specifically, then he has supposed incorrectly.

For the meaning of the verse is: "Say: It is made lawful for you, O people, when you are owners of dogs, the good things, and the game of what you have taught to hunt from the beasts of prey and birds." So His saying "trained (mukallibin)" is a description of the hunter, even if he hunts with other than dogs at some times. It is like the saying of one who addresses a people: "The good things are made lawful for you, and what you have taught of the hunting animals, trained, believers." It is known that the speaker only meant to inform the people that God, mighty is His remembrance, made lawful for them, while they are people of faith, the good things and the game of the hunting animals which He informed them that only what they hunt with them is lawful for them. [In the printed edition: "what they hunted with them", and the manuscript's reading is also correct.] Likewise His saying "Lawful for you are the good things and what you have taught of the hunting animals, trained" is like that, in that the training of the hunter, with dogs whether they hunt or with others, is not a statement from God, mighty is His remembrance, that only what dogs catch is lawful of game.
* *
The interpretation of His saying: "You teach them from what God has taught you"

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying "you teach them," may He be praised, He means: you train the hunting animals so that you teach them to pursue game for you. "From what God has taught you" means by that: from the training which God has trained you in, and the knowledge which He has taught you. [See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 302.]
* *
Some interpreters have said: the meaning of His saying "from what God has taught you" is "as God has taught you."
Those who said this:
11157 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "You teach them from what God has taught you," he says: you teach them the pursuit as God has taught you.
* *
= We do not know in the speech of the Arabs "min" used in the sense of "ka" (like), because "min" enters their speech in the sense of partitive, and "ka" in the sense of comparison. A particle is only put in the place of another when their meanings are close. But when their meanings differ, there is no precedent in their speech for placing one after the other. The Book of God and its revelation are most worthy of speech that avoids what departs from the intelligible and from eloquence, from the speech of the one in whose tongue it was revealed. ........... [It is likely that before this report some speech of Abu Ja'far has fallen out, and this is indicated by his later saying: "It was said: the interpreters differed on that." What I deduce from his speech at the end of this context, these views of the differing Imams (p. 564), is that Abu Ja'far, as is his custom, posed a question about the meaning of "teaching the hunting animals," then answered it by mentioning the differences of the interpreters. I did not consider it proper to place anything in place of the dots I have placed to indicate this omission, because I fear I might err in joining the speech with the report he narrated after it under no. 11158. See p. 553, notes 2, 3.]
11158 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Subayh narrated to us, saying: Abu Hani' 'Umar ibn Bashir narrated to us, saying: 'Amir narrated to us: that 'Adi ibn Hatim al-Ta'i said: A man came to the Messenger of God ﷺ asking him about the game of dogs, and he did not know what to say to him, until this verse was revealed: "You teach them from what God has taught you." [The report: 11158 - "Isma'il ibn Subayh al-Yashkuri," trustworthy, passed under no. 2996, 8640. And "Abu Hani'," "Umar ibn Bashir al-Hamdani," Ahmad said: "Salih al-hadith." Yahya ibn Ma'in said: "Weak." Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy, and Abu Hatim al-Razi said: "Not strong, his hadith is written, and Jabir al-Ju'fi is dearer to me than him." Ibn Shahin and al-'Uqayli mentioned him among the weak. Biography in Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/100, Lisan al-Mizan 4: 287, and passed also under no. 4422. In the printed edition it read: "Abu Hani' narrated to us from Abu Bishr," which is a pure error and a bad alteration of what was in the manuscript: "Abu Hani' 'Umar ibn Bashr," and the correct is what is established. "'Amir" is al-Sha'bi. It is a weak hadith because of the weakness of Abu Hani'. al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 260, and attributed it also to 'Abd ibn Humayd, and the story in it is: "that 'Adi ibn Hatim al-Ta'i came to the Messenger of God ﷺ."]
* *
It was said: the interpreters differed on that. [See the preceding note p. 552, note 2, and the following note.]
Some of them said: it is that he incites himself to pursue the game when his owner releases him, and holds it for him when he catches it and does not eat from it, and responds to him when called, and does not flee from him when he wants it. When this is repeated from him several times, he is "trained." This is the view of a group of the people of the Hijaz and some of the people of Iraq. [Note: "yastashli" here means he is incited to pursue game.]
Those who said this:
11159 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj informed us, saying: 'Ata' said: Anything your hunter kills before it is trained, holds, and hunts, is carrion. Its killing is not a slaughter until it is trained, holds, and hunts. If that happens and then it kills, that is its slaughter.
11160 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The trained dog is one that holds its game and does not eat from it until its owner comes to it. If it eats from its game before its owner comes to it, then its slaughter is lost, so do not eat from its game.
11161 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Uyayna narrated to us, from 'Amr, from Tawus, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: If the dog eats, do not eat, for it held only for itself.
11162 - Abu Kurayb and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, both saying: Isma'il ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Mu'alla narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: If a man releases the dog and it eats from its game, it has spoiled it, even if he mentioned God's name when he released it. He claimed that it held only for itself, and God says: "trained, you teach them from what God has taught you." He claimed that if it eats from its game before its owner comes to it, it is not trained, and that it should be beaten and trained until it abandons that habit. [Note: "He claimed" here is Sa'id ibn Jubayr's report of Ibn 'Abbas's statement, meaning "said." It is frequent in their speech.]
11163 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ma'mar al-Raqqi narrated to us, from Hajjaj, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas who said: If the dog takes and kills and then eats, it is a beast of prey.
11164 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from 'Amir, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Do not eat from it, for if it were trained it would not have eaten from it, and it would not have learned what you taught it. It held only for itself and did not hold for you.
11165 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Dawud informed us, from al-Sha'bi, from Ibn 'Abbas, similarly.
11166 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: If the dog eats, do not eat.
11167 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Sha'bi, from Ibn 'Abbas, similarly.
11168 - Humayd ibn Mas'ada narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Awn narrated to us, saying: I said to 'Amir al-Sha'bi: A man releases his dog and it eats from it; may we eat from it? He said: No, it did not learn what you taught it.
11169 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Umar who said: If the dog eats from its game, strike it, for it is not trained.
11170 - Sawwar ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Tawus, from his father who said: If the dog eats, it is carrion, so do not eat it.
11171 - al-Hasan ibn 'Arafa narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr = and Sayyar, from al-Sha'bi = and Mughira, from Ibrahim = that they said concerning the dog when it eats from its game: do not eat, for it held only for itself.
11172 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj informed us, saying: 'Ata' said: If you find the dog has eaten from the game, then what you find dead, leave it, for it is what did not hold game for you. It is only a beast of prey that held for itself and not for you, even if it was trained.
11173 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, similarly.
* *
Others said similar to this view, except that they set a limit for knowing the dogs' training: that his dog has accepted training and become one of the hunting animals whose game is lawful, by doing that three times. This is a view reported from Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan.
* *
Others among those who held this view said: there is no limit to the dog's training by its owner, beyond that the dog does what we described as training. They said: when it does that, it has become trained, and its game is lawful. This is the view of some later scholars.

Some of those who held this view distinguished between the training of the falcon and other birds of prey, and the training of the dog and predatory beasts, saying: eating from the game of which the falcon has eaten is permitted. They said: the training of the falcon is that it flies when incited and responds when called, and does not flee from its owner when he wants to take it. They said: it is not one of the conditions of its training that it not eat from the game.
Those who said this:
11174 - Hannad ibn al-Sarri narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Mughira, from Ibrahim and Hajjaj, from 'Ata' who said: There is no harm in the game of the falcon even if it eats from it.
11175 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq al-Shaybani narrated to us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from Ibn 'Abbas that he said concerning birds: If you release it and it kills, eat. For the dog, when you strike it, does not return. The training of birds is that they return to their owner, and it is not struck when it eats from the game and plucks feathers. [In the printed edition: "If it eats from the game and plucks feathers, then eat," with the addition "then eat," from the manuscript; the manuscript had the same as the printed: "If it eats..." I judged the correct reading to be "if it eats..." without the fa', and the sentence stands with the translation.]
11176 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: Abu Hamza narrated to us, from Jabir, from al-Sha'bi who said: The falcon and the hawk are not like the dog. If you release them and they hold and eat, then you call them and they come to you, eat from it.
11177 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu Zubayd narrated to us, from Mutarraf, from Hammad, Ibrahim said: Eat the game of the falcon even if it eats from it.
11178 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Hammad, from Ibrahim = and Jabir, from al-Sha'bi, they both said: Eat of the falcon's game even if it eats. [In the printed edition: "game of the bazi" with a final ya, and the manuscript's reading is correct. See above p. 548, note 4.]
11179 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughira, from Hammad, from Ibrahim: If the falcon and the hawk eat from the game, then eat, for it is not trained. [Meaning: it is not trained not to eat from the game as the dog is trained.]
11180 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim who said: There is no harm in what the falcon has eaten from.
11181 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Hammad, that he said concerning the falcon when it eats from it: eat. * *
Others among them said: the training of birds, beasts and predators is equal; no kind of these is trained except by what makes all the other kinds trained. They said: it is not lawful to eat any game that a hunting animal has caught and then eaten from, whatever that hunting animal is, beast or bird. [In the manuscript: "does not make every game lawful..." and the printed is correct. In the manuscript: "beast or bird" in the nominative; the printed is correct.] They said: because among the conditions of its training by which its game becomes lawful is that it holds what it catches for its owner and does not eat from it.
Those who said this:
11182 - Hannad and Abu Kurayb narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Salim narrated to us, from 'Amir who said: 'Ali said: If the falcon eats from its game, do not eat. [The report: 11182 - "Muhammad ibn Salim al-Hamdani," Abu Sahl al-Kufi, weak in hadith, abandoned. Biography in al-Tahdhib. Passed in the chain under no. 4824.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 4 (part 3 of 5):

11184 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Salim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "If the falcon eats, do not eat."

11185 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Amr ibn al-Walid al-Shanni, who said: I heard Ikrimah say: "If the falcon eats, do not eat." [[The report: 11185 - "Amr ibn al-Walid al-Shanni", Abu Salamah al-Abdi, of the tribe of Abd al-Qays. He narrated from Ikrimah and Shihab ibn Abbad al-Asri. Waki' and Abu Nu'aym narrated from him. He said: "If you reach it and it has not eaten, then eat." He said this more than once.

* *

Others said: The teaching of every hunting animal, whether beast or bird, is one. They said: Its teaching by which its game becomes lawful is that it is sent upon the game, responds to the sending, seizes the game, its owner calls it and it comes, and it does not flee from him when he has taken it. They said: When the hunting animal does this, it becomes "trained" (mu'allam), included in the meaning God stated: "And what you have taught of the trained hunting animals (mukallibin), teaching them of what God has taught you, eat of what they catch for you." They said: It is not a condition of such teaching that it not eat of the game. They said: How could that be a condition of it, when it is disciplined by its eating?

Mention of those who said this:

11187 - Ibn Abi al-Shawarib narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Sa'id - or Sa'd - from Salman, who said: "If you send your dog upon game and mention the name of God, and it eats two-thirds and one-third remains, eat what remains." "Salman" is Ibn al-Islam, Salman al-Khayr al-Farisi, companion of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). In the manuscript, in this report and the next, it read "Sulayman", then the manuscript was corrected to the right reading. After this report, no. 11211, Abu Ja'far notes that it is not known that Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab heard from Salman al-Farisi.
As for his saying "or Sa'd", I do not know what he meant by it, nor do I know who the "Sa'd" is from whom Qatadah narrates, and who narrates from Salman. In the following reports, a similar narration from "Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas" will come. I fear there is an inversion in the isnad: "Qatadah, from Sa'id, from Salman, or Sa'd." * *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the statements on the meaning of His saying "teaching them of what God has taught you" is that the "teaching" God mentioned in this verse for hunting animals is only that a man teaches his animal to respond when sent upon game, to pursue it when urged on, or to hold it for him when it has taken it without eating any of it, and not to flee from him when he wants it, and to come when he calls it. That is the teaching of every hunting animal, bird and beast alike. If the hunter's animal eats from the game, then his animal is at that point not trained. If its owner reaches his game alive and slaughters it, it is lawful for him to eat. If he reaches it dead, it is not lawful for him to eat, because it is what the beast has eaten, which God forbade in His saying: "And what the beast of prey has eaten" (﴿وَمَا أَكَلَ السَّبُعُ﴾), and he did not reach its slaughter.

We said that this is the most correct of the statements on this matter because of the widespread reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), namely:

11209 - Ibn Humayd narrated this to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Asim ibn Sulayman al-Ahwal, from al-Sha'bi, from Adi ibn Hatim: that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about game, and he said: "When you send your dog, mention the name of God over it. If you reach it after it has been killed and has eaten from it, do not eat anything from it, for it has held it only for itself." [[The report: 11209 - a sound hadith. Narrated by al-Bukhari (al-Fath 9: 527), Muslim 13: 78, 79, Ahmad in al-Musnad 4: 257, 379, Abu Dawud in his Sunan 3: 145 no. 2849, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan 9: 236, 238, 242, 244, from several chains, in full.]]

11210 - Abu Kurayb and Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i narrated to us, both saying: Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Bayan ibn Bishr, from 'Amir, from Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "We are a people who hunt with these dogs?" He said: "When you send your trained dogs and mention the name of God over them, then eat what they hold for you, even if they kill, unless the dog eats. If it eats, do not eat, for I fear it has held it only for itself." [[The report: 11210 - a sound hadith. Narrated by al-Bukhari through Qutaybah ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Fudayl (al-Fath 9: 527, 528), and by Muslim through Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, from Muhammad ibn Fudayl 13: 75, Ahmad in his Musnad 4: 258, al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan 9: 236, 237, and Abu Dawud in his Sunan 3: 145, no. 2848, in full.]]

If someone says: What do you say about what was narrated to you:

11211 - Imran ibn Bakkar al-Kala'i narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Dinar narrated to us, from Abu Ilyas, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Salman al-Farisi, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "If a man sends his dog upon game, and he reaches it after it has eaten from it, then let him eat what remains." [[The report: 11211 - "Imran ibn Bakkar al-Kala'i", Abu Ja'far's teacher, mentioned at nos. 149 and 2071.
"Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa ibn Rawh al-Lahouni", Abu Rawh, al-Bahrani al-Himsi. Abu Hatim said: "Truthful, trustworthy, reliable." Biographed in al-Tahdhib.
"Muhammad ibn Dinar al-Azdi al-Tahi", who is "Ibn Abi al-Furat", and "Abu Bakr ibn Abi al-Furat". Al-Nasa'i said: "There is no harm in him," and said elsewhere: "weak." Abu Dawud said: "He changed before he died." al-Daraqutni said: "weak," and said once: "abandoned." Biographed in al-Tahdhib.
"Abu Ilyas" is Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah ibn Iyas al-Muzani, a trustworthy Successor. Biographed in al-Tahdhib.
Abu Ja'far discusses the isnad of this report below, and Ibn Kathir in his tafsir 3: 75 cited what al-Tabari said, then followed it with: "What Ibn Jarir said is correct, but this meaning has been related as a marfu' report by other routes." He then cited Abu Dawud's hadith in his Sunan 3: 147, no. 2857, and said: "Thus Abu Dawud related it, and al-Nasa'i has also related it. Abu Dawud also related it through Yunus ibn Sayf, from Abu Idris al-Khawlani, from Abu Tha'labah..." and he cited Abu Dawud's hadith in his Sunan 3: 147, no. 2856, then said: "These are two good chains."]] It is said: This report has a problem in its isnad, for it is not known that Sa'id heard from Salman, and the trustworthy transmitters among the people of narrations stop this statement at Salman, and narrate it from him without it being traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). When trustworthy memorizers agree in transmitting something with a particular description, and a single transmitter who lacks their memory differs from them, the agreeing reliable group has more right to the soundness of what they transmitted than the lone transmitter who lacks their memory. [[See the note on the preceding report, no. 11211.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Since the matter regarding the dog is as I have stated, that if it eats from the game it is not trained, then the ruling for every hunting animal is likewise: that whatever it eats from the game is not trained, and it is not lawful to eat its game unless one reaches its slaughter.

* *

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying: ﴿فَكُلُوا مِمَّا أَمْسَكْنَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying "then eat of what they hold for you," He means: eat, O people, of what your hunting animals have held for you.

* *

The interpreters differed on the meaning of this.

Some of them said: It is according to its outward and general sense, as God made it general: it is lawful to eat everything that the dogs and trained hunting animals hold for us of lawful game, whether the animal eats from it or does not eat from it, whether we reach its slaughter and slaughter it, or do not reach its slaughter until the hunting animals kill it by its wounding or without wounding.

This is the view of those who said: "The teaching of hunting animals by which their game becomes lawful is that they are taught to respond when sent upon game, to pursue it when sent, to seize it, and not to flee from their owner, apart from not eating from their game when they hunt it." We have already mentioned the statement of the proponents of this view and the reports from them with their chains cited above.

* *

Other scholars said: Rather, that [the permission] is specific, not general. They said its meaning is: "So eat of what they (the trained animals) catch for you" of the game as a whole, not part of it. They said: If the hunting animals eat part of the game and hold back part of it, then the part they held back is not lawful to eat, since they ate some of it. For they only held back what they held back of that game after eating from it, for themselves and not for us. God, exalted is His remembrance, only permitted us to eat what our trained animals held back for us, by His saying: "So eat of what they hold back for you," and not what they held back for themselves. This is the view of those who said: "The training of hunting animals which makes their game lawful is that they be sent out to the prey when they are released, so they pursue it and seize it, and hold it for their owner without eating any of it and without fleeing from their owner." We have already mentioned among those who said this earlier a large group, and we will mention here another group. [[See the earlier reports, from no. 11182 onward.]] [[In the printed edition: "another group of others"; I have kept what is in the manuscript.]]

11212. Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: "So eat of what they hold back for you." He said: "Eat of what they kill." 'Ali said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say: If it kills and eats, then do not eat; and if it holds back and you reach it alive, then slaughter it.

11213. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: If the trained dog eats from its game before its master comes and reaches its slaughter, then it should not be eaten.

11214. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding "So eat of what they hold back for you": When the dog hunts and holds back the game after killing it without eating from it, then it is lawful. But if it eats from it, it is said: It only held it back for itself, so do not eat any of it, for it is not trained.

11215. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding "They ask you what has been made lawful for them," up to His saying "So eat of what they hold back for you, and mention the name of God over it." He said: When you release your trained dog, or your bird, or your arrow, and you mention the name of God, and it seizes or kills, then eat.

11216. It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say: If you release your trained dog and mention the name of God when you release it, and it holds back or kills, then it is lawful. But if it eats from it, then do not eat it, for it only held it back for itself.

11217. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from 'Asim, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adiyy, regarding His saying: "So eat of what they hold back for you." He said: I said: O Messenger of God, my land is a land of game? He said: "When you release your dog and say the name of God, then eat of what your dog holds back for you, even if it killed. But if it eats, then do not eat, for it only held it back for itself." [[Report no. 11217: a sound hadith, related by al-Bukhari (al-Fath 9: 527), in nearly its wording. Ahmad also related it in this fuller wording in his Musnad 4: 257. See the note on the earlier report no. 11209.]]

We have already shown which of the two views is closer to the truth, so there is no need to repeat it here. [[See above, p. 564.]]

* *

If someone asks: What is the function of "min" (from) in His saying "So eat of what they hold back for you," when God has made lawful to us the game of our lawful hunting animals, and "min" only enters speech to indicate a part of what it modifies?

It is said: The grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyya) have differed about the meaning of its occurrence in this place.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: "Min" enters in this place without any meaning, as the Arabs use it in their saying: "There was (min) rain," and "There was (min) talk." He said: Among this is His saying: "And He will remove from you (min) your misdeeds" [Q. 2:271], and His saying: "And He sends down from the sky (min) mountains (of hail) in which is (min) hail" [Q. 24:43]. He said: The sense of it, as it has been explained, is: "And He sends down from the sky mountains in which is hail." He said: Some of them said: "And He sends down from the sky (min) mountains in which is (min) hail," meaning: from the sky (min) hail, by making the "mountains of hail" to be in the sky, and by making the sending down to be from them.

* *
