They were brought to the Prophet ﷺ, and he cut off their hands and feet and branded (samal) their eyes [["samal 'aynahu": he gouged them out with a heated iron, or with a thorn, or something similar. He did this to them only because they had done the same to the shepherds, so he repaid them in kind for their deed.]], and left them in al-Harrah until they died [["al-Harrah" (with a fatha on the ha'): land of black, cracked stones, as if burned by fire. The city of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lies between two harrahs.]]. It was related to us that this verse was revealed concerning them: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger."

11809 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Rawh narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Abi 'Abd Allah narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet ﷺ, with the like of this account. [[The two narrations 11808 and 11809: "Rawh ibn 'Ubadah al-Qaysi," trustworthy, from whom the authors of the six canonical books related. Previously mentioned under nos. 3015, 3355, 3912. In the second narration, "Hisham ibn Abi 'Abd Allah" is "al-Dastawa'i."
This is a sound report, related by Ahmad through several chains in his Musnad 3: 163, by way of Ma'mar from Qatadah; 170, by way of Sa'id from Qatadah; 233, by way of Sa'id also; 287, by way of Hammad from Qatadah; and 290, by way of 'Affan from Qatadah. It was related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (al-Fath 7: 351) by way of 'Abd al-A'la ibn Hammad, from Yazid ibn Zuray', from Sa'id, with the like of it. Muslim pointed to it in his Sahih 11: 157. Abu Dawud in his Sunan 4: 186, no. 4368, by way of Hisham from Qatadah; al-Nasa'i in his Sunan through several chains 7: 97; and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan 8: 62.]]

11810 - Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqiq narrated to us, saying: I heard my father say: Abu Hamzah informed us, from 'Abd al-Karim, and he was asked about camel urine, and he said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated to me concerning the muharibun, saying: Some people came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "We pledge to you upon Islam!" They pledged to him, but they were liars, and they did not want Islam. Then they said: "We find Medina unhealthy!" [["ijtawa al-ard wa al-balad": when one dislikes staying in a place, even if it agrees with his body. It is said: "al-ijtiwa'" is not to digest food and drink in the land, but when you love to stay there and its food does not agree with you, you are "mustawbil" (one for whom it is unhealthy), not "mujtawi." It is said in explaining the hadith of the 'Uranites that they were afflicted with "al-jawa," which is illness and internal disease when it lingers.]] The Prophet ﷺ said: "These milch camels will go out to you and come back, [["al-laqah" (with a kasra on the lam), plural of "laqhah" (kasra then sukun), meaning milch camels.]] so drink from their urine and milk." He said: While they were in that state, the cry (al-sarikh) came, and he cried out to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ [["al-sarikh" and "al-sarikh": one who seeks help. His words "sarikha ila rasul Allah" seem to mean: his plea reached the Messenger of Allah. This is an expression rarely found in the references, so I have noted it.]], saying: "They killed the shepherd and drove off the camels!" So the Prophet of Allah commanded, and it was proclaimed among the people: "O horsemen of Allah, mount!" [[Ibn al-Athir said: "This is by elision of the modifier; he meant: O cavalry of the horses of Allah, mount! This is among the finest and most subtle figures of speech." It occurs in the revelation: "And incite against them with your horse and your foot," meaning with your cavalry and your infantry.]] He said: So they mounted, and no horseman waited for another horseman. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ rode after their tracks, and they continued pursuing them until they brought them into their place of safety. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned, having taken some of them captive, and brought them to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah revealed: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger," the verse. He said: Their banishment was that they were exiled until they were brought into their place of safety and their land, and they were expelled from the land of the Muslims. The Prophet of Allah killed some of them, crucified some, cut off hands and feet, and branded their eyes. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had not mutilated before, nor after. He said: He forbade mutilation (muthlah) and said: "Do not mutilate anything." He said: Anas ibn Malik used to say that, except that he said: "He burned them with fire after he had killed them." [[Narration: 11810 - "Abu Hamzah" is "Maymun, Abu Hamzah al-A'war al-Qassab," very weak, already mentioned under no. 6190.
"'Abd al-Karim" is "'Abd al-Karim ibn Malik al-Jazari," Abu Sa'id, trustworthy, related by the group, already mentioned under no. 892.]]
* *
He said: Some say they were people from Banu Sulaym, and among them from 'Uraynah, and some people from Bajilah.

[Those who said that:]
11811 - Muhammad ibn Khalaf narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan ibn Hammad narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Hashim, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, from Jarir, who said: A group from 'Uraynah came to the Prophet ﷺ, barefoot and afflicted, [["al-madrur" and "al-darir": the sick, emaciated person struck by harm.]] so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave orders concerning them. [[By his words "he gave orders concerning them," he means: he ordered that they be treated for their illness and that their condition be cared for.]] When they became healthy and strong, they killed the shepherds of the milch camels [["al-ru'a'" and "al-ru'ah": plural of "ra'in" (shepherd).]], then went out with the milch camels, intending to take them to the land of their people. Jarir said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me with a company of Muslims until we overtook them after they had reached the lands of their people, and we brought them to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides, branded their eyes, and they began saying: "Water!" while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Fire!" until they died. He said: Allah, mighty and majestic, disliked the branding of eyes, so He revealed this verse: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger," to the end of the verse. [[Narration: 11811 - "Muhammad ibn Khalaf ibn 'Ammar al-'Asqalani," the teacher of al-Tabari, already mentioned under nos. 126, 6534.
"al-Hasan ibn Hammad ibn Kasib al-Hadrami," known as "Sajjadah." He related from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Umawi, Abu Khalid al-Ahmar, Abu Malik al-Janbi, Waki', and others. Related from him Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and others. Trustworthy. Ahmad said: "A man of the Sunnah; I have not heard of him except good." He died in 241. In the printed edition it was "al-Hasan ibn Hannad," an error; the correct reading is in the manuscript and in Tafsir Ibn Kathir.
"'Amr ibn Hashim" is "Abu Malik al-Janbi," truthful but makes errors, weak in memory. Already mentioned under no. 1530.
"Musa ibn 'Ubaydah ibn Nashit al-Rabadhi," very weak; Ahmad said: "The narration from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah is not lawful for me to relate." Already mentioned under nos. 1875, 3291, 8361, 11134. In the printed edition and manuscript it was "Musa ibn 'Ubayd," which is an error; the correct form is from Tafsir Ibn Kathir.
As for "Muhammad ibn Ibrahim," he is apparently "Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith ibn Khalid al-Taymi," who saw Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and related with mursal narrations from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. I do not know whether he heard from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah or not. Jarir died in 51.
This report is very weak, and it is also not sound, because Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, the Companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, came to the Prophet ﷺ in the year he died, whereas the incident of the 'Uraynites was in Shawwal of the sixth year according to the narration of al-Waqidi (Ibn Sa'd 2/1/67), and the leader of the expedition was Kurz ibn Jabir al-Fihri. That was years before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died in Rabi' al-Awwal of the eleventh year after the Hijrah.
This report was mentioned by the hafiz Ibn Hajar in the biography of "Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali," and he declared it very weak. As for Ibn Kathir, he mentioned it in his Tafsir 3: 139, and said: "This is a strange hadith, and in its chain is al-Rabadhi, who is weak. And in its chain there is a benefit: the mention of the leader of this expedition, who is Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali. It was stated in Sahih Muslim that this expedition consisted of twenty horsemen from the Ansar. As for his words, 'Allah disliked the branding of eyes,' it is objectionable. It was mentioned in Sahih Muslim that they branded the eyes of the shepherds, so what was done to them was retribution, and Allah knows best." 
I wonder at Ibn Kathir: he thinks there is a benefit in what has no benefit, for the leader of this expedition was, without doubt, Kurz ibn Jabir al-Fihri, and no one has related that its leader was Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, except in this objectionable report.]]

11812 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Lahi'ah informed me, from Abu al-Aswad Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr= (transition) And Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Yahya ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Salim informed me, and Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and Ibn Sam'an, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, who said: Some people from 'Uraynah raided the milch camels of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, drove them off, and killed a boy of his who was with them, so he sent in their pursuit, they were seized, and he cut off their hands and feet and branded their eyes. [[Narration: 11812 - "Abu al-Aswad," "Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Nawfal al-Asadi," is "the orphan of 'Urwah," trustworthy. Previously mentioned under nos. 2891, 11510.
"Yahya ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Salim ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab," trustworthy, sound in narration. Biography in al-Tahdhib.
"Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Humayl al-Jumahi," judge of Baghdad. Trustworthy; Ahmad said: "There is nothing wrong with him, and his narrations are close." Ibn Abi 'Adi said: "He has strange good narrations, and I hope they are sound, but he errs in one thing after another, raising mawquf reports and connecting mursal ones, not by deliberate intent." Biography in al-Tahdhib.
"Ibn Sam'an" is "'Abd Allah ibn Sulayman ibn Sam'an al-Makhzumi," weak and a liar. Malik was asked about him and said: "A liar." Hisham ibn 'Urwah (from whom this report is related here) said: "He related hadiths from me, but by God, I did not relate them to him, and he lied about me." They agreed that his hadith should not be written, as al-Nasa'i said. Ibn 'Adi said: "The people who related most from him are Ibn Wahb, and the weakness of his hadiths and narrations is evident." As for Ibn Wahb, the transmitter from him here, Ahmad ibn Salih asked him about him, saying: "What did Malik say about Ibn Sam'an?" He said: "One does not accept what some say about others."
This report, which al-Tabari related with this chain, is sound, apart from the weakness and abandonment of Ibn Sam'an, and for this reason al-Nasa'i related it in his Sunan 7: 99, 100, giving al-Tabari's chain but omitting the mention of Ibn Sam'an, saying: "Akhbarana Ahmad ibn 'Amr ibn al-Sarh, qala: anba'ana Ibn Wahb, qala: wa akhbarani Yahya ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Salim and Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, and he mentioned another, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr," thus omitting the mention of "Ibn Sam'an," because he is abandoned in his view.
This report has also been related through other sound chains traced to 'A'ishah. See al-Nasa'i's Sunan 7: 99.]]

11813 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: 'Amr ibn al-Harith informed me, from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal, from Abu al-Zinad, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd Allah, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar= or 'Amr, Yunus doubted=, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, with that, and the verse of hirabah was revealed concerning them. [[Narration: 11813 - "'Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ya'qub al-Ansari al-Misri," trustworthy and a hafiz, already mentioned under nos. 1387, 5973, 6889.
"Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal al-Laythi al-Misri," trustworthy, one of the followers of the Successors. Already mentioned under nos. 1495, 5465. "Abu al-Zinad" is "'Abd Allah ibn Dhakwan al-Qurashi." It is said that his father was a brother of Abu Lu'lu'ah, the slayer of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Trustworthy; in Medina after the senior Successors, there was no one more knowledgeable than him.
"'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab." He related from his uncle 'Abd Allah, and Abu al-Zinad related from him. Trustworthy. Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i related one hadith from him, which is this hadith.
In the manuscript and the printed edition it was "'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah," which is a plain error.
As for Yunus's doubt over whether it was "'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab" or "'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As," that doubt has no standing. The correct reading is "'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab."
This hadith was related by Abu Dawud in his Sunan 4: 186-187, no. 4369, in full. Al-Nasa'i related it in his Sunan 7: 100 with the same wording as Abu Ja'far's narration.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 33 (part 2 of 5):

11814 - Ali ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: al-Awza'i narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Abu Qilabah, from Anas, who said: Eight men of 'Ukl came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and embraced Islam. Then they found Madinah unhealthy for them (ijtawu al-Madinah), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered them to go to the camels of the charity (ibil al-sadaqah) and drink from their urine and milk.
They did so, killed their herdsmen, and drove off the camels. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent after them a qafah [["al-qafah" is the plural of "qa'if": one who recognizes footprints and follows them. "qaf al-athar yaqufuhu qiyafah, wa-iqtafahu iqtiyafan".]] and they were brought back. He cut off their hands and feet, [["hasama al-dam yahsimuhu hasman": that is, staunched it by cauterizing with fire.]] and left them without cauterizing, until they died. [[Note on the report: Ahmad transmitted this report in the Musnad of Anas, through the chain of Yahya ibn Abi Kathir from Abu Qilabah al-Jarmi, 3:198, through the same route of Abu Ja'far, and in it: "they killed its herdsmen, or its shepherds," and in it an addition: "and he did not cauterize them until they died, and he blinded their eyes."
Al-Bukhari transmitted it in his Sahih through the route of Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah (al-Fath 1:289/6:108/7:352/12:99), and he also transmitted it through the route of Abu Raja' the client of Abu Qilabah, from Anas (al-Fath 8:206), and al-Hafiz completed the discussion in its explanation and clarification.
Muslim transmitted it in his Sahih through several routes, 11:153-157.
Abu Dawud transmitted it in his Sunan 1:185, 186 through several routes.
al-Nasa'i transmitted it in his Sunan through several routes, 7:93-95.]]
11815 - Ali narrated to us, saying: al-Walid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to me, from Qatadah, from Anas, who said: They were four men from 'Urayna and three from 'Ukl. When they were brought, he cut off their hands and feet, blinded their eyes, did not cauterize them, and left them to chew stones in al-Harrah, [["yatalaqqamun al-hijarah": that is, they put stones in their mouths from thirst, so that saliva would flow. It is explained in other wordings of the hadith. Anas said: "I saw one of them gnawing the ground with his mouth from thirst." It is said: "laqama al-ta'am, wa-talaqqamahu, wa-iltaqamahu".]] so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed concerning that: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger..." the verse. [[Note: See the two preceding reports, nos. 11808 and 11809.]]
11816 - Ali narrated to me, saying: al-Walid narrated to us, from Ibn Lahi'ah, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib: that Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan wrote to Anas asking him about this verse, and Anas wrote to him informing him that this verse was revealed concerning those men of 'Urayna, who were from Bajilah. Anas said: They apostatized from Islam, killed the herdsman, drove off the camels, terrorized the road, and committed unlawful sexual intercourse. [[Note: See Sunan al-Nasa'i 7:98, and the words of Commander of the Faithful Abd al-Malik to Anas while he related to him the hadith of the 'Urayniyyin: "For disbelief or for a sin?" and Anas said: "For disbelief." This report will come later in full, with Abu Ja'far's remark on it, and its takhrij there under no. 11854.]]
11817 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption...": he said: It was revealed concerning the black men of 'Urayna. He said: They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and had the yellow disease (al-ma' al-asfar), so they complained of that to him. He ordered them to go out to the camels of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the charity, and said: Drink from their milk and urine! So they drank from their milk and urine, until when they recovered and were healed, they killed the herdsmen and drove off the camels.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The most preferable of the sayings concerning this, in my view, is to say: Allah revealed this verse to His Prophet (ﷺ), informing him of His ruling on those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption, after what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did to the 'Urayniyyin, what he did.
We only said this is the most preferable of sayings regarding the truth, because the narratives which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related before this verse and after it are from the stories and reports of the Children of Israel, so that this should come in between, [["mutawassitan", in the accusative as a circumstantial state.]] from the explanation of the ruling concerning them and their counterparts, is more fitting and more appropriate.
And we said: the revelation of that was after what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did to the 'Urayniyyin, because of the widespread reports from the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that.
* *
Since that is more fitting for the verse for the reason we described, its interpretation is: For this reason We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, other than for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is as if he had killed all mankind, and whoever gives life to it, it is as if he had given life to all mankind. And indeed Our messengers came to them with clear proofs; then indeed many of them after that upon the earth are transgressors. He says: they are striving upon the earth with corruption, killing souls without a soul, and other than striving upon the earth with corruption, waging war against Allah and His Messenger. So whoever of them does that, O Muhammad, his penalty is only that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land.
* *
If someone says to us: How is it permissible for the verse to have been revealed in the circumstance you mentioned, from the situation of a disbelieving man of the Children of Israel breaking his covenant? And from your saying that the ruling of this verse is a ruling from Allah concerning the people of Islam, [["wa-min qawlika", the waw is the waw of the circumstantial state; meaning: how is that permissible when you say such and such.]] to the exclusion of the people of war among the polytheists?
It is said: That may be so, because the ruling on whoever wages war against Allah and His Messenger and strives upon the earth in corruption is one for the people of our dhimmah and our religious community. Those referred to by the verse were people of covenant and dhimmah, although every dhimmi and member of our community is included in its ruling, and it does not invalidate the validity of its revelation concerning those it was revealed about that people from among mankind entered under its ruling.
* *
The scholars differed concerning the abrogation (naskh) of the Prophet's (ﷺ) ruling regarding the 'Urayniyyin.
Some of them said: That is an abrogated ruling, abrogated by his prohibition of mutilation (al-muthlah) through this verse, meaning by His saying: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption..." the verse. And they said: This verse was revealed as a rebuke to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he did to the 'Urayniyyin.
* *
Others said: Rather, the act of the Prophet (ﷺ) toward the 'Urayniyyin is a ruling established for their counterparts forever, not abrogated and not changed. And His saying: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger" the verse, is a ruling from Allah concerning whoever wages war and strives upon the earth in corruption by hirabah. ["al-hirabah" (with a kasrah on the ha') is a verbal noun like "al-'ibadah", "al-ri'ayah", "al-tijarah", meaning: "waging war against Allah and His Messenger, and striving upon the earth in corruption". It is a verbal noun from their saying "harabahu", meaning he plundered him, took his property and left him with nothing. It is not the verbal noun of "harib", for the verbal noun of that is "muharabah wa-hirab", like "qatala muqatalah wa-qitalan". This word, despite its frequent occurrence in the books of the imams, is not mentioned in the books of lexicography; it seems they took it as used by jurists, and the linguistic transmission did not bring it. It is, God willing, a correct Arabic formation.]]
They said: The 'Urayniyyin apostatized, killed, stole, and waged war against Allah and His Messenger, so their ruling is other than the ruling for the one who wages war and strives upon the earth in corruption from among the people of Islam or dhimmah. [["al-Islam wa-l-dhimmah" in the printed edition; I have kept what is in the manuscript.]]
* *
Others said: The Prophet (ﷺ) did not blind the 'Urayniyyin, but he had intended to blind them, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse to His Prophet, informing him of the ruling concerning them, and forbade him from blinding their eyes.
Mention of those who said what we have described:
11818 - Ali ibn Sahl narrated to me, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: I discussed with al-Layth ibn Sa'd what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did in blinding their eyes and his leaving them uncauterized until they died. He said: I heard Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan say: This verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rebuking him for that, and taught him the punishment for their like: cutting, killing, and banishment, and he did not blind anyone after them. He said: This statement was mentioned to Abu 'Amr, ["Abu 'Amr" means al-Awza'i.] and he denied that it was revealed as a rebuke, and said: Rather, it was the punishment of those particular men, and then this verse was revealed concerning the punishment of others who waged war after them, and blinding was lifted from them.
11819 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to me, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for them, and they were brought — meaning the 'Urayniyyin — and he wanted to blind their eyes, but Allah forbade him from that, and commanded him to establish the prescribed punishments upon them as Allah had revealed them to him. [[See the disagreement on the abrogation of this verse in al-Nahhas's "al-Nasikh wa-l-mansukh": 123-128, which is an important section.]]
* *
The scholars differed over who deserves the title "one who wages war against Allah and His Messenger", upon whom the ruling of this verse is binding. Some of them said: He is the highwayman who cuts the road.
Mention of those who said that:
11820 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah and 'Ata' al-Khurasani concerning His saying: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption..." the verse, the two of them said: This is the highwayman who cuts the road, [["hadha huwa al-lis" in the printed edition is an addition with no benefit; he added it from himself.]] so he is a muharib.
* *
Others said: He is the thief who openly displays his thievery, the one who overpowers others in a city and elsewhere. [[In the manuscript: "al-mukathir" with a thaa'; the correct reading is that of the printed edition: "kabarahu 'ala haqqih" means he denied him his right and overpowered him over it. "Innahu la-mukabir 'alayh" means when he took it from him by force and coercion. It occurs frequently in al-Shafi'i's Kitab al-Umm in this section of jurisprudence. See al-Umm 6:140, and elsewhere.]]
Among those who said that was al-Awza'i.
11821 - al-'Abbas narrated to us with that, from his father, from him. [[Report 11821: "al-'Abbas" means al-'Abbas ibn al-Walid ibn Mazid al-'Udhri al-Amili al-Bayruti, teacher of Abu Ja'far, passed as no. 891.
And his father: al-Walid ibn Mazid al-'Udhri al-Bayruti. He narrated from al-Awza'i, and his son al-'Abbas narrated from him. It is reported from al-Awza'i that he said: "No book was presented to me more sound than the books of al-Walid ibn Mazid." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.
In the manuscript here it reads: "al-'Abbas narrated to us with that, from his father, and from him, from Malik and al-Layth ...", which is undoubtedly an error, for al-Walid ibn Mazid is not recorded as transmitting from Malik, al-Layth or Ibn Lahi'ah. Those who transmitted from them was al-Walid ibn Muslim, mentioned in the following reports. For this reason part of what is in the printed edition is correct, and I corrected what it omitted. In the printed edition: "... from his father, from him and from Malik ...", which I made "and from him, and from Malik ..." because he will narrate in this regard the saying of al-Awza'i also through the route of al-Walid ibn Muslim, no. 11824, as will come. The sentence is thereby sound.]]
* *
=And from him, and from Malik, and al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and Ibn Lahi'ah.
11822 - Ali ibn Sahl narrated to me, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: I said to Malik ibn Anas: Does hirabah occur in a city? He said: Yes, and the muharib according to us is one who bears arms against Muslims in a city or in the open, and that was from him not due to any strife between them, nor vengeance, nor enmity, ["al-nair'ah": a strife arising from enmity and rancor; "nar al-harb" and "nair'atuha" mean its evil and its agitation. "al-dhahl" is vengeance.] cutting off the road, the path, and the dwellings, terrifying them with his weapon, so that he kills one of them: the imam kills him as the killing of the muharib, [["kaqatlat al-muharib", in the printed edition and the manuscript; the manuscript is unpointed, so this is the correct reading. "al-qitlah" is the manner of killing.] with no pardon or retaliation (qawad) for the guardian of the slain.
11823 - Ali narrated to me, saying: al-Walid narrated to us, saying: I also asked al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Ibn Lahi'ah about that. I said: Does hirabah occur in the houses of a city, the cities and the villages? They said: Yes, when they enter upon them with swords openly, or at night with fires. I said: So if they killed, or took property without killing? He said: Yes, they are the muharibun. If they kill, they are killed; if they do not kill but take property, they are cut off from opposite sides when they leave the house with it. Is one who wages war against Muslims in the open and on the road any more a muharib than one who wages war against them in their sanctuaries and their houses? [[The word "I said" here is not in the manuscript; the first editor added it, and he did well.]]
11824 - Ali narrated to me, saying: al-Walid narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Amr said: [["al-Walid ibn Muslim" and "Abu 'Amr" is al-Awza'i; see the earlier note p. 254, no. 3.] And hirabah occurs in a city, when one brandishes his weapon against its people by night or by day. Ali said, al-Walid said: Malik also informed me that the killing by ghilah is equivalent to hirabah according to him. I said: And what is qatl al-ghilah? He said: It is a man who deceives a man or a boy, leads him into a house or isolates him, then kills him and takes his property. The imam is the guardian of the killing of this one, and the guardian of the blood and the wound has no qawad or retaliation.
* *
=And this is the saying of al-Shafi'i.
11825 - Al-Rabi' narrated to us with that from him.
* *
Others said: "The muharib" is the highwayman. As for "the mukabir in the cities," he is not the muharib who has the ruling of the muharibun. Abu Hanifah and his companions said so.
11826 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, who said: We discussed the muharib while we were with Ibn Hubayrah, among people of Basra, and their opinion agreed that the muharib is one who goes out of the city.
* *
Mujahid said:
11827 - al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Juraj, from Mujahid concerning His saying: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption..." he said: Fornication, theft, killing people, and destroying crops and offspring.
11828 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Anbasah, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid: "and strive upon the earth in corruption" he said: "corruption" is killing, fornication, and theft.
The most preferable of these sayings to me as correct is the saying of the one who said: "The muharib against Allah and His Messenger" is one who wages war on the roads of the Muslims and their dhimmis, and who raids them in their cities and villages as hirabah. [[See what I said on "hirabah" above, p. 252, note 2.]]
That is the most preferable of sayings as correct, because there is no disagreement among the authorities that whoever sets up war against the Muslims through injustice toward them is a muharib against them, and there is no dispute on this. Whoever has the description we have described, there is no doubt that he has set up war against them unjustly. Since that is so, whether his setting up war against them is in their cities and villages or on their roads and paths, he is a muharib against Allah and His Messenger, by waging war against the one whom Allah and His Messenger forbade to be warred against.
* *
As for His saying: "and strive upon the earth in corruption," it means: they work in the land of Allah with sins: by terrifying the roads of His believing servants or the roads of their dhimmis, cutting their paths, taking their property unjustly and aggressively, and attacking their sanctity with immorality and wickedness. [[See the explanation of "corruption in the earth" above, p. 232, note 2, and the references there.]]
* *
Concerning the interpretation of His words, Mighty is His mention: ﴿That they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land﴾
Abu Ja'far said: He, may His mention be exalted, says: For the one who wages war against Allah and His Messenger and strives upon the earth in corruption, from among the people of the religion of Islam or their dhimmis, there is nothing but some of these characteristics which He, may His praise be exalted, mentioned.
* *
Then the people of interpretation differed about these characteristics: are they binding upon the muharib by virtue of his deserving the title "hirabah", or is what is binding on him from that according to the measure of his crime, varying with the variation of his crimes?

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 33 (part 3 of 5):**

[Some of them said: the one who wages war (*muharib*, a highway brigand) must receive a punishment proportionate to his deserving, and he is obliged to bear what is due from that in proportion to his crime, varying with the variation of his crimes.] [[The addition between the brackets is necessary, for Abu Ja'far will mention this view and the other view on the matter in which they differed. It is his custom to introduce each view the scholars held with a heading stating their view. The heading for this section has dropped out, so I have reconstructed it from his earlier question, from the meaning of the reports that follow, and from Abu Ja'far's preference between these two interpretations later on, p. 264. The scribe apparently erred, the end of one sentence became confused with the end of another, and the heading was omitted.]]

Mention of those who said this:

11829 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his words: ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger...﴾ up to his words ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾. He said: If he wages war and kills, then he is to be killed if he is overpowered before he repents. [["Overpowered" (in the passive): that is, he was defeated and seized.] If he wages war, takes property and kills, then he is to be crucified if he is overpowered before he repents. If he wages war, takes property, but does not kill, then the hand and foot are to be cut off on opposite sides if he is overpowered before he repents. If he wages war and terrorises the road, then he is only to be exiled.

11830 - Ibn Wakī' and Abu al-Sā'ib related to us, both saying: Ibn Idris related to us, from his father, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, regarding ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger...﴾ He said: If he goes out, terrorises the road and takes property, his hand and foot are cut off on opposite sides. If he terrorises the road, does not take property, but kills, he is crucified.

11831 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, I think, concerning a man who goes out as a brigand. He said: If he cuts the road and takes property, his hand and foot are cut off. If he takes property and kills, he is killed. If he takes property, kills and mutilates, he is crucified.

He said: If he kills, takes property and terrorises the road, he is crucified. If he kills and does not exceed that, he is killed. If he takes property and does not exceed that, it is cut off. If he only causes corruption, he is exiled.

He said: If he terrorises the road but does not kill and does not take property, he is exiled.

As for one who commits both bloodshed and theft, he is crucified. As for one who commits bloodshed but refrains from taking property, he is killed. One who takes property but refrains from bloodshed has his hand cut off. One who commits neither of these is exiled.

He looked at the one who had killed but not taken property, and killed him. He looked at the one who had taken property and killed, and crucified him. Likewise, it is required for everyone who terrorises the road of the Muslims and commits highway robbery, to be dealt with thus if he is seized: if he has taken property, his hand is cut off for taking property and his foot for terrorising the road; if he has killed but not taken property, he is killed; if he has killed and taken property, he is crucified.

[[His words "exile by the sword" mean that he is pursued until he leaves the land, until they reach their place of safety and their land, as has already passed in report no. 11810.] If he takes property, his hand is for the property and his foot for what he did to terrify the Muslims. He said: This is the thief who cuts the road, and he is a brigand. If he kills and takes property, he is crucified. If he kills and does not take property, he is killed. If he takes property and does not kill, his hand and foot are cut off. [[In the manuscript: "If he kills and does not take property and does not kill, his hand and foot are cut off," which is a pure error; its correct form is what is in the printed edition, beyond doubt.] If he is seized before doing any of that, he is exiled.

Whoever kills but does not acquire property, is killed as he killed. Whoever acquires property but does not kill, has his hand cut off on opposite sides. And if he terrorises the road of the Muslims, he is exiled from his land to another, according to the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾.

Others waged war and seized property but did not exceed that, so their hands and feet were cut off. Others waged war and withdrew, and did not exceed that, and those were expelled from the land.

11841 - Hannad related to us, saying: Abu Usamah related to us, from Abu Hilal, saying: Qatadah related to us, from Muwarriq al-'Ijli, concerning the brigand, who said: If he went out, killed and took property, he is crucified. If he killed and did not take property, he is killed. If he took property and did not kill, he is cut off. If he went out opposing the Muslims, he is exiled.

11842 - Hannad related to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from Hajjaj, from 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the brigand goes out, terrorises the road and takes property, his hand and foot are cut off on opposite sides. If he goes out, kills and takes property, his hand and foot are cut off on opposite sides, and then he is crucified. If he goes out and kills but does not take property, he is killed. If he terrorises the road, does not kill and does not take property, he is exiled.

11843 - Ibn al-Barqi related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Maryam related to us, saying: Nafi' ibn Yazid informed us, saying: Abu Sakhr related to me, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi= and from Abu Mu'awiyah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding this verse ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive in the land to cause corruption﴾. Both said: If he terrorises the Muslims and seizes property without shedding blood, he is cut off. [[In the printed edition: "fa-iqtata'a al-mal," and I have kept what is in the manuscript; they have the same meaning.] If he sheds blood, he is killed and crucified. If he combines both, seizing property and shedding blood, he is cut off, then killed, then crucified, as if crucifixion were mutilation, and as if the cutting were the words: ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands﴾, [[In the manuscript: "wa-kāna al-sāriq wa-al-sāriqah...," and the correct form is what is in the printed edition. This and what follows is an incorporation of the two verses on the two judgements: on theft and on the killing of a soul.] and as if the killing were the words: ﴿a life for a life﴾. If he refuses, then it is the duty of the imam and of the Muslims to pursue him until they seize him, and then to enforce upon him the judgement of the Book of Allah: ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾, from the land of Islam to the land of disbelief.

Abu Ja'far said: The proponents of this view argued for their position by saying: Allah has made retaliation (*qawad*) obligatory for the killer and amputation obligatory for the thief. They said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except by one of three things: a man who kills and is killed in retaliation, a man who commits adultery after being married and is stoned, and a man who apostatises after his Islam." [[This is a sound hadith, agreed upon in meaning. He related it without its chain. See Muslim 11: 164, 165.] They said: So the Prophet ﷺ prohibited the killing of a Muslim man except by one of these three things. As for killing someone merely for terrorising the road, without his having killed or taken property, that is an advancing ahead of Allah and His Messenger, a contradiction of them both regarding the ruling. They said: The meaning of the words of the one who said: "The imam has the choice regarding him when he kills, terrorises the road and takes property" is that the imam's choice, in their view, lies between killing, or killing and crucifixion, or cutting off the hand and foot on opposite sides. As for crucifying him in the name of waging war, without his having done anything of killing or taking property, that is something no scholar has said.

* *

Others said: The imam has a choice in the matter: he may do whichever of these things Allah mentioned in His Book.

Mention of those who said this:

11844 - Ya'qub related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Jawaybir informed us, from 'Ata' [[and from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid], regarding the brigand: the imam has the choice in his case, whichever he wishes he may do.

11845 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, from 'Ubaydah, from Ibrahim: The imam has the choice regarding the brigand, whichever he wishes he may do. If he wishes he may kill, if he wishes he may cut off, if he wishes he may exile, if he wishes he may crucify.

11846 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from 'Asim, from al-Hasan, regarding his words ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger...﴾ up to his words ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾. He said: The imam takes whichever of them he likes.

11847 - Sufyan related to us, saying: my father related to us, from Sufyan, from 'Asim, from al-Hasan: ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger...﴾ He said: The imam has the choice among them.

11848 - Ibn Wakī' related to us, saying: my father related to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Juraj, from 'Ata', the same.

11849 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Qays ibn Sa'd, who said: 'Ata' said: The imam does in this whatever he wills. If he wills he kills, or cuts off, or exiles, according to the words of Allah: ﴿that they be killed or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be exiled from the land﴾. That is up to the ruling imam; he does with it whatever he wills.

11850 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Abd Allah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding his words ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger...﴾, the verse. He said: Whoever draws a weapon in the dome of Islam [[In the printed edition: "in the fi'ah (faction) of Islam," which has no meaning; the manuscript is undotted and was misread. The correct reading is what I have read, "qubbat al-Islam," meaning under its shade and where its authority is established. That is why they called Basra "the dome of Islam." The poet said: "Qays built the dome of Islam for its people, and had they not raised it, its shelter would have been long in coming undone." The root "qubbah" means a round tent of leather. This is like their saying "dar al-Islam" in the sense I have explained.] and terrorises the road, and then is overpowered and seized, the imam of the Muslims has the choice regarding him: if he wishes he kills him, if he wishes he crucifies him, if he wishes he cuts off his hand and foot.

11851 - Hannad related to us, saying: Abu Usamah related to us, saying: Abu Hilal informed us, saying: Qatadah informed us, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that he said regarding the brigand: That is up to the imam; when he seizes him, he does with him whatever he wills.

11852 - Hannad related to us, saying: Abu Usamah related to us, from Abu Hilal, who said: Harun related to us, from al-Hasan regarding the brigand, who said: That is up to the imam; he does with him whatever he wills.

11853 - Hannad related to us, saying: Hafs ibn Ghiyath related to us, from 'Asim, from al-Hasan: ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger...﴾, He said: That is up to the imam.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The proponents of this view argued by saying: We found that the conjunction "aw" (or), when used in the Qur'an to link obligations that Allah imposed as a religious duty, carries the sense of choice. An example is His words regarding the expiation for an oath: ﴿Its expiation is the feeding of ten needy persons, from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 89]; and His words: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom of fasting or charity or sacrifice﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 196]; and His words: ﴿Then the penalty is the like of what he killed of the cattle, judged by two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah, or an expiation of feeding the needy, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 95]. They said: Since the conjunction "aw" throughout the Qur'an, in every obligation Allah imposed as a duty, carries the sense of choice, then likewise in the verse about the brigands: the imam has a choice regarding what he sees fit to impose on the brigand when he is seized before repentance.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation most correct in our view is the interpretation of the one who holds that the brigand's punishment is proportionate to his deserving, and that the ruling concerning brigands varies with their actions. He obligates, for the one of them who terrorises the road, when he is seized before repentance and before taking property or killing, exile from the land. And when he is seized after taking property and killing a soul whose killing is forbidden, crucifixion, for the reason I mentioned earlier against the proponents of that view.

* *

As for the argument of those who said the imam has the choice in this matter, that "aw" in coordination carries the sense of choice in an obligation, that is a view with no meaning, [[In the printed edition: "fa-naqūlu: lā ma'nā lahu" ("so we say: it has no meaning"). That is a feeble sentence; the correct text is what is in the manuscript.] because "aw" in the speech of the Arabs comes with various meanings. Were it not for disliking to lengthen the book by mentioning them, I would have mentioned them. I have already explained many of its meanings above, and I will cover the rest where they occur hereafter, God willing. [[See what has passed: 1: 336, 337; 2: 235-237; 4: 75, 76; 6: 513; 7: 194.]]

= As for in this place, its meaning is sequence (*ta'qib*, i.e., alternatives in sequence, one after another according to the case), and that is like the statement of one who says: "The reward of the believers with God on the Day of Resurrection is that He admits them to Paradise, or raises their ranks in the Illiyyun, or settles them with the prophets and the truthful." It is known that the speaker of that does not intend that the reward of every believer who believed in Allah and His Messenger is one and the same of these ranks and one and the same of these stations by his faith. Rather, what is understood from him is that the reward of the believer will not be free, with God, Mighty is His remembrance, of some of these stations. So the moderate one's station is below the station of the one who is foremost in good deeds, and the one who is foremost in good deeds is higher in station, and the one who wrongs himself is below both, [[Read the verse, Surah Fatir: 32: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from Our servants; of them is one who wrongs himself, and of them is one who is moderate, and of them is one who is foremost in good deeds, by Allah's permission. That is the great bounty.﴾]] and all of them are in Paradise, as He, whose praise is majestic, said: ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter﴾ [Surah Fatir: 33]. Likewise, the meaning of "aw" in His words "Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger", the verse, is only sequence.

**Its interpretation:** The one who wages war against Allah and His Messenger and strives on earth to cause corruption cannot escape deserving the punishment by one of these four categories that Allah, mighty is His remembrance, has mentioned. It is not that the ruler (al-imam) has discretion in the matter and may choose freely, whatever the state of the offender, whether his crime is grave or light. [Printed edition: "wa-'azhamat" with a waw, which has no place here.] For if that were so, the ruler could kill someone who brandishes a weapon to terrify the road and crucify him, even if he has taken no property and killed no one, and he could banish one who has killed, taken property, and terrorised the road. That is a view which, if anyone held it, would contradict what has been authentically transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: a man who kills a man, so he is killed for it; or one who commits adultery after having been married, so he is stoned; or one who apostatises from his religion." [See the takhrij of this report earlier, p. 261, note 3.] It would also contradict his words: "Amputation is for a quarter dinar and above," [This report is agreed upon in the authentic collections; see Fath al-Bari 12:89–91, and its takhrij will follow under no. 11912.] and it would contradict the rulings that are not known.

* *

If someone says: "These rulings you have mentioned were from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning someone other than the muharib (the one who wages war), and the muharib has a separate ruling distinct from them."

It is said to him: "Then what is the ruling that is specific to the muharib in the Sunnah?"

If he claims a ruling from him ﷺ different from what we have mentioned, all the scholars will refute him, because that is not established by the transmission of a single narrator or of a group.

If he asserts that this ruling is what appears in the apparent meaning of the Book, it is said to him: "At best, even if it is granted to you, the apparent meaning of the verse may bear what you have said and what your opponent has said. So what is your proof that your interpretation is more deserving than his interpretation of the verse?"

Furthermore, if the ruler has discretion in passing judgment on the muharib because, in your view, "aw" in this context means choice, does he have the right to crucify him while he is alive and leave him on the cross until he dies, without killing him?

If he says, "That is permitted to him," he has opposed the community on this point.

And if he claims that this is not permitted to him, and that he may only kill him and then crucify him, or crucify him and then kill him, he has abandoned his own reason, namely that the ruler has the choice in judging the muharib because "aw" comes to mean choice.

It is said to him: "How then did he have the choice between killing, banishing, or amputation, but not the choice of crucifixion alone, so that another punishment must be added to it? And it is said to him: Is there any difference, by principle or by analogy, between you and the one who grants the choice where you refuse it, and refuses it where you grant it to him?" [The context: "Is there between you and the one who granted the choice... a difference of principle or analogy?"] He will not say anything about one of them except that the other is obliged to the same.

* *

It has been transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in support of what we have said on this matter, something whose chain of transmission is questionable, namely what follows:

11854. Ali ibn Sahl related to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim related to us, from Ibn Lahi'ah, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, that Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan wrote to Anas ibn Malik asking him about this verse. Anas wrote back to him, informing him that this verse was revealed concerning those men of 'Uraynah, who were from Bajilah. Anas said: They apostatised from Islam, killed the shepherd, drove off the camels, terrorised the road, and committed unlawful sexual intercourse. Anas said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked Jibril, upon him be peace, about the judgment concerning one who wages war. He said: "Whoever steals and terrorises the road, cut off his hand for his theft and his foot for his terrorising. Whoever kills, kill him. Whoever kills, terrorises the road, and makes lawful unlawful sexual intercourse, crucify him." [Report 11854: al-Walid ibn Muslim al-Dimashqi al-Qurashi is a trustworthy, meticulous hafiz, one of Ahmad's teachers, whose biography has been mentioned several times before.
Ibn Lahi'ah is Abd Allah ibn Lahi'ah, about whom the scholars have spoken at length. My brother al-Sayyid Ahmad has graded him as trustworthy earlier (nos. 160, 2941), but some say: "His hadith is not to be used as evidence."
Yazid ibn Abi Habib al-Misri is trustworthy, and the collectors all narrated from him; he has appeared earlier (nos. 4348, 5418, 5493).
The defect of this report is the weakness of Ibn Lahi'ah, according to those who consider him weak and reject using his hadith as evidence. Furthermore, Yazid ibn Abi Habib did not meet Anas, and it is not mentioned that he heard from him.
The first part of this report has passed earlier as no. 11816, so see the commentary there. It will come in report 11885 that Yazid ibn Abi Habib's transmission of this report is from Anas ibn Malik's letter to Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan.]

* *

As for His saying: "or their hands and feet be cut off on opposite sides" (aw tuqatta'a aydihim wa-arjuluhum min khilaf), He, mighty is His praise, means by it that their hands are cut off while differing in the cutting from the cutting of their feet. That is, the right hands are cut off and the left feet. Thus "khilaf" (opposition) between them lies in the cutting.

Had the word "min" in this place been "ala" or "bi", so that it said, "or their hands and feet be cut off on opposition" or "by opposition," they would have conveyed the same meaning that "min" conveys.

* *

The interpreters differed over the meaning of "banishment" (nafy) mentioned by Allah in this place.

Some said: It means that he is pursued until he is captured, or flees the territory of Islam.

Those who said this:

11855. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, concerning His words "or be banished from the land": He said: The ruler pursues them with horsemen and men until he seizes them and carries out the judgment against them, or they are banished from the land of the Muslims.

11856. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: His banishment is that he is pursued.

11857. al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abd Allah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas: "or be banished from the land": he says: or they flee until they leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war.

11858. Ali ibn Sahl related to me, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim related to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Lahi'ah informed me, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Anas ibn Malik's letter to Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: that he wrote to him: "As for his banishment, it is that the ruler pursues him until he seizes him; then, when he seizes him, he imposes upon him one of these punishments that Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned, according to what he has made lawful." [Report 11858: see the earlier commentary on report 11854.]

11859. Ali ibn Sahl related to me, saying: al-Walid related to us, saying: I mentioned that to al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and he said: His banishment is his being pursued from town to town until he is seized, or his being pursued drives him out of the abode of Islam to the abode of polytheism and war, if he is a muharib who has apostatised from Islam. Al-Walid said: I asked Malik ibn Anas, and he said the same.

11860. Ali related to me, saying: al-Walid related to us, saying: I said to Malik ibn Anas and al-Layth ibn Sa'd: "Is it likewise that the muharib who remains upon his Islam is pursued, forced by pursuit from town to town until he reaches a frontier of the frontiers of the Muslims, or the furthest boundary (hawz) of the Muslims?" [In the printed edition: "until he reaches a frontier of the frontiers of the Muslims or the furthest neighbourhood of the Muslims," but the correct reading is "hatta" and "aqsa hawz al-muslimin," as in the manuscript. "Al-hawz" (with fatha and sukun) means land that a man takes possession of, marking its boundaries so that he is entitled to it and no one has a right against him in it; that is "hawz." From it comes "hawz al-dar" (the courtyard of the house), and also "hawzat al-Islam," meaning its borders and regions. In a hadith: "He protected the hawzat al-Islam."] "If they pursue him, does he enter the abode of polytheism?" They both said: "A Muslim is not compelled to do that."

11861. Hannad ibn al-Sari related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: "or be banished from the land," he said: That they pursue him until they fail to catch him.

11862. It was related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman related to me, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, and he mentioned something similar.

11863. Ibn Wakī' related to us, saying: Hafs ibn Ghiyath related to us, from Asim, from al-Hasan: "or be banished from the land," he said: He is banished until he cannot be caught.

11864. al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Abd Allah related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, concerning His words "or be banished from the land": He said: They are expelled from the land, wherever they are found they are driven out until they join the land of the enemy.

11865. al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq related to us, saying: Ma'mar related to us, from al-Zuhri, concerning His words "or be banished from the land": He said: His banishment is that he is pursued but not caught; whenever he is heard of in a land, he is pursued.

11866. Ali ibn Sahl related to me, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim related to us, saying: Sa'id informed me, from Qatadah: "or be banished from the land": He said: If he did not kill and did not take property, he is pursued until he is exhausted.

11867. Ibn al-Barqi related to me, saying: Ibn Abi Maryam related to us, saying: Nafi' ibn Yazid informed me, saying: Abu Sakhr related to me, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi; and from Abu Mu'awiyah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "or be banished from the land," from the land of Islam to the land of disbelief.

* *

Others said: The meaning of "banishment" in this place is that when the ruler has seized him, he banishes him from his town to another town other than it.

Those who said this:

11868. al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Qays ibn Sa'd, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "or be banished from the land," he said: Whoever terrorises the road of the Muslims is banished from his town to another, because of the words of Allah, mighty and majestic: "or be banished from the land."

11869. al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: al-Layth related to me, saying: Yazid ibn Abi Habib and others related to me, from Hayyan ibn Surayj: that he wrote to Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz concerning highwaymen, describing their brigandage to him, and that he imprisoned them. He said: Allah said in His Book: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides," and omitted: "or be banished from the land." Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz wrote back to him: "To proceed: You wrote to me mentioning the words of Allah, mighty and majestic: 'Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides,' and you left out the words of Allah: 'or be banished from the land.' Are you a prophet, O Hayyan?! You do not move things from their places. Have you devoted yourself to killing and crucifixion as if you were the slave of the Banu Aqil, [The Arabic "tajarrada li-l-amr" means to strive in it with great exertion and to devote oneself to it fully, as a man strips off his garments to be unhindered. It is said, "So-and-so devoted himself to worship," and al-Akhtal said: "And I extinguished from myself the fire of Nu'man after it had been prepared for a wicked matter and had stripped (tajarrada)." And Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said: "They strip off (tajarradu) and strike their falsehood with the truth until the lie becomes clear."
The correct phrase is "slave of the Banu Abi Aqil," for Abu Aqil is the grandfather of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn al-Hakam ibn Abi Aqil ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Thaqif, the highest ancestor of al-Hajjaj, was, as they say, "Qasy (Thaqif) ibn Munabbih ibn al-Nabit ibn Mansur ibn Yuqdim ibn Afsa ibn Da'mi ibn Iyad ibn Nizar," and it is not as is mentioned in the lineage of Thaqif, that he is from "Mudar ibn Nizar." Thaqif, according to what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, was a slave of the wife of the prophet of Allah Salih, who gave him to Salih, and he is "Abu Righal," whose grave is stoned. Hassan ibn Thabit says in satire of Thaqif (his Diwan: 341–342):
"When the Thaqafi boasts to you, say: 'Come, let us count the mother of Abu Righal.'
Your father is the most wicked of fathers entirely, and you are resembling him in his pattern."
In this poem Hassan claims that Thaqif was a slave of al-Fizr, who is Sa'd ibn Zayd Manat ibn Tamim, and he says:
"The slaves of al-Fizr, he bequeathed them to his sons, and swore not to sell them for wealth.
They were not imprisoned for honour, but the nights desired to humiliate them, the other way."
As for the satire of al-Hajjaj that he is "a slave from Iyad," Malik ibn al-Rayb says (al-Kamil 1:302):
"What will al-Hajjaj reach with his utmost effort, if we pass beyond the Hayr of Ziyad?
Were it not for the sons of Marwan, Ibn Yusuf would have been, as he was, a slave from the slaves of Iyad,
A time when he was the slave who acknowledges humiliation, who goes out and comes back with the boys of the villages."
For al-Hajjaj was a teacher in al-Ta'if, and he was mocked for that. This is the explanation of "slave of the Banu Abi Aqil." Al-Hajjaj, as you know, was excessive in killing, and that is why Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said what he said.] other than the one I resemble you to? When this letter of mine comes to you, go forth to Shaghb."

11870. Yunus related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: al-Layth related to me, from Yazid and others, with something like this report; except that Yunus said in his report: "as if you were the slave of the Banu Abi 'Aqal, [I have not found a basis for the phrase "Ibn Abi 'Aqal," for his grandfather to whom he is attributed is Abu Aqil, as has passed in the previous report.] without my resembling you to him."

11871. Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Lahi'ah informed me, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, that al-Salt, the secretary of Hayyan ibn Surayj, informed them that Hayyan wrote to Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz: "That some people of the Copts had been established against by evidence that they had waged war against Allah and His Messenger and striven upon the earth in corruption, and that Allah says: 'Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption...'" and he recited until he reached "and their feet on opposite sides," and he was silent about the banishment. And he wrote to him: "If the Commander of the Faithful sees fit to carry out the judgment of Allah concerning them, let him write accordingly." When Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz read his letter, he said: "Hayyan has been satisfied with too little!" Then he wrote to him: "Your letter has reached me and I understood it. You have indeed been satisfied with too little, as if you had written by the letter of Yazid ibn Abi Muslim, or the non-Arab (ilj) of the Iraq, [Yazid ibn Abi Muslim and Yazid ibn Dinar were clients of Thaqif, not clients of manumission, and he was a foster-brother of al-Hajjaj. He was among the companions and governors of al-Hajjaj, and he imitated him in his conduct, and he governed Iraq and Ifriqiya. Ibn Abd al-Hakam said in the biography of Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz (pp. 34–35): "He displayed piety and enforced everything the ruler commanded, whether great or small, in tyranny and opposition to the truth. He used to frequently mention Allah and glorify Him, and he would order people, and they would be tortured before him, while he said: 'Glory be to Allah and praise be to Allah; strike, O boy, the place of such and such,' referring to some places of torment, and he would say: 'There is no god but Allah and Allah is greatest; strike, O boy, the place of such and such.' His condition was the worst of those conditions."
Yazid was, on the day Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz succeeded, governor of Ifriqiya. Umar had scarcely finished burying the corpse of Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik when he hastened, called for paper and ink, and wrote three letters, which he did not think it right, between himself and Allah, to delay, and he carried them out immediately. People began to find fault with Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz because of his haste, saying: "What is this hurry? Could he not have waited until he returned to his house? This is love of power! This is one who dislikes what he has entered into!" But Umar had no haste and no love for what he had come to, but he held himself to account and saw that delaying this was not right for him. One of these three letters was his letter dismissing Yazid ibn Abi Muslim. (Sirat Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz: 34–35; and al-Wuzara' of al-Jahshiyari: 42.)
As for "ilj sahib al-Iraq": the ilj is a man from the non-Arab unbelievers and others. It means al-Hajjaj himself, who was governor of Iraq, and he called him "ilj," as if he were a coarse client, just as he called him "slave" in the previous report.] without my resembling you to them, so you wrote the beginning of the verse and were silent about its end, while Allah says: 'or be banished from the land.' If the evidence has been established against them with what you have written, then fetter them in iron around their necks, then send them off to Shaghb and Bada." [Reports 11869–11871: Yazid ibn Abi Habib al-Misri, who has passed recently in report no. 11854.
As for "al-Salt," he is al-Salt ibn Abi Asim; I have not found a biography for him, and I saw his mention in the book Futuh Misr of Ibn Abd al-Hakam, p. 90.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 33 (part 5 of 5):

As for "Hayyan ibn Surayj al-Misri," he was an official (ʿamil) of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz over Egypt. Ibn Abi Hatim has a biography of him at 1/2/247, and al-Bukhari's al-Kabir at 2/1/52. The "Surayj" is vocalized with an unpointed sin, and the jim is in al-Mu'talif of ʿAbd al-Ghani ibn Saʿid al-Azdi al-Misri, p. 76. The editor of al-Tarikh al-Kabir said in his note: "Likewise Ibn Makula vocalized it in al-Ikmal... and in this place in the original it appears as 'Shurayh'."
"Shurayh" also occurs in many books, and it was so in the printed edition in all other places. As for the manuscript, it is unpointed. I followed the vocalization of the Hafiz ʿAbd al-Ghani, because he was Egyptian, and he knows the genealogies of the Egyptians best.
In the printed edition it was "Hayyan" with a single initial ba, which is pure error.
* *
Abu Jaʿfar said: "Shaghb" and "Bada" are two places. "Shaghb" (with a fatha and then a sukun) is a watering place between the road of Egypt and Syria, and "Bada" is a valley near Ayla, on the seashore, and both are among the abodes of the Banu ʿUdhra. Kuthayyir says: "You are the one who made Shaghb beloved to me, and Bada as well, while my homelands are other than these two."
ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Sa'ib says: "When they ascended Shaghb, I realized that it had cut off my ties with the people of the Hijaz."
His son replied: "May they never cease to be exhausted and lame, why did they carry us to a distant land of few friends!?"
This supports that it is a distant place of exile for the people of the Hijaz and Syria, as comes in this report.
* *
Others said: the meaning of "banishment from the land" in this place is imprisonment.
Those who related this from him:
This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions.
* *
Abu Jaʿfar said: The most correct of these sayings in my judgment is the view of the one who said: the meaning of "banishment from the land" in this place is his exile from one city to another city besides it, and his imprisonment in the prison of the city to which he was exiled, until his repentance from his wickedness and his turning away from his disobedience to his Lord becomes evident.
I said this is the most correct of the sayings, because the commentators differed about the meaning of this on one of the three aspects I mentioned. Since that is so, and it was known that God, mighty is His praise, only made the penalty for the muharib: killing, or crucifixion, or the cutting of hand and foot from opposite sides, after power over him, not while he is refusing, it was known that banishment too is his penalty after power over him, not before it. If his fleeing from pursuit were banishment from the land, [the printed edition has "hurubuhu"; the manuscript has "hu bihi"; "al-hurub" is not an Arabic verbal noun, though its use has become common in our time; the proper verbal noun is "al-harab" (with two fathas), so the correct reading is "harabahu" as I have set it] then cutting his hand and foot from opposite sides while he refuses and wars in the manner of fighting would be the enforcement of the prescribed penalty upon him after power over him. And there is consensus of all that this does not stand in place of his banishment, which God, mighty and majestic, made a prescribed penalty for him after power over him, [it became void that his banishment from the land is his fleeing from pursuit]. [This addition between brackets is one that cannot be dispensed with for the sentence to be sound. I have deduced it from Abu Jaʿfar's speech earlier and what comes after it.]
Since that is so, it is known that only the other two remain: banishment from one city to another city besides it, or imprisonment. Since that is so, there is no doubt that when he is exiled from one city to another city besides it, he is not banished from the land; rather he is banished from one land and not another. Since that is so, and God, mighty is His praise, only commanded his banishment from the land, it is known that there is no way to banish him from the land except by confining him in one plot of it apart from the rest, so that he is then banished from all of it, except from what there is no way to banish him from.
* *
As for the meaning of "nafy" (banishment) in the speech of the Arabs, it is expulsion (al-tard). Among examples of this is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:
"They are driven away from the paths of the noble, as the mallets drive off what the carded wool has left (qard)."
[Sharh al-Mufaddaliyyat: 827. It is not in the Diwan of Aws, but it is from his poetry, from the fifth qasida whose opening is: "O sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand, except a hand that has no forearm (ʿadud)," and he is satirizing them. The Mufaddaliyyat version is "min turuq al-kiram" (from the paths of the noble). "Al-matariq" is the plural of "mitraqa" and "mutraq," the rod with which wool or cotton is beaten so that it fluffs up, and it drives off the qard. "Al-qard" (two fathas) is what has been shed of the fur and wool, matted and clumped with its edges knotted; it is the refuse of wool, and then it was applied to other fur, hair and flax. His saying "ma yalI al-qard" means what the qard has come upon, from the expression "waliyahu yaliyahu," meaning he came close to it and drew near to it. It means: what the qard came close to and touched and clung to by its knotting.
In the printed edition it was "ma yali al-fardaa," which is an error and contrary to the manuscript, where it is pointed, against the usual practice in such things.]
And from this the bad dirhams and other things of every kind are called "al-nufaya" (refuse). ["Al-nufaya" here (with a damma on the nun) is beyond doubt. See the following note.] As for the verbal noun from "nafaytu," it is "al-nafy" and "al-nafaya," ["Al-nafaya" here (with a kasra on the nun), because he counted it as a verbal noun, like "raʿat al-mashiya raʿyan wa raʿaya" (with a kasra on the ra'). This is what I deduced. The lexicographical books mention only "nafyan" and "nafyanan" among the verbal nouns of "nafa," so this is a verbal noun to be added if it has a valid poetic or reported witness.] and it is said: "The bucket nafy (throws out) the water." And what flies up from the water from the bucket is called "al-nafiyy," and from it is the saying of the rajaz poet: [He is al-Akhyal al-Ta'i.]
"As if between its two flanks from the nafiyy are the places where birds alight upon the stone (safiyy)."
[The line, its explanation and its sources were mentioned previously at 3:225 / 5:523, and I did not point there to its occurrence in this place in the exegesis, so I note it here.]
From this it is said: "His hair nafa," when it falls out. It is said: "Your colour has changed, and your hair has nafa." [This is in the report of Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz when he became caliph, and saw him disheveled, and said:
"...Our knowledge of him in Medina was as a governor over us, of fine body and full flesh, and I began to look at him a look, hardly turning my gaze from him. He said: 'O son of Kaʿb, why do you look at me a look you did not used to look at me before?' I said: 'Out of wonder!' He said: 'And what amazed you?' I said: 'At how your body has wasted, your hair has nafa, and your colour has changed.' He said: 'And how would it be if you saw me after three days in my grave, when my eyes fall upon my cheek, and worms and pus flow from my nostrils and mouth; you would be even more repulsed by me than you are today!'"
"Nafa al-sha'r" means it has risen up, departed, become disheveled and fallen out.]
* *
The discussion of the words of God, exalted is His mention: ﴿That is their disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter there is a great punishment﴾ (33).
Abu Jaʿfar said: God, mighty is His praise, by His saying "that" means this penalty with which I have requited those who waged war against God and His Messenger, and strove in the land to cause corruption, namely killing, or crucifixion, or cutting of hand and foot from opposite sides. "For them" means: for these combatants. "Disgrace in this world" means: it is for them evil, shame, humiliation, disgrace and punishment in the hasty part of the world before the Hereafter.
* *
It is said from this: "akhzaytu fulanan, fa-khziya huwa khizyan" (I disgraced so-and-so, and he was disgraced).
* *
As for His saying "and for them in the Hereafter there is a great punishment," it means, mighty is His mention: for these who waged war against God and His Messenger, and strove in the land to cause corruption, and did not repent of their deed until they died, in the Hereafter, [the context: "for these who waged war against God and His Messenger... in the Hereafter..."] along with the disgrace with which I requited them in the world, and the punishment with which I punished them there, "a great punishment," meaning: the punishment of Hell. [See the explanation of "a great punishment" earlier in the indices of vocabulary (ʿadhaba) (ʿazuma).]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He and remembered: ﴿Except those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (5:34).

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: The meaning is: "except those who repent of their polytheism and their waging war against Allah and His Messenger and their striving on earth to cause corruption, by embracing Islam and entering into faith, before the believers gain power over them. For there is no way for the believers to inflict upon them any of the punishments that Allah has made the recompense for those who wage war against Him and His Messenger and strive on earth to cause corruption, namely killing, crucifixion, cutting off a hand and a foot on opposite sides, or banishment from the land. Thus, no claim (tiba'ah) against them belongs to anyone for what they had inflicted during their state of disbelief and their warring against the believers, [Tiba' (with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the ba') and tiba'ah (with a kasra on the ta'): that which contains a sin for which its perpetrator is held accountable. It is said: "He has no claim (tiba'ah) or accountability (tibah) before Allah concerning this."] whether in property, in blood, or in sanctity. They said: As for a Muslim who wages war against the Muslims or against those under covenant, and commits some act that makes the punishment obligatory, his repentance does not remove the punishment for his sin. Rather, his repentance concerns what is between him and Allah, and it is incumbent upon the ruler to carry out the prescribed penalty (hadd) that Allah has made obligatory upon him, and to take from him the rights of the people.

Mention of those who said this:

11872 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, from al-Husayn ibn Waqid, from Yazid al-Nahwi, from Ikrimah and al-Hasan al-Basri, that both of them said concerning His words, "The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive on earth..." up to His words, "So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful": This verse was revealed concerning the polytheists. Whoever of them repents before he is overpowered, no way (sabil) shall be against him. This verse does not protect a Muslim man from the prescribed penalty if he kills, or causes corruption on earth, or wages war against Allah and His Messenger, and then joins the disbelievers before he is overpowered. That penalty shall be carried out against him for what he committed. [Report 11872 has passed as no. 11806, see the comment on it.]

11873 - Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Rawh ibn Ubadah narrated to us, he said: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Except those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." He said: This is for the people of polytheism: if they committed something during their polytheism, then Allah is Forgiving and Merciful to them when they repent and submit (aslamu).

11874 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, he said: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive on earth to cause corruption": fornication, theft, killing a soul, and destroying crops and progeny.
