Indeed, what destroyed those before you were the leaders of hardship, [[His words "the leaders of hardship" mean those who begin asking about things which become forbidden to people because of their questions. They are like the leaders who preceded the people and imposed hardship upon them. "Hardship" is the narrowest constriction.]] by God, if I had made lawful for you everything on earth, and forbidden you a hoof's-width of it, you would have fallen into it!" He said: So God, exalted, revealed at that moment: "O you who have believed, do not ask about things," to the end of the verse. [[The narration: 12807 - "Zakariya ibn Yahya ibn Aban al-Misri", from whom Abu Ja'far narrated earlier, no. 5973, and my brother al-Sayyid Ahmad said there: "I have not found a biography of him in the books before me," and he was right; his name has not appeared specified as it does here and there. But Abu Ja'far narrated from him in several places of his History 1: 39, saying: "Zakariya ibn Yahya ibn Aban al-Misri narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿUfayr narrated to us." Then he narrated from him in al-Muntakhab from the book Dhayl al-Mudhayyal (13: 39): "Zakariya ibn Yahya ibn Aban al-Misri narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih, secretary of al-Layth, narrated to us," then (13: 63): "Zakariya ibn Yahya ibn Aban al-Misri narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn Ashkab narrated to us," then (13: 109): "Zakariya ibn Yahya narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn Yunus narrated to us." All those from whom he narrated are Egyptian.
I fear that he is "Zakariya ibn Yahya al-Waqqar al-Misri", Abu Yahya, biographed in Lisan al-Mizan 2: 485, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/601, and Mizan al-I'tidal 1: 350. He narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Wahb al-Misri and those after him, and from Zakariya ibn Yahya al-Adam al-Misri, and al-Qasim ibn Kathir al-Misri. Zakariya ibn Yahya al-Waqqar was born in 174 and died in 254, so it is likely that Abu Ja'far narrated from him. He was among the pious worshippers and jurists. But Ibn ʿAdi said: "He fabricates hadith; Salih Jazarah declared him a liar. Salih said: Zakariya al-Waqqar narrated to us, and he was among the great liars." He also said: "I saw the shaykhs of Egypt praising Abu Yahya for his worship, striving, and virtue, and he has many hadiths, some of which are sound and some of which are fabrications, and he was accused of fabricating them, for he narrated from trustworthy people fabricated hadiths. The pious have become known for this: that they narrate fabricated hadiths, and a group of them are accused of fabricating them."
As for "Abu Zayd": "ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Ghamr", the Egyptian jurist, one of al-Bukhari's teachers, narrated from outside the Sahih, passed under no. 4329. In the printed edition it reads "ibn Abi al-ʿAmr" with an unpointed ʿayn, which is an error.
"Abu Mati'": "Muʿawiyah ibn Yahya al-Shami al-Atrabulusi", trustworthy. Ibn Ma'in said: "He is not that strong," and al-Daraqutni said: "Weak." Biographed in al-Tahdhib and al-Kabir 4/1/336, where no criticism is mentioned, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/384; Abu Zur'ah deemed him trustworthy.
"Safwan ibn ʿAmr ibn Harim al-Sakasiki", trustworthy, passed under no. 7009.
"Salim ibn ʿAmir al-Kala'i al-Khabairi", trustworthy, narrated from Abu Umamah and other Companions. Biographed in al-Tahdhib and al-Kabir 2/2/126, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/211.
This report was cited by al-Haythami in Majma' al-Zawa'id in abridged form 3: 204, and he said: "al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Kabir and its isnad is good and sound."
Ibn Kathir quoted it from this place of the Tafsir 3: 251, and said: "There is weakness in its isnad." It seems that the cause of its weakness in his view is "Zakariya ibn Yahya ibn Aban al-Misri." There is an error in the isnad as given in Ibn Kathir, where it is written "ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Abi al-Ghamr", which is a clear error.
al-Suyuti takes it out in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 335, adding its attribution to Ibn Mardawayh. Then see what Abu Ja'far concluded this section with, p. 112, that the sources of these reports are sound in his view.]]

12808 - Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding his words: "O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you." That was because the Messenger of God announced to the people and said: "O people, the Hajj has been prescribed for you!" A man from the Banu Asad stood up and said: "O Messenger of God, every year?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) became exceedingly angry, and said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if I had said 'yes,' it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory you would not have been able to do it, and then you would have disbelieved. So leave me as long as I leave you. When I command you to do something, do it, and when I forbid you from something, refrain from it!" So God, exalted, revealed: "O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you." He forbade them from asking about the like of what the Christians asked about from the Table, and they became disbelievers because of it. God, exalted, forbade that and said: Do not ask about things which, if the Qur'an were revealed concerning them with harshness, would trouble you; but wait, and when the Qur'an is revealed, you will not ask about anything without finding its explanation. [[The narration: 12808 - my brother al-Sayyid Ahmad has already shown, in report no. 305, the weakness of this isnad which recurs in the Tafsir, and he said: "It is an isnad uniformly weak, from a single family." Then he explained the isnad in detail.]]

12809 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, saying: ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah narrated to us, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding his words: "O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you, and if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you." He said: When the verse of the Hajj was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) called out to the people and said: "O people, God has prescribed the Hajj for you, so perform it!" They said: "O Messenger of God, is it once or every year?" He said: "No, rather once; and if I had said 'every year,' it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory you would have disbelieved." Then God, exalted in remembrance, said: "O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you." He said: They had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about things, and he admonished them, and they desisted.

12810 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from ʿIsa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: "O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you." He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) mentioned the Hajj, and it was said: "Is it obligatory, O Messenger of God, every year?" He said: "No; if I had said it, it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory you would not have been able to bear it, and if you had not been able to bear it you would have disbelieved." Then he said: "Ask me! No man will ask me in this gathering of mine about anything except that I will inform him, even if he asks me about his father!" A man stood up and said: "Who is my father?" He said: "Your father is Hudhafah ibn Qays." Then ʿUmar stood up and said: "O Messenger, we are content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad (ﷺ) as Prophet, and we seek refuge in God from His anger and the anger of His Messenger."

* *

Others said: Rather, this verse was revealed because they asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the Bahirah, the Sa'ibah, the Wasilah, and the Ha'mi.

Mention of those who said that:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 101 (part 3 of 3):

11. 12811: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim ibn Habib ibn al-Shahid narrated to me, saying: Attab ibn Bashir narrated to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Do not ask about things﴾. He said: They are the baheera (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released), the saiba (a animal set free), the wasila (a she-camel or ewe giving twins), and the ham (a stallion camel released after a set number of uses). Do you not see that He says after that: ﴿Allah has not appointed any such thing, nor any such⁠﻿﻿ ...﴾? [The narrator of this report is Khusayf.] Ikrimah, however, said: They used to ask him about the signs, so they were forbidden from that. Then he recited: ﴿A people before you asked about them, and then became disbelievers because of them﴾. He (Khusayf) said: I said, "Mujahid has narrated to me something contrary to this from Ibn Abbas, so why do you say this?" He said: Hayhah. [Note on "hayhah": here it is pronounced with a fatha on the first ha, a sukun on the ya, and a fatha on the final ha. It is said to a thing that is being pushed away and driven off. As for "hayh" (with kasra on the first ha and kasra or fatha on the last), it is like "ayh," said to a man to ask him for more of a familiar conversation between the two of you. Ikrimah's gesture of driving away and pushing off was because of the enmity between Mujahid and Ikrimah. See what has preceded of Mujahid's poor opinion of Ikrimah in the commentary on reports nos. 10445 and 10469.]

12. 12812: Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Ibn Awn, from Ikrimah, who said: He is the one who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Who is my father?" Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They are the ones who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the baheera and the saiba.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these opinions is the view of the one who said: This verse was revealed because of the frequent questions that the questioners put to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), such as Ibn Hudhafah's question about who his father was, and the questioner's question when he said, "Allah has made the Hajj obligatory upon you, is it every year?" and similar questions. This is because the reports are widely attested from the Companions, the Successors, and the majority of the exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil).

As for the view that Mujahid narrated from Ibn Abbas, it is not far from the truth, but the widely attested reports from the Companions and the Successors contradict it, so we dislike holding it for this reason. Moreover, it is not objectionable that the question about the baheera, the saiba, the wasila, and the ham was among the questions they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about, which Allah disliked for them, just as Allah disliked for them the question about the Hajj, "Is it every year, or only once?" and just as He disliked Abdullah ibn Hudhafah's question about his father. So the verse came forbidding all questions, and each reporter mentioned some of what the verse was revealed for, and for other things. [In the printed edition it reads "aw ajal ghayrihi" ("or for other than it"), where the "aw" was introduced in place of the conjunctive "wa," which corrupts the sentence badly.] This view, in my opinion, is the most correct of these views, because the chains of transmission for all the meanings mentioned are sound, so directing them toward the correct sense in their various aspects is preferable.

* * *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made clear to you. Allah has pardoned them, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾ (5:101).

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says to those Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) whom He forbade from asking the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about what they were forbidden to ask him about, namely obligations that Allah had not imposed upon them, and the permitting of matters that He had not permitted for them, and the forbidding of things that He had not forbidden them before the Qur'an was revealed with that: O believers who ask about what they asked my messenger about, things about which I have not sent down a book or revelation, do not ask about them. For if clarification of them is made manifest to you by revelation and sending down, it will displease you, because when the revelation about it comes to you, it comes with what will test and examine you: either by imposing a deed upon you and an obligation binding upon you, which involves hardship, burden, and difficulty for you; or by forbidding what, had revelation not come with its prohibition, you would have been free and at ease in doing; or by permitting what you believe to be forbidden, which causes you displeasure because it shifts you from what you considered true to what you considered false. But if you ask about them after the Qur'an has been revealed about them, and after the beginning of the clarification of their matter in My Book to My messenger sent to you, it will be made easy for you by what I have sent down to him from the clarification of My Book and the interpretation of My revelation. [In the printed edition: "bayyana lakum ma anzaltuhu ilayhi min ityan kitabi" ("He made clear to you what I sent down to him from the coming of My Book"), which is also meaningless. The manuscript reads: "lassas 'alaykum ma anzaltuhu ilayhi min asay kitabi," and the correct reading, God willing, is what I have adopted.]

This is similar to the report transmitted from some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which is:

13. 12813: Hannad ibn al-Sarri narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Makhul, from Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, who said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, has prescribed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; He has set limits, so do not transgress them; and He has pardoned things out of other than forgetfulness, so do not search into them. [Report 12813: Abu Ja'far transmitted this as a statement (mawquf) attributed to Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani. Al-Suyuti, in al-Durr al-Manthur (2:336), cited it as a prophetic report (marfu') and attributed it to Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound. Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his commentary (3:252), saying: "And in the sound hadith also," but I was unable to find it in al-Mustadrak or in other sound collections.]

14. 12814: Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'idah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Juraij informed us, from Ata', who said: Ubayd ibn Umayr used to say: Allah, may He be exalted, made lawful and made unlawful. So what He made lawful, accept as lawful, and what He made unlawful, avoid. And He left some things without declaring them lawful or unlawful, and that is a pardon from Allah, by which He pardoned. Then he recited: ﴿O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made apparent to you, would distress you﴾.

15. 12815: Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: al-Dahhak narrated to us, saying: Ibn Juraij informed us, saying: Ata' informed me, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, that he used to say: Indeed Allah made unlawful and made lawful, and then he mentioned something similar.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Allah has pardoned them﴾, He means: Allah has pardoned you for asking about the things you asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about, which Allah disliked for you to ask him about, so that He would not take you to account for them or punish you for them, if He knows of your repentance and return. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾, meaning: Allah conceals the sins of those who repent from them, and refrains from exposing him in the Hereafter. ﴿Forbearing﴾ [meaning: patient and slow] in not punishing him for them, because He covers the one who repents from them with His mercy and pardon, sparing him punishment for them. [See the explanation of "Forgiving" in the lexical indexes earlier, and the explanation of "Forbearing" in earlier volumes: 5:117, 5:521, and 7:327. I have added what is between the brackets from Abu Ja'far's earlier explanation, since the statement is not well-formed without it or something similar.]

* * *

In accordance with what we have said on this, the report from Ibn Abbas that we mentioned earlier was transmitted. It is this:

16. 12816: Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿Do not ask about things﴾, meaning: Do not ask about things which, if the Qur'an were revealed about them with a severe ruling, would distress you. Rather, wait, and when the Qur'an is revealed, you will not ask about anything without finding its clarification. [Report 12816: This is part of the report mentioned earlier, no. 12808.]

The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿Certainly a people before you asked such questions, then they became disbelievers in them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: A people before you asked for signs, and when God gave them to them, they became deniers, rejecting that they were evidence for the truth of what they were presented as proof of, and a proof of the soundness of what they were made a proof to establish. This is like the people of Salih who asked for a sign, and when the she-camel came to them as a sign, they hamstrung her. And like those who asked Jesus for a table to descend upon them from heaven, and when it was given to them, they disbelieved in it, and what is similar to that.

So God, may He be exalted, warned the believers in His Prophet (ﷺ) against following the path of those nations before them that were destroyed for their disbelief in God's signs when they came to them after asking for them. He said to them: Do not ask for signs, and do not search for things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you. A people before you asked for signs, and when they were given them, they became disbelievers in them. As the following report states:

12817 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾: He forbade them to ask about the like of what the Christians asked about, concerning the table, and so they became disbelievers in it, and God forbade that. [Note on the report: this is part of the earlier report No. 12808.]

12818 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿Certainly a people before you asked such questions﴾: A people before you asked for signs, and that was when it was said to him: Turn the Safa into gold for us.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 103 (part 1 of 3):

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿God did not ordain any bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah, or ha'm﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: God did not ordain any bahirah (a she-camel whose ear was slit), nor did He make any sa'ibah (a camel set free to roam), nor any wasilah (a she-camel given as a dedication), nor did He make any ha'm (a stallion camel released after fulfilling a number of mounts) as protected. Rather, it is you, O disbelievers, who did that, and forbade them, fabricating against your Lord, as in what was narrated:

12819 – Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam told me, saying: my father and Shu'ayb ibn al-Layth told me, from al-Layth, from Ibn al-Had; and Yunus told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf told us, saying: al-Layth told me, saying: Ibn al-Had told me, from Ibn Shihab, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "I saw 'Amr ibn 'Amir al-Khuza'i dragging his intestines in the Fire, and he was the first to release the sawa'ib (free-roaming animals)."

[Editor's note: This report is narrated by Abu Ja'far through two chains. The first includes Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam ibn A'yan al-Misri, trustworthy, previously mentioned under no. 2377. His father, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam ibn A'yan, the jurist of Egypt, trustworthy, biographied in al-Tahdhib; and Shu'ayb ibn al-Layth ibn Sa'd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Fahmi al-Misri, trustworthy, previously mentioned under nos. 3034 and 5314. His father al-Layth ibn Sa'd, the eminent imam, previously mentioned under nos. 186, 187, 2072, 2584, 9507. "Ibn al-Had" is Yazid ibn al-Had, named after his grandfather, namely Yazid ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Usamah ibn al-Had, trustworthy, previously mentioned under nos. 2031, 3034, 4314. As for the second chain: "Yunus" is Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la al-Sadafi, trustworthy, previously mentioned under nos. 1679, 3503 and others. And 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf al-Tinnisi al-Kala'i, trustworthy, one of al-Bukhari's teachers, biographied in al-Tahdhib.

This report of Abu Hurayrah, through al-Layth ibn Sa'd, from Yazid ibn al-Had, from Ibn Shihab, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, was narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad, no. 8773, and al-Bukhari alluded to it in his Sahih (al-Fath 8: 214). He had earlier narrated it through Salih ibn Kaysan, from Ibn Shihab, from Sa'id. Ahmad also narrated it earlier in a broken (munqati') form, no. 7696, through 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Hurayrah. My brother al-Sayyid Ahmad has fully explained this in his commentary. As for Muslim, he narrated it in his Sahih 17: 189 through Salih ibn Kaysan, from Ibn Shihab, from Sa'id.

Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his Tafsir 3: 253, and cited the narration of al-Bukhari mentioned above. He said: "al-Hakim said: al-Bukhari meant that Yazid ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Had narrated it from 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Bakht, from al-Zuhri." This was related thus by our teacher Abu al-Hajjaj al-Mizzi in al-Atraf, and he remained silent and did not point it out. Ibn Kathir said: "There is scrutiny in what al-Hakim said, for Imam Ahmad and Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir both narrated it from the hadith of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, from Ibn al-Had, from al-Zuhri himself; and God knows best." The meaning of Ibn Kathir's words is that Ibn al-Had's hearing from al-Zuhri is established. He did not clarify what Abu al-Hajjaj meant by what he said, nor did he explain it. The hafiz Ibn Hajar in al-Fath (8: 214) did not refer to anything of what al-Mizzi said.

As for "al-qasab" (with a dammah and then a sukun), it means all the intestines. As for his saying "sayyab al-sayyab," "sayyab the animal, or the she-camel, or the thing" means to leave it to roam wherever it wishes, i.e., to go wherever it wishes. As for "al-sayyib" (with a dammah on the sin and a shaddah on the yaa with a fathah), it is the plural of "sa'ibah" on the pattern of "na'ihah / nawh" and "na'im / nawm," as preceded in my note on the report no. 10447. Its evidence: Ibn Hisham narrated in his Sirah this verse (1: 93):

"Around the wasa'il in Shuraif ... are the hiqqah, and the hamiyat whose backs..."

"Al-suyyab" is also pluralized as "sawa'ib," which is the analogical form. In one of the two narrations of Sahih Muslim (17: 189) there is: "the first to release the suyub" (with a dammah on the sin and the yaa). Al-Qadi 'Iyad said in Mashariq al-Anwar: "the first to release the sawa'ib; in the other narration: the first to release the suyub," and he did not explain it. Its explanation is that "suyub" is the plural of "sayb" (with a fathah then a sukun), a verbal noun by which "al-sa'ibah" was named. It has come in the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf on the day of the consultation (shura): "Indeed, a stratagem with speech is more eloquent than the suyub in speech." They explained it in two ways. The first is what is in Lisan al-'Arab: "al-suyub: what is released and left, so it runs (sa'a), i.e., goes." The other is what al-Zamakhshari said in al-Fa'iq: "al-suyub is a verbal noun of sa'a. It is analogical that the plural of sa'ib and sa'ibah is suyub, for whatever has a verbal noun in fu'ul, its plural of the active participle (fa'il) comes in fu'ul, like shahid / shuhud, qa'id / qu'ud, and hadir / hudur." I have mentioned this in a previous note; see also Sharh al-Shafiyah 2: 158. This is the explanation that al-Qadi 'Iyad and al-Nawawi in the commentary on Sahih Muslim overlooked.

In the printed edition it read: "the first to release the sa'ibah," which differs from the manuscript, and is a shameful distortion of the trust of knowledge!! Written by Mahmud Muhammad Shakir.]

12820 – Hannad ibn al-Sari told us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith told me, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to Aktham ibn al-Jawn: "O Aktham, I saw 'Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif dragging his intestines in the Fire, and I have not seen a man more resembling a man than him, nor him more than you!" Aktham said: "Perhaps his resemblance will harm me, O Messenger of God!" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No, you are a believer and he is a disbeliever. He was the first to change the religion of Isma'il, to slit the bahirah, to release the sa'ibah, and to protect the ha'm."

[Editor's note: "Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith al-Taymi," whom the authors of the six books narrated from, a trustworthy follower with many narrations, previously mentioned under no. 4249. "Abu Salih" is Dhakwan al-Sammān, a trustworthy follower, previously mentioned many times. As for "Muhammad ibn Ishaq," the author of the Sirah, my brother al-Sayyid Ahmad's affirmation of his reliability has passed under no. 221 and in his other works. Ibn Kathir narrated this report in his Tafsir 3: 254, together with no. 12822, and in al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah 2: 189, then said: "These two chains are not in the books in this form," meaning the authentic collections. Otherwise this report is established through the chain of Muhammad ibn Ishaq in Ibn Hisham's Sirah 1: 78, 79. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned it in al-Isti'ab without a chain, p. 55; Ibn al-Athir mentioned it with its chain 1: 123, 124; and Ibn Hajar in al-Isabah (entry: Aktham ibn al-Jawn) attributed it to Ibn Abi 'Urwah and Ibn Mandah through Ibn Ishaq. al-Suyuti extracted it in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 338 but confused its takhrij greatly, saying: "Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim narrated it and he authenticated it," whereas that is actually no. 12822 that follows. This report will come later in full through another chain, no. 12827, which is Abu Ja'far's second chain in the narration of Ibn Ishaq's Sirah.

As for his saying "'asa an yadurrani shabahuh" (perhaps its resemblance will harm me), it means: perhaps its resemblance will harm me, he fears that this may be so. In the printed edition: "akhsha an yadurrani shabahuh" (I fear its resemblance will harm me), which contradicts the narration. It was merely confused by the manuscript copyist's writing, as he wrote it jumbled: "tahti," as if he meant to write something, then returned to it until "'asa" became dotted, and the same as the printed edition appeared to me in al-Durr al-Manthur. The frequency of such things showed me that this manuscript copy that we are publishing is the one that fell into al-Suyuti's hands, and the correct reading is what I have established from the Sirah and from those who quoted from it.

The manuscript also had: "wa hima al-himan," which is pure error; its correct form is from the sources of this report.]

12821 – Hannad told us, saying: Yunus told us, saying: Hisham ibn Sa'd told me, from Zayd ibn Aslam, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I know the first to slit the bahair (slit-eared camels): a man from Mudlij who had two she-camels. He slit their ears, forbade their milk and their backs, and said: 'These are for God!' Then he needed them, so he drank their milk and rode their backs." He said: "Indeed I saw him in the Fire, harming the people of the Fire with the smell of his intestines."

[Editor's note: "Hisham ibn Sa'd al-Madani," the orphan of Zayd ibn Aslam, was among the most reliable people from Zayd, and he is trustworthy, though some have spoken about him, previously mentioned under no. 5490. This is a mursal report. It will come through the chain of Ma'mar, from Zayd ibn Aslam, under no. 12824.]

12822 – Hannad told us, saying: 'Abdah told us, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The Fire was displayed to me, and I saw in it 'Amr ibn so-and-so ibn so-and-so ibn Khindif dragging his intestines in the Fire. He was the first to change the religion of Ibrahim, to release the sa'ibah, and he resembled Aktham ibn al-Jawn more than anyone I have seen." Aktham said: "O Messenger of God, will his resemblance harm me?" He said: "No, because you are a Muslim and he is a disbeliever."

[Editor's note: "'Abdah" is "'Abdah ibn Sulayman al-Kilabi," trustworthy, previously mentioned shortly before under no. 12729. In both the printed and manuscript editions it reads "'Ubaydah," which is an error; the correct form is in Ibn Kathir's Tafsir. "Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn 'Alqamah ibn Waqqas al-Laythi" and "Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf" also passed in a similar chain under no. 12729, and this chain's narrators are trustworthy.

This report was narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 4: 605, through Abu Hatim al-Razi, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr, and in it is explicitly: "I saw in it 'Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif." He then said: "This is a sahih hadith according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not include it," and al-Dhahabi agreed.

You have already seen that Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir 3: 254 and in al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah 2: 189 that it is not in the books, meaning the sahih collections, and he added nothing more.

As for the hafiz Ibn Hajar, he extracted it in al-Isabah (entry: Aktham ibn al-Jawn) through Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Muhammad ibn Bishr al-'Abdi, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr, from Abu Salamah, with the same wording, and then pointed to al-Hakim's chain in al-Mustadrak. But I was unable to find Ahmad's report in the Musnad.

As for the imam and hafiz Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm, he narrated it in his book Jamharat al-Ansab, p. 223, through 'Ali ibn 'Umar al-Daraqutni, from al-Husayn ibn Isma'il al-Qadi al-Muhamili, from Sa'id ibn Yahya al-Umawi, from his father, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr. Then Abu Muhammad said, after listing the hadiths of al-Bukhari and Muslim and this hadith, which are four, of which this is the third: "As for the first, third, and fourth hadiths, they are in the utmost soundness and firmness," thereby judging this report to be sound.

In the printed edition here it reads: "'Amr ibn fulan ibn fulan ibn fulan ibn Khindif," with "fulan" three times, which contradicts the manuscript; and it is an error thereafter, for between "'Amr" and "Khindif" there are two names, not three. Likewise in the manuscript and the printed edition: "la li-annaka muslim" (no, because you are a Muslim). Were it not for their agreement, I would have preferred "la innaka muslim" (no, you are a Muslim), as in other narrations.]

12823 – Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: I saw 'Amr ibn 'Amir al-Khuza'i dragging his intestines in the Fire, and he was the first to release the sawa'ib.

[Editor's note: As you see, this is a mursal report; 'Abd al-Razzaq did not raise it.]

12824 – Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I know the first to release the sawa'ib, and the first to change the covenant of Ibrahim!" They said: "Who is he, O Messenger of God?" He said: "'Amr ibn Luhayy, brother of the Banu Ka'b. I saw him dragging his intestines in the Fire, his smell harming the people of the Fire. And indeed I know the first to slit the bahair!" They said: "Who is he, O Messenger of God?" He said: "A man from the Banu Mudlij, who had two she-camels. He slit their ears and forbade their milk, then afterward drank their milk. I saw him in the Fire, and they were biting him with their mouths and trampling him with their hooves."

[Editor's note: This too is a mursal report, and it is another chain for the earlier report no. 12821. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned it in al-Fath (8: 214, 215), then said: "The first is more sound," meaning the mention of this man from the Banu Mudlij as the first to slit the bahair, and that the correct version is what came in the sound reports earlier, that it was 'Amr ibn Luhayy.

"Banu Mudlij" are the Banu Mudlij ibn Murrah ibn 'Abd Manat ibn Kinanah ibn Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah ibn Ilyas ibn Mudar ibn Nizar ibn Ma'd; they were not from Quraysh. Among them was the practice of qiyafah and 'iyafah (reading tracks and omens), and among them was Mujazzaz al-Mudlaji, whose skill in qiyafah pleased the Prophet (ﷺ) (Jamharat al-Ansab: 176, 177).]

And "al-bahirah" is the fa'ilah form from the saying of the speaker: "I slit this she-camel's ear," when he split it: "abhuruha bahran" (I slit it, a slitting), and the she-camel is "mabhurah" (slit), and then the form "mafulah" is changed to "fa'ilah," so one says: "she is bahirah." As for "al-bahir" among camels, it is the one afflicted by a disease from excessive drinking of water; one says of it: "bahira al-ba'ir yabhar bahameans" (the camel became bahir), [This is on the pattern of "farih yafrah farahan" (fariḥa, yafrahu, farahan).] and from it is the saying of the poet: [I was unable to find who said it.]

la-a'lat-tannahu wasman la yufariquhu ... kama yuhazzu bi-hamyi al-mīsami al-bahiru

[It will come in the commentary (29: 19, Bulaq). Lisan al-'Arab (bahr). "'Allata al-ba'ir ya'lituhu 'alatan" means to brand the camel with a 'ala (mark). The "'alat" (with a kasrah on the 'ayn) is a mark on the breadth of a camel's neck; if it is on the length of the neck, it is "sita'" (with a kasrah on the sin). This is the linguistic explanation that it is on the neck. As for Abu Ja'far al-Tabari, he said in his commentary (29: 19): "The Arabs say: 'By God, I will brand you with a mark that will not leave you,' meaning the nose," then he mentioned the verse and said: "al-Najr" is a disease that affects camels, so they are branded on their noses. He mentioned it there with the nun and jim as I have recorded it, and it has a valid form that will come, except that I fear the correct reading there is, as it is here, with the ba' and ha', and his saying "bi-hamyi al-mīsami": one says: "hamā al-mismār hamiyan wa hamuwan" (the nail became hot), meaning it was heated in the fire; and "ahmaytu al-mismar fi al-nar ihma'an" (I heated the nail in the fire). "Al-mīsam" is the branding iron with which animals are branded. As for "al-bahr," Abu Ja'far explained it, but al-Azhari said: "The disease that afflicts a camel so that it cannot be quenched with water is al-najr, with the nun and jim; and al-bajr, with the ba' and jim; and as for al-bahr, it is a disease that causes consumption (sull)."

This verse is in mockery of a man and a threat of evil that leaves its trace.

In the printed edition it reads: "la-a'taynannaka," with a kaf at the end, and the correct reading is from the manuscript, from what will come in the printed commentary (29: 19), and from Lisan al-'Arab.]

And in a manner similar to what we have said regarding the meaning of "bahirah," a report came from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

12825 – 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Bayan told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yazid informed us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from his father, who said: I entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: [In the printed edition, "lahu" was dropped, but it is present in the manuscript, and it is correct.] "Did you not see your camels, that they bring forth their young with healthy ears, and you take the knife and slit them, saying: 'This is a bahirah,' and split their ears, and you say: 'This is sarm'?" He said: "Yes!" He said: "Indeed the help of God is stronger, and the knife of God is sharper! All your property is lawful for you; nothing of it shall be forbidden to you."

[Editor's note: This report was narrated by Abu Ja'far through two chains, this and the one that follows. "'Abd al-Hamid ibn Bayan al-Qannad," a teacher of Abu Ja'far, previously mentioned many times. "Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Kala'i" al-Wasiti, whom Ahmad declared trustworthy and who is among his teachers, previously mentioned under no. 11408. "Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid al-Ahmasi," trustworthy, previously mentioned under nos. 5694, 5777. "Abu Ishaq" is al-Sabi'i the imam, previously mentioned many times. "Abu al-Ahwas" is 'Awf ibn Malik ibn Nadlah al-Jushami, a trustworthy follower, previously mentioned under no. 6172. And his father: "Malik ibn Nadlah ibn Khudayj al-Jushami," and it is said: "Malik ibn 'Awf ibn Nadlah," and Ibn Sa'd so biographied him in al-Tabaqat 6: 17. As for al-Bukhari's al-Tarikh al-Kabir 4/1/303, I saw in it: "Malik ibn Yaqzah al-Khuza'i, the father of Abu al-Ahwas, has a companionship (sohbah)." But the famous Abu al-Ahwas is "'Awf ibn Malik ibn Nadlah," so my opinion is that what is in the Tarikh is an error, for I did not find this name among the Companions; the error would be in "Yaqzah," which is "Nadlah," and in "al-Khuza'i," which is "al-Jushami"; and God knows best.

This report came in the manuscript as I have recorded it, and in the printed edition: "wa tashiqqu adhanaha wa taqulu" (in the singular), so I have recorded what is in the manuscript.

As for his saying "musallamah adhanuha," it means: healthy, sound. I will explain its wording at the end of the following report, and what was in error in the printed and manuscript editions regarding "sarm," after its takhrij there.]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 103 (part 2 of 3):**

12826. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, from Abu Ishaq, who said: I heard Abu al-Ahwas, from his father, who said: I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Do the camels of your people give birth to ears intact, so that you go to the knife and cut their ears and say, 'This is a *bahir*,' and slit them or slit their hides and say, 'This is a *surum*,' and so forbid them to yourself and your family?" He said: "Yes!" He said: "Verily, what Allah has given you is lawful to you, and the helper of Allah is stronger, and the knife of Allah is sharper." Sometimes he said: "The helper of Allah is stronger than your helper, and the knife of Allah is sharper than your knife."

[[The report: 12826. This report is a repetition of the one before it.
Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi transmitted it in full in his Musnad (p. 184, no. 1303), by way of Shu'bah from Abu Ishaq.
Ahmad transmitted it in his Musnad by way of Muhammad ibn Ja'far, from Shu'bah, from Abu Ishaq; then by way of Affan, from Shu'bah, in the Musnad 3:473.
Al-Bayhaqi transmitted it in al-Sunan al-Kubra 10:10, by way of Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Abu Ishaq.
Ibn Kathir cited it in his Tafsir from the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim 3:256, in full, and did not attribute it to anyone else.
Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 2:337, in very full form, and attributed it to Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat. As for its wording in al-Suyuti, I do not know whose wording it is, for it is not the wording of any of those I mentioned above in their books.
Then Ahmad transmitted it in the Musnad 4:136, 137, by way of Sufyan ibn Uyaynah, from Abu al-Zar'a Amr ibn Amr, from his uncle Abu al-Ahwas, from his father, with a different wording that differs entirely.]]

These are the explanations of the difficult terms in these two reports. "*Nataja al-naqah yantijuha nitajan*" (on the pattern of *daraba*): when one takes charge of her birthing, i.e., her delivery. As for his saying in the second report, "Do the camels of your people give birth," it is in the passive voice. One says, "*nutijat al-naqah tuntaj*" (in the passive voice): when she gave birth.

"*Jad' al-anf wa al-udhun wa al-shafah*": when part of these is cut off. As for his saying, "This is a *surum*," it was written in the manuscript and the printed edition in both reports as "*hurum*" with a *ha*, and likewise it occurs thus in Ibn Kathir's Tafsir. The correct reading, from the sources I have cited and from the lexicographical works in explaining this report, is otherwise.

"*Surum*" in the first report is read with a *fatha* on the *sad* and a *sukun* on the *ra*, and "*al-sarm*" means cutting. He named it *al-masrumah* (the cut one) by the verbal noun, as the correct reading of it is shown by what appears in the explanation of the term in Lisan al-Arab under the root (*s-r-b*). As for the second report, his saying "This is a *bahir*" (with a *damma* on the *ba* and the *ha*) is the plural of *bahirah*; and his saying "This is a *surum*" (with a *damma* on the *sad* and the *ra*) is the plural of *sarimah*, which is the one whose ear has been cut and severed. This is the clear statement of the author of Lisan in his entries on *s-r-m* and *s-r-b*, and of al-Zamakhshari in al-Fa'iq under *s-r-b*. Ahmad transmitted in the Musnad 4:136, 137: "*sarma'*" (a female with a severed ear), and the lexicographical works did not point to it. As for al-Zamakhshari and the author of Lisan, they transmitted: "And one says: *sarbi*" (on the pattern of *sukra*). He said in explaining it: when they slit the ear of the *bahirah*, they left her unmilked except for the guest, so the milk gathers in her udder, from their saying "*sarab al-laban fi al-dar*" (the milk accumulated in the udder) when he withholds it and does not milk it. They both transmitted that it is said that the *ba'* is a substitution for the *mim*, as in their saying "*darbah lazim wa lazib*" (a firm blow), and that this is the more correct of the two explanations.

As for "*al-sa'ibah*": it is the one let loose and left free. In the Jahiliyyah, one of them would do this with some of his livestock, forbidding the benefit of it to himself, just as some people of Islam would free their slave as a *sa'ibah*, so he would derive no benefit from him nor from his *wala'* (right of patronage).

[[See the explanation of "*al-sa'ibah*" above, 3:386, note 1.]]

"*Al-musayyabah*" was brought out with the wording "*al-sa'ibah*," as it is said: "*'ishah radiyah*," in the sense of "*mardiyah*" (a pleasing life).

* * *

As for "*al-wasilah*" (the connected one): when a female among their cattle in the Jahiliyyah gave birth to a male and a female in one birth, it was said: "The female has connected her brother," by her being spared slaughter on his account, so they named her *wasilah*.

* * *

As for "*al-ham*": it is the stallion of the cattle whose back is protected from riding and benefit because of the succession of offspring produced from his mating.

* * *

The people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) have differed about the characteristics of those named by these names, and about the cause for which they used to do that.

Mention of the narrations on what has been said about that:

12827. Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, from Ibn Ishaq,

[[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "from Abu Ishaq," and this is a pure error, as is evident in its takhrij.]]

from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith al-Taymi: that Abu Salih al-Samman told him that he heard Abu Hurayrah say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say to Aktham ibn al-Jawn al-Khuza'i: "O Aktham, I saw Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif dragging his intestines in the Fire, and I have never seen a man more similar to a man than he is to you, nor than you are to him!" Aktham said: "Will his resemblance harm me, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "No, for you are a believer and he is a disbeliever, and he was the first to change the religion of Isma'il, and set up the idols, and let loose the *sawa'ib* among them."

[[It was mentioned in report 12820: "I have never seen a man," and this is another narration.]]

[[In the printed edition: "No, because you are a Muslim," differing from it; but it is in the manuscript and in Ibn Hisham as I have established it.]]

[[In the printed edition: "he let loose the *sawa'ib* among them," and I have kept what is in the manuscript, though the copyist wrote "*al-sa'ib* among them," and the correct form is from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.
This part of the report is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, which passed earlier under no. 12820, and its takhrij was given there. As for the second part, which I placed at the beginning of the line, it is from the words of Ibn Ishaq himself, as you will see in the takhrij.]]

= And that is because the she-camel, when she gave birth to twelve females in succession with no male among them,

[[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "when she gave birth to twelve females with no male among them," though in the manuscript it reads "with no male among them," and both are a pure error. The correct form of this phrase is what I have established from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham and others, except that I made "*fihinna*" (among them, feminine) in place of "*baynahunna*" (between them) in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, because of what comes later in the report, "*fihinna*" in place of "*baynahunna*" in the corresponding part of the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.]]

was let loose, and her back was not ridden, her wool was not sheared, and her milk was not drunk except by a guest. Then, whatever she bore after that of a female, her ear was slit, and then she was let go with her mother among the camels; her back was not ridden, her wool was not sheared, and her milk was not drunk except by a guest, as was done with her mother. So she is the *bahirah*, the daughter of the *sa'ibah*.

And the *wasilah*: when the ewe gave birth to ten females in succession across five births, with no male among them, she was made a *wasilah*. They said: "She has connected." So whatever she bore after that was for their males and not for their females,

[[Report 12827: The beginning of this report up to his saying "let loose the *sa'ib* among them" is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned earlier under no. 12820, and it is in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham 1:78, 79, and I have traced it there.
As for the second part to the end of the report, it is from the words of Ibn Ishaq, and it is in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham 1:91, 92.]]

except that if one of them dies, they all share in eating it, males and females alike.

[[In the printed edition: "for their males, not for their females." In the manuscript: "for their males among them," unpointed; the correct form is from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.]]

As for the *ham*: when a stallion had ten females produced for him in succession with no male among them, his back was protected, he was not ridden, his wool was not sheared, and he was let loose among his camels to mate with them, benefiting from him in no other way. Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah*, nor *sa'ibah*, nor *wasilah*, nor *ham*" up to His saying "and they do not understand."

12828. Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu al-Duha, from Masruq, concerning this verse: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah*, nor *sa'ibah*, nor *wasilah*, nor *ham*." = Abu Ja'far said: I think that some words of his fell from me [i.e., were omitted by the transmitters]. = He said: "So I came to Alqamah and asked him, and he said: What do you want with a thing that the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do?"

[[In the printed edition: "that they used to do," and the correct form is from the manuscript.]]

12829. Yahya ibn Ibrahim al-Mas'udi related to me, saying: My father related to us, from his father, from his grandfather, from al-A'mash, from Muslim, who said: I came to Alqamah and asked him about the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah*, nor *sa'ibah*, nor *wasilah*, nor *ham*." He said: "And what would you do with this? It is only a thing from the deeds of the Jahiliyyah!" He said: "So I came to Masruq and asked him, and he said: 'The *bahirah*: when a she-camel gave birth to five or seven [births], they split her ear and said, "This is a *bahirah*."' = He said: 'Nor *sa'ibah*: a man would take some of his property and say, "This is a *sa'ibah*."' = He said: 'Nor *wasilah*: when a she-camel gave birth to a male, they ate it, the males only and not the females; and when she gave birth to a male and a female in one birth, they said, "She has connected her brother," and they did not eat them both. He said: When the male died, the males only, not the females, ate it.' = He said: 'Nor *ham*: when a camel had offspring and offspring of his offspring, they said, "This one has finished what is upon him," and they did not benefit from his back. They said, "This is a *hima*" (a protected thing).'"

[[Report 12829: "Yahya ibn Ibrahim al-Mas'udi," the teacher of al-Tabari, is: "Yahya ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Ubaydah al-Mas'udi," mentioned under nos. 84, 5379, 8811, 9744.
His father is: "Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Ubaydah al-Mas'udi," mentioned under nos. 84, 5379, 8811, 9744.
His father is: "Muhammad ibn Abi Ubaydah al-Mas'udi," also mentioned there.
His grandfather is: "Abu Ubaydah ibn Ma'n al-Mas'udi," also mentioned.
In the printed edition here it was: "this is a *ham*," and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]]

12830. Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us, from al-A'mash, from Muslim ibn Subayh, who said: I asked Alqamah about the saying of Allah: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah* nor *sa'ibah*," and he said: "What do you do with this? This is a thing that the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do."

12831. Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman and Yahya ibn Adam related to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah*." He said: The *bahirah* is the one that has borne five births and then was left alone.

12832. Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir ibn Abd al-Hamid related to us, from Mughirah, from al-Sha'bi: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah*." He said: The *bahirah* is the *mukhdaramah*

[["*Al-mukhdaramah*" refers to she-camels and sheep whose ear is half cut off, or whose ear-tip is cut, or one of whose two ears is cut; it was a mark of the Jahiliyyah. In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us on the day of sacrifice from a *mukhdaramah* she-camel."]]

"nor *sa'ibah*," and the *sa'ibah* is what was let loose for the *'idi*

[["*Al-'idi*" (with a *kasra* on the *'ayn* and an open *dal*): the strangers, meaning the guests, as it comes in the other reports. This is how it is in the manuscript, "*al-'idi*." As for the printed edition, it has "*lil-hadi*" (for the offering), which is a distortion and a pure error. If there is an error in the copyist's writing, the nearest likelihood is that it is "*lil-mu'tari*" (for the one who comes seeking). It is said: "*'arahu yi'ruhu wa i'taraha*" when he visits him seeking his kindness. And it is said: "So-and-so is visited by guests and *ta'tarihi*," meaning he is approached by them. It is on this basis that they explained the saying of al-Nabighah: "I came to you naked, my garments worn, / in fear, suspicion may be cast upon me." That is: a guest seeking your bounty.]]

= and the *wasilah*, when she gives birth after four births, in the view of Jarir, and then gives birth to a fifth, a male and a female; she has connected her brother = and the *ham*, the one whose offspring's offspring have mated among the camels.

12833. Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mughirah, from al-Sha'bi, in a similar manner = except that he said: and the *wasilah* is the one that gave birth after four births, a male and a female; they said, "She has connected her brother." And the rest of the report is like the report of Ibn Humayd.

12834. Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Ishaq al-Azraq related to us, from Zakariyya, from al-Sha'bi: that he was asked about the *bahirah*, and he said: It is the one whose ears are slit. He was asked about the *sa'ibah*, and he said: They used to give the camels and sheep as offerings to their gods, leaving them with their gods, so they would go and mingle with the sheep of the people,

[[In the printed edition: "... with their gods, to be slaughtered, and mingle with the sheep of the people," differing from the manuscript, which ruins the sentence. As for his saying, "so they go and mingle," I noted in 7:457, note 6, that the Arabs use "*dhahaba*" (went) among the words of assistance that enter speech to depict a movement or clarify an action, such as their saying: "So-and-so sat, no one passes him but he reviles him," where neither the meaning of "going" nor of "sitting" is intended. Similar examples are many in their speech. See also this, pp. 250–251, note 1.]]

so none drink their milk except the men, and if one of them dies, the men and the women eat it together.

12835. Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the saying of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah*," and what comes with it: "The *bahirah*" is a camel whose wool, back, flesh, and milk the people of the Jahiliyyah forbade, except to men. Whatever it bore of a male and a female was in its condition; and if it died, men and women shared in eating its flesh. When the male camel mates with one of the offspring of the *bahirah*, he is the *hami*. And *al-hami* is a noun. [[In the printed edition, the phrase "*wa al-hami ism*" was omitted, thinking it was an addition with no meaning. But he meant that "*al-hami*" is the name of this camel from the offspring of the *bahirah*, and is not an active participle.]] As for the *sa'ibah*, it is of the sheep in a similar way, except that whatever it bore from its offspring up to six young was in its condition. When it bore a male or a female or two males at the seventh, they slaughtered it, and its men ate it, not its women. If it gave birth to a female and male twins [*tawammat*], it was a *wasilah*, to leave off slaughtering the male for the female. [[The word "*tawammat*" occurs thus in the printed edition and the manuscript, and I have not found them using this sense except "*atamat al-mar'ah wa kullu hamil*" (the woman and every pregnant one gave birth to twins), meaning she gave birth to two in one womb. This is a word I do not know what to say about except that it occurs thus here.]] And if they were two females, they were left alone.

[[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "*tark*" without a *lam*, and what I have established seems closer to the correct form to me.]]

12836. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah* nor *sa'ibah*." The *bahirah* is the she-camel: when a man's she-camel gave birth to five young, he would intend the fifth, so long as it was not a *saqab* (male),

[[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "so long as it was not a male," and what I have established is the correct form. The *saqab* is the male of the camel's offspring. Al-Asma'i said: when the she-camel gives birth to her young, the young one at the moment of delivery is called *salil*, before it is known whether it is male or female. When it is known, if it is male, it is a *saqab*.]]

and he would slit its ears, and not shear its wool, and not drink its milk. That is the *bahirah*. = "Nor *sa'ibah*": a man would let loose from his property whatever he wished. = "Nor *wasilah*": it is the ewe when she gave birth to seven; he would intend the seventh, and if it was a male, he slaughtered it, and if it was a female, he left it; and if there were in her womb a male and a female, and she gave birth to both, they said, "She has connected her brother," and both were left, not slaughtered. That is the *wasilah*. = And his saying, "Nor *ham*": a man would have a stallion, and when he impregnated ten she-camels, it was said: "*Ham*, so leave him alone."

12837. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to us, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning his saying: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah* nor *sa'ibah*": they let them loose for their idols. = "Nor *wasilah*": he says: the sheep. = "Nor *ham*": he says: the stallion of the camels.

12838. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, concerning his saying: "Allah has not instituted any *bahirah*, nor *sa'ibah*, nor *wasilah*, nor *ham*": it was a severity that Satan imposed upon the people of the Jahiliyyah concerning their wealth, and a strictness upon them. So the *bahirah* was among the camels: when a man had five from his camels give birth, he looked at the fifth birth; if it was a *saqab* (male), he slaughtered it and the men ate it, not the women; if it was dead, its males and females shared in it; and if it was a *ha'il* (barren female), which is the female, she was left alone, and her ear was slit, and her wool was not sheared, and no milk was drunk from her, and no back was ridden, and the name of Allah was not mentioned over her.

[[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "like the camels," and this is an undoubted error.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 103 (part 3 of 3):

And the *sa'iba* (a camel or other beast set free, left to graze without restriction): they would let loose whatever of their property they wished, so it was not prevented from a watering-trough it wished to drink from, [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "فلا تمتنع", and the correct reading is what I have set down.]] nor from a pasture it wished to graze in. And the *wasila* (a ewe that gives birth to twins, a kind of ewe-sacrifice practice) among sheep, from the seventh birth: if it was a male, they would slaughter it and only the men would eat it, not the women. And if it was dead, both their males and females shared in it. And if it brought forth a male and a female together, it was said: "She has joined her brother, so she has prevented him from being slaughtered." And the *ham* (a stallion freed from labour): when a stallion had sired ten offspring from his own line, or had sired his grandchildren, it was said: "He has been protected; his back has been shielded." So he was not burdened, not bridled, and not ridden.

12839 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, concerning the words of God: ﴿God did not appoint any bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and set free), nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham﴾. As for the *bahira*, it was of camels: when a she-camel had given birth to five young, if the fifth was a male calf they would slaughter it and offer it to their gods, and its mother was of the choicest camels. And if it was a female (*rubaa*, a young camel born in spring, the first of the year's births, and the female of it is called *rubaa*), they would let it live, slit its mother's ear, shear its wool, and leave it in the open land. It was not permitted for them to milk it for any purpose, they did not milk it for milk, nor shear its wool, nor ride upon its back; it was one of the livestock whose backs were forbidden. And as for the *sa'iba*: it is the man who lets loose from his property whatever he wishes, as a form of thanksgiving, if his wealth increased, or if he recovered from an ailment, or if he rode a she-camel and succeeded; then he names her "sa'iba," lets her go, and none of the Arabs would encounter her without being struck by a punishment in this world. And as for the *wasila*: it is from sheep. It is the ewe that gave birth to three or five young, and the last of them was a male kid; they would slaughter it and offer it to the house of their gods. But if it was a female kid (*anaq*), they would let it live; and if it was a male and a female kid together, they would spare the male kid on account of the female, for she was a *wasila* who had joined her brother. And as for the *ham*: it is the stallion that mates with the camels for ten years. It is also said: when he has mated with his grandchildren, it is said: "He has protected his back," and they leave him, never touched nor slaughtered, and he is not prevented from any pasture he wants; and he is one of the livestock whose backs were forbidden.

12840 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from al-Zuhri, from Ibn al-Musayyab, concerning the words of God: ﴿God did not appoint any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham﴾. He said: "The *bahira*" is of camels, whose milk was withheld for the idols (*tawaghit*). [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "يمنع" with ʿayn; the correct reading is with ḥāʾ.]] "The *sa'iba*" is of camels; they would let them loose for their idols. "The *wasila*" is of camels: a she-camel would bear a female first, then bear a second female, [[In the printed edition: "تبكر", and the correct reading is from the manuscript. It is said: "ابتكرت الحامل" when she bore her first-born, and "أثنت" for the second, and "ثلثت" for the third.]] and they would call her the "wasila," saying: "She has joined two females with no male between them." So they would slit her ear for their idols, or slaughter her — the doubt is from Abu Jaʿfar. "The *ham*" is the stallion of camels, which used to mate a counted number of times. [[In the printed edition: "المعدود" without the final tā'; I have set down what is in the manuscript, which is correct.]] When it reached that number they would say: "This is a ham; he has protected his back," and he was left, and so they named him "the ham." Maʿmar said: Qatada said, "when he has mated ten times."

12841 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada, who said: "The *bahira*" is of camels: when a she-camel had given birth to five young, if the fifth was a male, it was for the men and not the women; but if it was a female, they would slit its ears and let it go, and they would not slaughter any of its offspring, nor drink its milk, nor ride its back. "The *sa'iba*": they would let loose some of their camels, so that it would not be prevented from a watering-trough it wished to drink from, nor from a pasture it wished to graze in. "The *wasila*" is a sheep: when it gave birth to seven young, if the seventh was a male, it was slaughtered, and the men only ate it, not the women; but if it was a female, it was left.

12842 - Related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh al-Fadl ibn Khalid say: ʿUbayd ibn Sulayman related to us, from al-Dahhak, concerning the words of God: ﴿God did not appoint any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham﴾. As for the *bahira*: when a she-camel had given birth to five young, they would slaughter the fifth if it was a male calf, and if it was a *rubaa*, they would slit its ear and let it live; and this is the *bahira*. As for the male calf, their women would not eat from it; it was exclusively for their men. But if the she-camel died, or they gave birth to it dead, then their men and women shared in it equally, and all ate from it. As for the *sa'iba*: a man would let loose some of his livestock, so it was left to graze freely, and no one would benefit from its back, its offspring, its milk, its hair, or its wool. As for the *wasila*: the sheep, when it gave birth to seven young, they would slaughter the seventh if it was a male kid; if it was a female kid, they would let it live; and if it was a male and a female kid together, they would spare both of them, and they said: "The male kid has been joined by its sister, so she has made it forbidden to us." As for the *ham*: the stallion, when they had ridden his grandchildren, they said: "This one has protected his back, and his grandchildren have secured him," [[In the printed edition: "وأحرز أولاد ولده"; the correct reading is from the manuscript. "أحرزه": he preserved it, guarded it, and shielded it.]] so they would not ride him, nor prevent him from any shrub-pasture or watering-trough he drank from, even if the trough did not belong to its owner. And among their camels there was a group upon which they never mentioned the name of God in any of their affairs: neither when they rode, nor when they carried loads, nor when they milked, nor when they gave birth, nor when they sold. Concerning this, God, may His remembrance be exalted, revealed: ﴿God did not appoint any bahira, nor sa'iba﴾, to His words: ﴿and most of them do not understand﴾.

12843 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning the words of God: ﴿God did not appoint any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham﴾: "This is a thing that the people of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance before Islam) used to practise, and it has passed away." He said: "The *bahira*": a man would slit the ears of his she-camel, then free her as he would free his slave-girl or his slave-boy; she was not milked nor ridden. "The *sa'iba*": he lets her loose without slitting. "The *ham*": when a stallion sired seven female offspring in succession, his back was protected; he was not ridden, nor was any work done upon him. "The *wasila*": from the sheep: when it gave birth to seven females in succession, its meat was protected from being eaten.

12844 - Yunus related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Yusuf related to us, saying: al-Layth ibn Saʿd related to us, saying: Ibn al-Hadi related to me, from Ibn Shihab, who said: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: "The *sa'iba*" is the one that was let loose so that no burden would be placed upon it. "The *bahira*" is the one whose milk was withheld for the idols, so that no one would milk it. "The *wasila*" is the young she-camel that gave birth first to a female, then gave birth again after that to a female; and they would dedicate it to the idols, calling it the "wasila," because it had joined its sisters, one to the other. [[In the printed edition the word "أخواتها" is omitted; there is no need to omit it, for the sentence is sound.]] "The *hami*" is the stallion camel, which mates ten camels. When its mating is "nafada" (the word is unclear in the printed text and manuscript, which read "نقص", but the correct reading is "نفض" with nūn, fāʾ and ḍād. It is said: "nafadat al-ibil and anfadat," meaning all of them gave birth. Dhu al-Rummah said: "Both her two cheeks, they shed, and she did not find for her a calf's scent in the two births that touches her." Meaning: each of the two cheeks (meaning the two births) expels what is in her womb of foetuses, so that females are found in them with no male among them. As for his phrase "nafada ḍirabahu," the lexicographers did not record this expression, but this is its explanation: that the she-camels he covered gave birth to females in succession, with no male among them, as was mentioned in the reports narrated by Abu Jaʿfar.] they dedicate him to the idols, and they relieve him of burden, so they do not load anything upon him, and they call him the "hami."

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: These are matters that existed in the Jahiliyya, and Islam nullified them, so we do not know of any people who practise them today.

Since this is so, and what the Jahiliyya used to practise cannot be known — because there is no trace of it in Islam today, nor in polytheism, that we might recognise it — except through a report, and the reports about what they used to do in this regard are varied in the variance we have mentioned, then the correct statement on this matter is to say: as for the meanings of these names, we have explained them at the beginning of our discussion of the interpretation (*ta'wil*, the meaning or explanation of a verse) of this verse. And as for the manner in which these people acted in this regard, we have no knowledge of it. Reports have come describing their practice as we have related, and ignorance of this does not harm when what is needed of knowledge is sufficient to reach its reality, which is that these people used to forbid for themselves from their livestock what God had not forbidden, [[In the printed edition: "كانوا محرمين من أنعامهم"; the good reading is from the manuscript.]] following the footsteps of Satan. So God, may His remembrance be exalted, rebuked them for that, and informed them that all of it is lawful. The forbidden in everything, according to us, is what God, may His remembrance be exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ) have forbidden, by explicit text or by indication; and the lawful in it is what God and His Messenger have likewise made lawful. [[In the printed edition: "ما أحله الله"; I have set down what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against God, and most of them do not reason﴾ (103).

Abu Jaʿfar said: The interpreters differed concerning who is meant by "those who disbelieve" in this place, and what is meant by His words "and most of them do not reason."

Some of them said: those meant by "those who disbelieve" are the Jews, and those "who do not reason" are the idol-worshippers.

Mention of those who said that:

12845 - Ibn Wakiʿ related to us, saying: Abu Usama related to us, from Sufyan, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Muhammad ibn Abi Musa, concerning ﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against God﴾, he said: the People of the Book. ﴿And most of them do not reason﴾, he said: the idol-worshippers. [[The report 12845: "Muhammad ibn Abi Musa" was mentioned under number 10556.]]

* *

Others said: Rather they are people of one religion, but "the inventors" are the leaders who are followed, and "those who do not reason" are the followers.

Mention of those who said that:

12846 - Related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: Kharija related to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Shaʿbi, concerning His words: ﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against God, and most of them do not reason﴾: they are the followers. As for "those who invented," they understood that they had invented. [[In the printed edition: "يعقلون أنهم افتروا"; I have set down what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The most preferable of the statements on this matter, according to us, as correct, is to say: the ones meant by His words "But those who disbelieve invent lies against God" are those who slit the *bahaʾir* (plural of bahira), let loose the *sawaʾib* (plural of sa'iba), joined the *wasa'il* (plural of wasila), and protected the *hawami* (plural of ham): such as ʿAmr ibn Luhayy and his like, from among those who established evil customs for the people of polytheism, changed the religion of God, the religion of truth, [[In the printed edition: "ممن سنوا لأهل الشرك... وغيروا" in the plural; I have set down what is in the manuscript, which is entirely correct and is not refuted by the plural "وأضافوا" that follows it.]] and attributed to God, may His remembrance be exalted, that He is the one who forbade what they forbade and made lawful what they made lawful, inventing lies against God while they knew, and fabricating falsehood against Him while they understood. So God, may His remembrance be exalted, declared them liars in their saying that, and in their attribution to Him of making lawful what they made lawful and forbidding what they forbade. Thus He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: "God did not appoint any bahira nor sa'iba; but those who disbelieve are the ones who do that, and invent lies against God."

= [[His words "and that it should be said" are coordinated with His words at the beginning of the paragraph: "The most preferable of the statements on this matter, according to us, as correct, is to say..."]] And it should be said: the ones meant by His words "and most of them do not reason" are the followers of those who established these customs for them from among the ignorant polytheists. Undoubtedly they are more numerous than those for whom those customs were established, so God, may His remembrance be exalted, described them as not reasoning, because they did not understand that those who established those customs for them, and informed them that they were from God, were liars in their reports, deceivers; rather they thought that they were right in what they said, and truthful in their reports. The meaning of the speech is only: "and most of them do not understand that this prohibition, which these polytheists forbade and attributed to God, may His remembrance be exalted, is a lie and falsehood." [[See the explanation of "افترى" (invented) in the earlier passages: 6:292 and 8:451.]] This statement that we have made on this matter is similar to the statement of al-Shaʿbi that we mentioned before. [[In the printed edition, "قبل" has been omitted, due to a poor writing in the manuscript.]] There is no sense in the saying of one who said: "What is meant by those who disbelieve are the People of the Book," because the rebuke at the beginning of the verse is from God, may His remembrance be exalted, upon the polytheists of the Arabs; so concluding with them is more fitting than with others, since nothing had appeared in the speech that would turn the reference away from them to others.

* *

Qatada used to say in a similar manner:

12847 - Bishr ibn Muʿadh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Saʿid related to us, from Qatada, concerning His words: ﴿and most of them do not reason﴾, he says: the prohibition of Satan which was forbidden to them was only from Satan, and they do not reason. [[In the printed edition: "يقول: لا يعقلون تحريم الشيطان الذي يحرم عليهم"; it adds "وغير", which corrupts the whole sentence, while the editor thinks he is correcting it.]]

The commentary of Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) on the verse: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ (5:104)

Abu Ja'far said: The Exalted, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "And when it is said to those who slit the ears of the she-camels (al-bahā'ir) and let loose the free-roaming camels (al-sawā'ib), who do not realize that by attributing the prohibition of these to Allah, the Exalted, they fabricate lies against Allah: 'Come to the revelation of Allah and the verses of His Book, and to His Messenger, so that the falsity of your claim may become clear to you, regarding what you attribute to Allah, the Exalted, of prohibiting these things that you prohibit'" [[See the explanation of "ta'ālaw" above: 6:474, 483, 485; 8:513.]]. They answered the one who invited them to that by saying: "Sufficient for us is what we found our forefathers doing, acting upon it," and they say: "We follow them, and they are our leaders and guides, and we have been content with what we took from them, and we are satisfied with what they were upon of prohibition and permission." [[See the explanation of "ḥasb" above: 4:244; 7:405.]]

The Exalted, may His remembrance be exalted, said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "Even though their forefathers, those who say this saying, knew nothing?" That is: They did not know that what they attribute to Allah, the Exalted, of prohibiting the bahīra, the sā'iba, the wasīla and the ḥām, is a lie and a fabrication against Allah, with no reality or validity to it. For they were followers of the fabricators who began the prohibition of these things, fabricating against Allah by their saying what they used to say, attributing to Allah, the Exalted, what they attribute. And they were not, in what they were doing of that, upon rectitude and correctness; rather, they were upon error and mistake. [[In the printed edition: "ma kānū fīmā hum bihi ʿāmilūn," while in the manuscript: "kānū" without "mā." The context requires what has been adopted, since it is coordinated with his earlier statement: "He says: they did not know..."]]

**The discussion on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:** ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul. No harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are [rightly] guided﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: Allah, dhikruhu (His remembrance is exalted), says: O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul, so set it right, work to free it from the punishment of Allah, dhikruhu, and look after it by that which brings it closer to its Lord. "No harm will come to you from those who have gone astray," meaning: those who disbelieved and took a path other than the path of truth will not harm you, when you are guided and believe in your Lord and obey Him in what He has commanded you and in what He has forbidden you, so that you make unlawful what He has made unlawful and make lawful what He has made lawful.

* *

The word ﴿anfusakum﴾ ("your souls") is in the accusative by way of *al-ighra'* (a form of warning or urging to attention). The Arabs use *'alayka* ("upon you"), *'indaka* ("with you"), *dunaka* ("beside you") and *ilayka* ("to you") in this manner, treating them as *sifat* (here meaning prepositions and adverbs of place, as is clear from their context). [[The word "al-sifat" here refers to the prepositions (huruf al-jarr) and adverbial expressions (al-zuruf), as is clear from the context. See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 322, 323.]]

The people of ta'wil (interpretation, i.e. the meaning and its ultimate application) differed concerning the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: its meaning is, "O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul," when you command the good and forbid the evil, but it is not accepted from you.

Those who said this include:

**12848** – al-Hasan reported that this verse was recited to Ibn Mas'ud: "O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided." Ibn Mas'ud said: "This is not its time. Say it as long as it is accepted from you; but when it is rejected from you, then upon you is your own soul." [[The narration 12848: Sawwar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sawwar al-'Anbari, the judge, the teacher of al-Tabari. Trustworthy (thiqah), whose biography is in al-Tahdhib. His father, 'Abd Allah ibn Sawwar al-'Anbari, the judge, is trustworthy, and his biography is in al-Tahdhib. Abu al-Ashhab is Ja'far ibn Hayyan al-Sa'di al-'Attaridi, trustworthy, whom the Six (Kutub al-Sittah) narrated from; he has passed as no. 11408. The narration will be traced in the note on no. 12850.]]

**12849** – Ibn Wakii' narrated to us: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Abu al-Ashhab, from al-Hasan who said: Ibn Mas'ud was mentioned [[In the printed edition: "dhukira Ibn Mas'ud" without "'inda"; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]] "O you who have believed," then he mentioned something similar.
