**12850** – Ya'qub narrated to us: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, from Yunus, from al-Hasan who said: A man said to Ibn Mas'ud: Did not Allah say, "O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided"? He said: This is not its time. Say it as long as it is accepted from you; but when it is rejected from you, then upon you is your own soul. [[In the narration 12848–12850: the report of al-Hasan from Ibn Mas'ud was recorded by al-Haythami in Majma' al-Zawa'id 7: 19, and he said: "It was narrated by al-Tabarani, and its narrators are the narrators of the authentic (sahih), except that al-Hasan al-Basri did not hear from Ibn Mas'ud."]]

**12851** – al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah narrated to us: Shababah ibn Sawwar narrated to us: al-Rabi' ibn Subaih narrated to us, from Sufyan ibn 'Iqal who said: It was said to Ibn 'Umar: "If you were to sit in these days and not command or forbid, since Allah, dhikruhu, says, 'Upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided'?" Ibn 'Umar said: "It is not for me, nor for my companions, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Let the present one convey to the absent one.' So we were the present ones, and you are the absent ones [[al-Ghayb (with a fatha on the ghayn and the ya') is the plural of ghd'ib (absent), like khadim and khadam.]], but this verse is for people who will come after us: if they say it, it will not be accepted from them." [[The narration 12851: al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah al-'Abdi al-Baghdadi, the teacher of al-Tabari, has passed as no. 9373. Shababah ibn Sawwar al-Fazzazi has passed as nos. 37, 6701, 10051. al-Rabi' ibn Subaih al-Sa'di has passed as nos. 6403, 6404, 10533. Sufyan ibn 'Iqal: his biography is in al-Kabir 2/2/94 and in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/219, and both said: "He narrated from Ibn 'Umar; al-Rabi' narrated from him," and they added nothing more. It was traced in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 340, and he attributed it additionally to Ibn Mardawayh.]]

**12852** – Ahmad ibn al-Miqdam narrated to us: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard my father say: Qatadah narrated to us, from Abu Mazin who said: I went to Madinah in the time of 'Uthman, and there was a group of Muslims sitting. One of them recited this verse, "Upon you is your own soul," and most of them said: The interpretation of this verse has not come today. [[The narrations 12852 and 12853: Abu Mazin al-Azdi al-Hadani was one of the righteous of the Azd. He came to Madinah in the time of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. Qatadah narrated from a companion of his, from him. Thus said Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/44. But in these two chains there is no mention of the "man" from whom Qatadah narrated, as Abu Hatim said. It will appear in the chain no. 12856: "from Qatadah, from a man who said: I was in the caliphate of 'Uthman in Madinah," and this "man" is Abu Mazin, without doubt. Then it will appear in no. 12857: "from Qatadah: Abu Mazin narrated to us, a man of the righteous of the Azd, of the Banu al-Huddan," where Qatadah explicitly states the narration from him, with no "man" between them as Abu Hatim said. So I fear there is an error in the words of Abu Hatim. This report was traced by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 340, and he attributed it additionally to 'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh.]]

**12853** – Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us: 'Amr ibn 'Asim narrated to us: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, from his father, from Qatadah, from Abu Mazin, similar to it. [[See the note on no. 12852.]]

**12854** – Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Ja'far and Abu 'Asim narrated to us, both saying: 'Awf narrated to us, from Sawwar ibn Shabib who said: I was with Ibn 'Umar when a man came to him, strong in the eye and sharp of tongue, and said: O Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, we are six, all of whom have recited the Qur'an and hastened in it, and all of whom are striving without falling short, and all of whom detest that he should commit a base act [[In Ibn Kathir 3: 259, he narrated from this place of the tafsir and added here: "...that he should commit a base act, except the good," which are not in our manuscript.]] – and in that, some of them bear witness against others of polytheism! A man among the people said: And what base act do you want, more than that some of them bear witness against others of polytheism! He said: The man said: I did not ask you, I am asking the Shaykh! So he repeated the account to 'Abd Allah, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said: Perhaps you think, may you have no father, that I will order you to go and kill them! Admonish them and forbid them, and if they disobey you, then upon you is your own soul, for Allah, dhikruhu, says: "O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided; to Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do." [[The narration 12854: Sawwar ibn Shabib al-Sa'di al-A'raji. Banu al-A'raj is a tribe of the Banu Sa'd. "al-A'raj" is al-Harith ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd ibn Zayd Manat ibn Tamim, whose leg was cut off on the day of Tayyas, so he was named "al-A'raj." He is trustworthy, from Kufah, narrated from Ibn 'Umar; 'Awf narrated from him, and 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar. His biography is in al-Kabir 2/2/168 and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/270. This report was quoted by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir 3: 259, and al-Suyuti traced it in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 341, limiting himself to attributing it to Ibn Mardawayh.]]

**12855** – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hasan, that Ibn Mas'ud was asked by a man about the words of Allah, "Upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided." He said: This is not its time; today it is accepted [[His words "today it is accepted" mean: the word of truth in commanding the good and forbidding the evil.]], but a time is about to come when you command the good and it is dealt with in such-and-such a way to you – or he said: it will not be accepted from you – then at that time: "Upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray." [[The narration 12855: see the note on the narrations 12848–12850. In the printed edition here was: "...from those who have gone astray when you are guided," with the addition, and what is in the manuscript has been restored.]]

**12856** – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, from a man who said: I was in the caliphate of 'Uthman in Madinah, in a circle in which were companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). There was among them an elder to whom they would refer [[His words "yusnidun ilayhi" ("they would refer to him") mean: they would turn to his knowledge, understanding and jurisprudence, and would seek him out for understanding what was unclear to them. It is said: "I entrusted my affair to him" (asnadtu amri ilayhi), meaning: I committed it to him and relied upon him. al-Farazdaq said: "To al-Abrash al-Kalbi I entrusted a need, which the living tribes of Tamim and Wa'il left to one another." All of this is something that should be noted in the books of lexicography, for it is not clear there.]]. A man recited: "Upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided," and the elder said: Its interpretation is only at the end of time.

**12857** – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah who said: Abu Mazin narrated to us, a man of the righteous of the Azd, of the Banu al-Huddan [[In the printed edition: "Banu al-Judan" with a jim, which is an error.]], who said: I went during the lifetime of 'Uthman to Madinah, and I sat in a circle of companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [[In the printed edition: "fiha ashab Rasul Allah," and in the manuscript: "fiha min ashab Rasul Allah"; the scribe struck the pen on "fiha" and restored it correctly.]], and a man from the people recited this verse, "No harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided." A man from the eldest of the people said: Leave this verse, for its interpretation is at the end of time. [[The two narrations 12856 and 12857: see the note on the two preceding narrations, nos. 12852 and 12853.]]

**12858** – al-Qasim narrated to us: al-Husayn narrated to us: Ibn Fudalah narrated to us, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr who said: I was in a circle in which were companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I was the youngest of the people. They discussed commanding the good and forbidding the evil, and I said: Does not Allah say in His Book, "O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided"? They turned towards me with one tongue and said: Do you bring a verse of the Qur'an that you do not know [[In the printed edition: "tanza'u bi-ayah min al-Qur'an" without the "in", which differs from the manuscript; and what differs is correct. But it is said: "intaza'a ma'nan jayyidan" and "nazaʿahu," meaning: he extracted and deduced it; and it is said: "intaza'a bi-al-ayah wa al-shi'r," meaning: he cited it as an example.]], and you do not know its interpretation!? until I wished that I had not spoken. Then they turned to talking among themselves, and when the time of their rising came, they said: "You are a young boy, and you brought a verse whose meaning you do not know. Perhaps you will live to see that time, when you see avarice obeyed, desire followed, and the admiration of every person of opinion for his own opinion; then upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided." [[The narration 12858: Ibn Fudalah is Mubarak ibn Fudalah ibn Abi Umayyah, Abu Fudalah al-Basri. In the tafsir of Ibn Kathir: "Abu Fudalah narrated to us," and he has passed as nos. 154, 597, 611, 1901. Mu'awiyah ibn Salih ibn Hudayr al-Hadrami, one of the great scholars, has passed many times, including nos. 186, 187, 2072, 8472, 11255. Mu'awiyah ibn Salih is not recorded as having a narration from Jubayr ibn Nufayr; rather his son 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr narrated from him. Jubayr ibn Nufayr was from the Islamic and pre-Islamic period, and has passed as nos. 6656, 7009. This report has a broken chain, and it was quoted by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir 3: 260, and al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 340, and he did not attribute it to anyone other than Ibn Jarir.]]

**12859** – Hannad narrated to us: Layth ibn Harun narrated to us: Ishaq al-Razi narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, concerning His words: "O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided; to Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do." He said: They were sitting with 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and between two men there was what there is between people, until each of them rose towards his companion. A man from among the companions of 'Abd Allah said: Shall I not rise and command them to the good and forbid them from the evil? Another beside him said: Upon you is your own soul, for Allah, dhikruhu, says: "Upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided." He said: Ibn Mas'ud heard it and said: Mah [[It is "mah" as in the printed edition, Ibn Kathir, and al-Durr al-Manthur; "mah" is a word of rebuke meaning: stop this. In the manuscript in its place: "mahl," and I fear it is an error by the copyist; if it were written "mahlan," it would be correct, as it is said: "mahlan ya fulan," meaning: gently and calmly, do not hasten.]], this has not yet come to its interpretation! The Qur'an was revealed where it was revealed, and among it are verses whose interpretation passed before they were revealed, and among it is what its interpretation occurred in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and among it are verses whose interpretation occurred shortly after the Prophet (ﷺ) [[In the printed edition: "ayy qad waqa'" with an addition; the manuscript has been restored.]], and among it are verses whose interpretation will occur after today, and among it are verses whose interpretation will occur at the Hour, according to what was mentioned of the Hour [[In the printed edition: "according to what was mentioned of the matter of the Hour," with the word "matter" added; in the manuscript the scribe omitted "'ala," and its restoration is correct.]], and among it are verses whose interpretation will occur on the Day of Reckoning, according to what was mentioned of the reckoning, the Garden and the Fire [[In the printed edition: "min amr al-hisab," with the addition; the manuscript has been restored.]]. So as long as your hearts are one, and your desires are one, and you are not clothed in sects, and some of you have not tasted the violence of others, then command and forbid. But when the hearts and desires differ, and you are clothed in sects, and some of you have tasted the violence of others, then each man is for himself, and at that time the interpretation of this verse has come. [[The narration 12859: "Layth ibn Harun" – I have found no biography of him nor any mention. "Ishaq al-Razi" is Ishaq ibn Sulayman al-Razi, who has passed as nos. 6456, 10338, 11240. See the following chain no. 12866. This report was quoted by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir 3: 258, 259, and al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 339, 340, and he attributed it additionally to 'Abd ibn Humayd, Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab. It will come with another chain in the one that follows.]]

**12860** – al-Qasim narrated to us: al-Husayn narrated to us: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ibn Mas'ud: that there was between two men some of what there is between people, until each of them rose towards his companion; then he mentioned something similar. [[The narration 12860: see the preceding report.]]

**12861** – Ahmad ibn al-Miqdam narrated to me: Harami [[The chain here has a gap in the text: "Harami ..........," the dots in the original indicate a missing name.]] narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Hasan say: Some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) interpreted this verse: "O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul; no harm will come to you from those who have gone astray when you are guided," and some of his companions said: Leave this verse, for it is not for you. [[The narration 12861: this is an incomplete chain, without doubt. Ahmad ibn al-Miqdam ibn Sulayman al-'Ijli, Abu al-Ash'ath. Al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from him; he is sound in narration. He was born around the year 156 and died in the year 253. Harami ibn 'Umarah ibn Abi Hafsah al-'Atki has passed as no. 8513. He died in the year 201, and it is impossible that he met al-Hasan or heard from him, for al-Hasan al-Basri died around the year 110, so the chain is defective; for this reason I placed dots between him and al-Hasan, indicating a gap in the chain.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 105 (part 2 of 3):

12862 - Ismail ibn Isra'il al-Lu'lu' al-Ramli related to me, saying: Ayyub ibn Suwayd related to us, saying: Utbah ibn Abi Hakim related to us, from Amr ibn Jariya al-Lakhmi, from Abu Umayya al-Sha'bani, who said: I asked Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani about this verse: ﴿O you who believe, take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾. He said: You have asked about it one who is well informed. I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and he said: "Abu Tha'laba, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. But when you see worldliness given preference, stinginess obeyed, every person of opinion admiring his own opinion, then take care of yourself. Indeed, after you there will be days of patience. Whoever holds fast on that day to what you are upon will have the reward of fifty workers!" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, the reward of fifty workers from among them?" He said: "No, the reward of fifty workers from among you." [[Narration 12862: It will come with another chain in the one that follows.
"Ismu'il ibn Isra'il al-Lu'lu' al-Ramli" has appeared under numbers 10236 and 12213, and I noted there that Ibn Abi Hatim has "al-Sallal" there, while 10236 has "al-Dallal," and here "al-Lu'lu'" (one who makes and sells pearls). We find nothing that prefers any one of the three.
"Ayyub ibn Suwayd al-Ramli" is trustworthy but spoken of (regarding his memory). It has appeared under number 12213.
"Utbah ibn Abi Hakim al-Sha'bani al-Hamdani, then al-Urduni" is trustworthy; Ibn Ma'in declared him weak. It has appeared under number 12213.
"Amr ibn Jariya al-Lakhmi" is trustworthy and his biography is in al-Tahdhib. In the printed edition it was "Amr ibn Khalid," which is a pure error. In the manuscript, it was written "Khalid" and then changed to "Jariya," which is correct.
"Abu Umayya al-Tha'labi" (the printed text reads "al-Sha'bani"): his name is "Yahmad" (with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the mim); it was also said his name is "Abdullah ibn Akhamar." He is trustworthy. His biography is in al-Tahdhib.
"Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani": there is much disagreement about his name and his father's name. He was a Companion.
His narration will come in the one that follows.]]

12863 - Ali ibn Sahl related to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim informed us, from Ibn al-Mubarak and others, from Utbah ibn Abi Hakim, [from Amr ibn Jariya al-Lakhmi], from Abu Umayya al-Sha'bani, who said: I asked Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani: How should we act regarding this verse: ﴿O you who believe, take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾? Abu Tha'laba said: You have asked about it one who is well informed. I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and he said: "Enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, until you see stinginess obeyed, desire followed, and every person of opinion admiring his own opinion; then take care of your own inner self (khuwaysat nafsika), and leave their common folk. Indeed, behind you there will be days in which the reward of the worker is the reward of fifty of you." [["Khuwaysa" is the diminutive of "khassa."
Narration 12863: "Utbah ibn Abi Hakim," in the manuscript is "Ubayda ibn Abi Hakim," which is an obvious error.
In the manuscript and the printed edition, the phrase [from Amr ibn Jariya al-Lakhmi] is omitted, so I have placed it between brackets.
This is the very same chain as al-Tirmidhi's.
This report was transmitted by al-Tirmidhi in the Book of Tafsir, by way of Sa'id ibn Ya'qub al-Talaqani, from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, from Uqba ibn Abi Hakim, with a wording similar to what is here. Then al-Tirmidhi said: "Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: Someone other than Utbah added to me: It was said: O Messenger of Allah, the reward of fifty men from us or from them? He said: No, rather the reward of fifty men from you." Then al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan gharib hadith."
Ibn Majah transmitted it in his Sunan, no. 4014, by way of Hisham ibn Ammar, from Sadaqa ibn Khalid, from Utbah ibn Abi Hakim, with a wording similar to its own.
Abu Dawud transmitted it in his Sunan 4:174, no. 4341, by way of Abu al-Rabi' Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Ataki, from Ibn al-Mubarak, with the like of it.
Ibn Kathir cited it in his Tafsir 3:258, and al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 2:339, adding its attribution to al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, who authenticated it.]]

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is that when a servant acts in obedience to Allah, the one who goes astray after him and perishes will not harm him.

Those who said this:

12864 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding his saying: ﴿O you who believe, take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray﴾. He says: If the servant obeys Me in what I have commanded him concerning the lawful and the unlawful, then the one who goes astray after him will not harm him, when he acts upon what I have commanded him.

12865 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, regarding his saying: ﴿Take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾. He says: Obey My command, and preserve My charge.

12866 - Hannad related to us, saying: Laith ibn Harun related to us, saying: Ishaq al-Razi related to us, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from Safwan ibn al-Jawn, who said: A young man from among the people of desires came to him and mentioned something of his affair. Safwan said: Shall I not direct you to the special favor of Allah, which He has reserved for His friends? ﴿O you who believe, take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray﴾, the verse. [[Narration 12866: "Laith ibn Harun" (printed as "Harun"): I have not found him; see the earlier chain no. 12859.
"Ishaq" is "Ishaq ibn Sulayman al-Razi"; see no. 12859.
As for "Safwan ibn al-Jawn," he is written thus in the manuscript as well, and I have not found a biography for him. In al-Durr al-Manthur 2:341 it reads "Safwan ibn Muhriz," and it attributes it to Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim.
"Safwan ibn Muhriz ibn Ziyad al-Mazini, or al-Bahili": he narrated from Ibn Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. Jami' ibn Shaddad, Asim al-Ahwal, and Qatada narrated from him. He was among the worshippers; he made for himself a cellar in which he would weep. He died in the year 74 AH. His biography is in al-Tahdhib. It appeared under no. 6496.]]

12867 - Abd al-Karim ibn Abi Umayr related to us, saying: Abu al-Mutarrif al-Makhzumi related to us, saying: Juwaybir related to us, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: ﴿Take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾, so long as there is no sword or whip. [[Narration 12867: "Abd al-Karim ibn Abi Umayr" has appeared under nos. 7578 and 11368. "Abu al-Mutarrif al-Makhzumi" (printed as "al-Mutawwaf"): I have found no mention of him.]]

12868 - Ali ibn Sahl related to us, saying: Damra ibn Rabi'a related to us, saying: al-Hasan recited this verse: ﴿O you who believe, take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾. Then al-Hasan said: Praise be to Allah for it, and praise be to Allah for what it contains. There was no believer in the past, nor a believer in what remains, except that beside him there is a hypocrite who dislikes his deeds. [[Narration 12868: "Damra ibn Rabi'a al-Filastini al-Ramli" is trustworthy; he has appeared under no. 7134. In the printed edition it was "Murra ibn Rabi'a," which was a failure to read the manuscript properly.
This statement of al-Hasan, though it was obscure to people in earlier times, its truth in our time is seen plainly by the believer in every place he goes in the morning and evening.]]

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: ﴿O you who believe, take care of your own selves﴾, so act in obedience to Allah, ﴿no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾, when you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

Those who said this:

12869 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Hakkam ibn Salm related to us, from Anbasa, from Sa'd al-Baqqal, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: ﴿no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾. He said: When you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, the one who goes astray will not harm you if you are on the right path.

12870 - Ibn Wakî' related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman related to us, from Sufyan, from Abu al-Amis, from Abu al-Bakhtari, from Hudhayfa: ﴿Take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾. He said: When you are commanded and forbidden.

12871 - Hannad related to us, saying: Waki' related to us; and Ibn Wakî' related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Ibn Abi Khalid, from Qays ibn Abi Hazim, who said: Abu Bakr said: You recite this verse: ﴿No harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾, but when people see the wrongdoer, (Ibn Wakî' says: and) they do not take hold of his hands, Allah will soon encompass them all with His punishment. [[Narration 12871: The report of Qays ibn Abi Hazim from Abu Bakr was transmitted by Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) with chains, nos. 12871 to 12878, all stopping at Abu Bakr (mawquf), except nos. 12876 and 12878, which he transmitted connected and traced to the Prophet (marfu'), and except no. 12874, which is mursal. Most of Abu Ja'far's chains are weak.
He transmitted it from the chain of "Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid," from Qays ibn Abi Hazim, in nos. 12871 and 12873. From this chain, Ahmad transmitted it in his Musnad, nos. 1, 16, 29, 30, 53, connected and traced to the Prophet. Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir 3:258: "This hadith has been transmitted by the authors of the four Sunan, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and others, by many routes, from a large number of people, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, connected and traced to the Prophet. Some transmitted it from him as stopping at al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr). Al-Daraqutni and others preferred its being traced to the Prophet."
"Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid al-Ahmasi" is trustworthy; he has appeared under nos. 5694 and 5777.
"Qays ibn Abi Hazim al-Ahmasi" is trustworthy; the Six (authors of the canonical collections) narrated from him; he narrated from a group of Companions, and he was precise in narration. His biography is in al-Tahdhib.
This is a sound chain.]]

[[Narration 12872: "Ibn Fudayl" is "Muhammad ibn Fudayl ibn Ghazwan al-Dabbi," who has appeared many times.

[[Narration 12876: "al-Harith" is "al-Harith ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Usama," who has appeared many times, the last under no. 10553, and his biography is under no. 10295.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of this verse is: ﴿no harm can come to you from those who have swerved from the right path and disbelieved in Allah from among the People of the Book﴾.

Those who said this:

12879 - Ya'qub related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾. He said: He means those among the People of the Book who have gone astray.

12880 - Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, saying: Shu'ba related to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding this verse: ﴿no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾. He said: It was revealed concerning the People of the Book.

* *

Others said: It means everyone who has gone astray from the true religion of Allah.

Those who said this:

12881 - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿O you who believe, take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾: A man, when he embraced Islam, they would say to him: You have made your fathers foolish and misguided them, and you did such and such, and you made your fathers like this and like that! It would have been fitting for you to support them and do such and such!

Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, take care of your own selves; no harm can come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are on the right path﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these views and the most sound interpretations of this verse, in our opinion, is what has been related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) concerning it, namely: "O you who believe, take care of yourselves" – keep to acting in obedience to Allah and to what He has commanded you, and refrain from what Allah has forbidden you – "the one who has gone astray cannot harm you if you are guided," meaning: the straying of one who has strayed will not harm you if you keep to acting in obedience to Allah, [[In the printed edition: "if you aspire (rumtum) to act in obedience to Allah," which has no meaning; the editor misread what is in the manuscript, due to its poor writing.]] and you discharge, regarding those among the people who have strayed, what Allah has obligated you to do concerning them, namely the obligation of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, regarding one who commits or attempts to commit it, and restraining his hands when he seeks to wrong a Muslim or a covenanted non-Muslim, and preventing him from it when he refuses to desist. There is no blame upon you for his persistence in his error and misguidance, if you are guided and you fulfil the right of Allah, exalted is His remembrance, concerning it.

We said that this is the most correct interpretation of this verse only because Allah, exalted is His remembrance, commanded the believers to uphold justice and to cooperate in righteousness and piety. Among upholding justice is restraining the hand of the oppressor, and among cooperating in righteousness and piety is enjoining what is right. This accords with what the reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) have amply attested concerning his command to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. Were people free to abandon this, there would be no meaning to the command to do it, except in the situation in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted its abandonment, namely the situation of being unable to carry it out with the outward limbs, in which case he is excused from abandoning it, provided that he then discharges the duty Allah has placed upon him in this matter with his heart.

Since the interpretation we have described is the more preferable for the verse, it is clear that what Hudhayfah and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said is included in the meaning of His words "if you are guided," namely that this means "if you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong," and it is also included in the meaning of what Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

* *

Concerning the interpretation of His words: ﴿To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ (105)

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, exalted is His remembrance, says to the believers among His servants: Act, O believers, by what I have commanded you, and refrain from what I have forbidden you, and command the people of deviation and error, and whoever has swerved from My path, with what is right, and forbid them what is wrong. If they respond, then it is for them and for you. But if they persist in their error and misguidance, then to Me is the return of all of you and your destination in the Hereafter, and theirs, and I am the Knower of what all of you do of good and evil. There I will inform each party of you of what it used to do in the world, and then I will recompense him for the deed he has brought before Me with his due recompense according to what he deserves, for no deed of any doer among you, male or female, is hidden from Me.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 106 (part 1 of 3):

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a witness] between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two just men from among you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, mentioning this to the believers in Him: "O you who have believed, let there be a witness between you," meaning: let there be a witness between you. "When death approaches one of you at the time of bequest," meaning: at the time of the bequest. "Two just men from among you," meaning: two men of sound judgment, intellect and reason from among the Muslims. [[See the explanation of the words of this verse in the earlier indexes of linguistic terms.]] As follows:

12882 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar and Ubayd Allah ibn Yusuf al-Jubayri related to us, both saying: Mu'ammal ibn Isma'il related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, from Qatadah, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, regarding His saying: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [Surah al-Talaq: 2], he said: "Men of intellect."

[[Report 12882: "Ubayd Allah ibn Yusuf al-Jubayri," "Abu Hafs al-Basri," a teacher of al-Tabari, reliable (thiqah). Ibn Majah related from him. He is biographied in al-Tahdhib. In the manuscript it reads "Abd Allah ibn Yusuf," which is an error. It occurred earlier as number 109, but he was not biographied there.
This report concerns the interpretation of the second verse of "Surah al-Talaq," and al-Tabari did not mention it there in the interpretation of that verse. This is one of the forms of his abridgement of the tafsir.]]

The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of His saying: "two just men from among you."

Some of them said: It means: from among the people of your religion (millah).

Those who said this:

12883 - Humayd ibn Mas'adah related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "Two witnesses, just men from among you," from among the Muslims.

12884 - Imran ibn Musa al-Qazzaz related to us, saying: Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Suwayd related to us, from Yahya ibn Ya'mar, regarding His saying: "two just men from among you," from among the Muslims.

12885 - Ibn Bashshar and Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, both saying: Ibn Abi Adi related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, regarding His saying: "two just men from among you," he said: "Two men from among the people of your religion."

12886 - Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, from Ash'ath, from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah, who said: I asked him about the words of Exalted is His mention: "two just men from among you," and he said: "From the millah."

12887 - Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, from Hisham, from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah, similar to it, except that he said in it: "From the people of the millah."

12888 - Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah related to us, from Hisham, from Ibn Sirin, who said: I asked Ubaydah about this verse: "two just men from among you," and he said: "From the people of the millah."

12889 - Ibn Wakic related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Ibn Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah, similar to it.

12890 - Ibn Wakic related to us, saying: Husayn related to us, from Za'idah, from Hisham, from Ibn Sirin, who said: I asked Ubaydah, and he mentioned something similar.

12891 - Ibn Wakic related to us, saying: Ibn Mahdi related to us, from Hammad, from Ibn Abi Najih; and he said: Malik ibn Isma'il related to us, from Hammad ibn Zayd, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similar to it.

12892 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "just men from among you," he said: "Just men from among the people of Islam."

12893 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "just men from among you," he said: "From among the Muslims."

12894 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, who said: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib used to say: "two just men from among you," i.e., from among the people of Islam.

* *

Others said: It means: just men from among the kin (hayy) of the one making the bequest. This is an opinion narrated from Ikrimah, Ubaydah, and a number of others besides them.

* *

They differed concerning the description of the "two" whom God mentioned in this verse: what are they, and what are they?

Some of them said: They are two witnesses who testify to the bequest of the one making it.

* *

Others said: They are two executors (wasiyy).

* *

The interpretation of those who claimed that they are two witnesses is His saying: "a witness between you": let two just witnesses from among you witness your bequest.

The interpretation of those who said: "They are two executors, not two witnesses," His saying: "a witness between you" means presence and attendance at what the sick person bequeaths to them, from your saying: "I witnessed the bequest of so-and-so," meaning: I was present at it. [[See the explanation of "shahida" in the earlier indexes of linguistic terms and the differences in its meanings.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two interpretations of His saying: "two just men from among you," is the interpretation of the one who interpreted it to mean that they are from the people of the millah, rather than the one who interpreted it to mean that they are from the kin of the one making the bequest.

We only said that this is the more correct interpretation of the verse because Exalted is He, mentioned, addressed the believers in general in His saying: "O you who have believed, let there be a witness between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two just men from among you." It is not permissible to turn what God, Exalted is He, mentioned in general to the specific, except by a proof that must be accepted. Since this is so, what returns from His mention must be general, just as their mention at the beginning was general. [[In the printed edition: "from their mention," and what is in the manuscript is pure correctness.]]

* *

The more correct of the two meanings of His saying: "a witness between you" is the oath, not the "testimony" by which one who has testimony for another, to whom it is due, against whom it is due, presents it before the judges. [[The beginning of this phrase in the manuscript read: "a witness between you, because the testimony. . .," omitting the word "oath," and making "not the testimony" into "because the testimony," which is corrupt. What is in the printed edition is the pure correctness, God willing, and it agrees with what al-Qurtubi related in his tafsir, 6:348, from Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.]] Because we do not know of any ruling of God, Exalted is He, mentioned, in which the witness must swear an oath, so that it would be permissible to turn "testimony" in this place to the "testimony" which some people give before judges and rulers.

In the ruling of this verse, in this matter, the oath on the just men, and on whoever stands in their place, by the oath in His saying: [[In the printed edition, "in the oath in His saying" here differs from the manuscript and corrupts the sentence. The context is: "In the ruling of the verse. . . by the oath. . . is the clearest proof. . ."]] "You shall detain them after the prayer, and they swear by God" = is the clearest evidence for the soundness of what we have said on this matter, that "testimony" here means oaths, not the testimony by which judgment is given for the one to whom testimony is due against the one against whom it is due, and for the refutation of what opposes it.

* *

If a speaker says: Have you found in the ruling of God, Exalted is He mentioned, an oath that is obligatory upon the claimant, so that your saying about testimony in this place is directed toward correctness?

If you say: "No," this shows the corruption of your interpretation as you interpreted it, because according to this interpretation the two swearers in His saying: "But if it is discovered that the two had incurred sin, then two others shall take their place from among those who have the prior claim against them, and they shall swear by God: our testimony is more worthy than their testimony," would have to be the claimants.

And if you say: "Yes," it is said to you: In which ruling of God, Exalted is He mentioned, did you find that? It is said: We found that in most meanings. That is in the ruling of a man who claims a debt from another man, and the one against whom he claims acknowledges it, but claims that he has paid it. Then the word of the creditor is accepted. [[His saying "and the man acknowledges" is joined to his saying "in the ruling of the man. . . ." In the printed edition here it reads "and the man acknowledges. . . and claims the acknowledging," which is an error; its correct form is what is established, as in the manuscript.]]

And a man acknowledges an item in the possession of another man, and the one in whose possession it is claims that he bought it from the claimant, or that the claimant gave it to him, and similar things that are too numerous to count. On this basis, God, Exalted is He mentioned, made the oath obligatory in this place upon the two claimants who discovered the two traitors in what they had betrayed. [[In the printed edition: ". . . upon the two sides in what they committed," which has no meaning here. In the manuscript: "upon the two sides in what they had wronged in it," and the correct reading is what is established.]]

Abu Ja'far said: The scholars of Arabic differed concerning what is in the nominative (raf') in His saying: "a witness between you," and His saying: "two just men from among you."

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: The meaning of His saying: "a witness between you" is the testimony of two just men. Then "the testimony" was dropped, and "the two men" was put in its place, so they took the nominative case with which "the testimony" would have been in the nominative if it had been included in the speech. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "with what the witness was in the nominative with," which is an error beyond doubt; its correct form is what is established.]] He said: And that, with the omission of what was omitted from it, and the placing of what was placed in its position, is like His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 82], and he means: "And ask the people of the town," and "the town" was put in the accusative in place of "the people" and took its place. Then His saying: "or two others" was joined to "the two."

* *

And some of the grammarians of Kufa said: "The two" is in the nominative by "the testimony," i.e., let two men from among the Muslims bear witness against you, or two others from among you.

* *

And another among them said: "The testimony" is in the nominative by "when there approaches." He said: It was nominative only by that, because he said: "when there approaches," making it "testimony" as an omitted, newly begun subject, not the testimony that has been made nominative for all creation, because He, exalted is His mention, said: "or two others from among you," and this is a testimony that occurs only in this situation, and it is not among what is established. [[In the printed edition: "from what is established," and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these opinions in my view is the saying of the one who said that "the testimony" is in the nominative by His saying: "when there approaches," because His saying "when there approaches" means: at the approach of death to one of you; and "the two men" is in the nominative by the implied meaning, which is: that two men should bear witness. So what was mentioned of "the testimony" in His saying: "a witness between you" sufficed in place of "that they should bear witness."

We only said that this is more correct because "the testimony" is a verbal noun (masdar) in this place, and "the two men" is a noun, and a noun cannot be a verbal noun. However, the Arabs sometimes place nouns in the positions of verbs. [["The verbs": the verbal nouns (masadir). See the indexes of technical terms in the earlier parts.] Therefore, even if this is so, directing all of that to its most correct aspect, as far as we are able to find a way, is more appropriate for us than directing it to its weakest aspect.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿or two others from among you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He mentioned to the believers: let there be a witness between you when death approaches one of you, two just men from among the Muslims, or two others from among those who are not Muslims.

* *

The people of interpretation have differed regarding the interpretation of His saying: "or two others from among you."

Some of them said: Its meaning is: or two others from among those other than the people of your religion, in the sense of what we have said about it.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: "or two others from among other than your clan and kin."

[[Report 12932: "ʿUthmān ibn al-Haytham ibn al-Jahm ibn ʿĪsā al-ʿAṣrī al-ʿAbdī," who is "al-Ashajj al-ʿAṣrī," a trustworthy narrator. Al-Bukhārī cited reports from him. [[Report 12933: "Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī al-Akhḍar al-Yamāmī," servant of al-Zuhrī, has passed as no. 9312.]]

1293 4- Bishr ibn Muʿādh narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, who said: "al-Ḥasan used to say, 'Two persons of justice among you' (﴿اثْنَانِ ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِنْكُمْ﴾), meaning from his clan, 'or two others from among other than yourselves' (﴿أَوْ آخَرَانِ مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ﴾), he said: from other than his clan."

1293 9- al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Ayyūb, from Ibn Sīrīn, from ʿUbaydah, his statement: "or two others from among other than yourselves," he said: "Muslims from outside your locality."

1294 0- al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to me, saying: ʿUqayl narrated to me, saying: I asked Ibn Shihāb about God's saying, may He be remembered: "O you who have believed, the testimony between you when death approaches one of you…" (﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا شَهَادَةُ بَيْنِكُمْ إِذَا حَضَرَ أَحَدَكُمُ الْمَوْتُ﴾), up to His saying: "And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people" (﴿وَاللَّهُ لا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الْفَاسِقِينَ﴾). I said: "Tell me, the two persons mentioned by God, from outside the family of the testator: are they from among the Muslims, or are they from the People of the Book? And the other two who stand in their place, do you think they are [from among non-] the family of the testator, or are they from among non-Muslims?" Ibn Shihāb said: "We have not heard about this verse from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), nor from the leading scholars of the common people, any sunnah that I can mention. We used to discuss it sometimes with some of our scholars, and they did not mention any known sunnah in it, nor any judgment from a just imam. Rather, their opinions differ concerning it. The most pleasing of their opinions to us was the view of those who said: It concerns the heirs among the Muslims, where some of them witness for the deceased whom they inherit from, while some of them are absent. Those who witnessed bear witness to what he bequeathed to his close relatives, and they inform those of them who were absent of what they witnessed of the bequest. If they accept it, his bequest is valid. But if they doubt that they had altered the words of the deceased and preferred with the bequest those they wished, from among those to whom the deceased had bequeathed nothing, then the two who witnessed to that swear after the prayer, which is the prayer of the Muslims, and they swear by God: 'If you doubt, we will not sell it for any price, even if it were a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of God, for then we would indeed be among the sinners' (﴿إِنِ ارْتَبْتُمْ لا نَشْتَرِي بِهِ ثَمَنًا وَلَوْ كَانَ ذَا قُرْبَى وَلا نَكْتُمُ شَهَادَةَ اللَّهِ إِنَّا إِذًا لَمِنَ الآثِمِينَ﴾). If they swear to that, their testimony and oaths are valid, so long as it is not discovered that they deserved sin in any of that. If it is discovered that they deserved sin in any of that, [[This sentence between brackets is not in the manuscript. The printed edition put "If it is discovered" in its place and stopped there. I inferred the sentence from al-Ṭabarī's context.]] then two others stand in their place from among the heirs, from the opponents who deny what the first two, who were made to swear the first time, testified against him. They swear by God: 'Our testimony is more worthy than your testimony [[This addition between brackets is necessary; I inferred it from the verse and the context.]] regarding your lying or your nullifying of what you testified to' (﴿لَشَهَادَتُنَا أَحَقُّ مِنْ شَهَادَتِهِمَا وَمَا اعْتَدَيْنَا إِنَّا إِذًا لَمِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾), 'and we have not transgressed, for then we would indeed be among the wrongdoers.' 'That is more likely that they will bring testimony in its proper form, or that they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths' (﴿ذَلِكَ أَدْنَى أَنْ يَأْتُوا بِالشَّهَادَةِ عَلَى وَجْهِهَا أَوْ يَخَافُوا أَنْ تُرَدَّ أَيْمَانٌ بَعْدَ أَيْمَانِهِمْ﴾), the verse."

* *

Abū Jaʿfar (al-Ṭabarī) said: The most correct of the two interpretations (taʾwīl; the explanation of a verse's meaning) according to us is the interpretation of those who explained it as: "or two others from among other than the people of Islam." That is because God, may He be exalted, identified for His believing servants, at the time of bequest, the testimony of two persons of just believers, or two from among non-believers. There is no way to say in the speech "the attribute of the testimony of believers from among you, or two men from outside your clan." Rather, it is said: "the attribute of the testimony of two men from your clan or from outside your clan," or "two men from among the believers or from among non-believers."

Since there is no way for that in the speech, it is not permissible to turn the meaning of God's speech, may He be remembered, except to its best aspects. [[In the printed edition: "turning the locked speech of God." In the manuscript: "locked (muʿallaq)." The correct reading is "meaning (maʿnā)."]]

We have already shown earlier that His saying, "two persons of justice among you" (﴿ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِنْكُمْ﴾), refers only to those of your religion and community, with what suffices for whoever has been granted understanding of it.

Since this has been established by what we have indicated, it is known that the meaning of His saying, "or two others from among other than yourselves" (﴿أَوْ آخَرَانِ مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ﴾), is only: "or two others from outside the people of your religion and community." Given that, it is the same whether the two others from outside our religion were Jews, Christians, Magians, or worshippers of idols, or whatever religion they were. For God, may He be remembered, did not specify two others from the people of one particular religion over another, after they are from [outside] the people of Islam. [[This addition between brackets is necessary, otherwise the sentence is corrupted.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: "If you travel in the land and the calamity of death befalls you" (﴿إِنْ أَنْتُمْ ضَرَبْتُمْ فِي الأَرْضِ فَأَصَابَتْكُمْ مُصِيبَةُ الْمَوْتِ﴾):

Abū Jaʿfar said: God, may He be remembered, says to the believers: the attribute of the testimony between you, when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest, is that two persons of justice from among you, O believers, bear witness, or two other men from outside the people of your religion, if you travel going and returning in the land.

* *

We have already explained earlier the reason why the traveler is called "one who strikes in the land" (al-ḍārib fī al-arḍ). [[See the explanation of "striking in the land" (al-ḍarb fī al-arḍ) in what has passed: 5:593, 7:332, 9:123.]]

"Then the calamity of death befalls you" (﴿فَأَصَابَتْكُمْ مُصِيبَةُ الْمَوْتِ﴾): he says, then death descends upon you. [[See the explanation of "affliction" (al-iṣābah) in what has passed: 8:514, 538, 555; 10:393, 404.]]

* *

Most interpreters directed this passage toward the meaning of sequence rather than choice. They said: its meaning is: "Testimony between you, when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two persons of justice from among you, if they are found; but if they are not found, then two others from outside you." They did that because they directed the meaning of "testimony" in His saying, "testimony between you," to the meaning of the testimony that obliges a party to have its holder stand before the judge, or that nullifies it.

Mention of some who interpreted it in this way:

1294 1- ʿImrān ibn Mūsā al-Qazzāz narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Wārith ibn Saʿīd narrated to us, saying: Isḥāq ibn Suwayd narrated to us, from Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar regarding His saying, "persons of justice among you" (﴿ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِنْكُمْ﴾), from among the Muslims. "If you do not find from among the Muslims, then from among non-Muslims."

1294 2- Muḥammad ibn Bashshār and Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Abī ʿAdī narrated to us, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab regarding His saying, "Two persons of justice among you, or two others from among other than yourselves" (﴿اثْنَانِ ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِنْكُمْ أَوْ آخَرَانِ مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ﴾), he said: "Two from the people of your religion, 'or two others from among other than yourselves,' from the People of the Book, if one is in a land where he cannot find anyone else."

1294 3- Ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, saying: Dāwūd narrated to us, from ʿĀmir, from Shurayḥ regarding this verse, "Testimony between you" up to His saying, "or two others from among other than yourselves" (﴿شَهَادَةُ بَيْنِكُمْ﴾ … ﴿أَوْ آخَرَانِ مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ﴾), he said: "If a man is in a land of strangeness and finds no Muslim to witness his bequest, and he calls a Jew or a Christian or a Magian to witness it, their testimony is valid."

1294 4- Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn narrated to me, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī regarding "O you who have believed, the testimony between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest: two persons of justice from among you" (﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا شَهَادَةُ بَيْنِكُمْ إِذَا حَضَرَ أَحَدَكُمُ الْمَوْتُ حِينَ الْوَصِيَّةِ اثْنَانِ ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِنْكُمْ﴾), he said: "This is in the case of the settled (al-ḥaḍar)," "or two others from among other than yourselves" (﴿أَوْ آخَرَانِ مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ﴾) "in the journey" (fī al-safar), "if you strike in the land and the calamity of death befalls you" (﴿إِنْ أَنْتُمْ ضَرَبْتُمْ فِي الأَرْضِ فَأَصَابَتْكُمْ مُصِيبَةُ الْمَوْتِ﴾). "This is the man whom death overtakes on his journey while no one from the Muslims is present with him, so he calls two men from the Jews, Christians, and Magians, and bequeaths to them." [[In the printed edition: "this man," with an added "fī." I kept what is in the manuscript. It will come in its correct form in no. 12954.]]

1294 5- al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Mughīrah informed us, from Ibrāhīm and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, that both of them said regarding this verse, "O you who have believed, the testimony between you" (﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا شَهَادَةُ بَيْنِكُمْ﴾), up to the end: "When death comes to a man on a journey, he calls two men from among the Muslims. If he does not find two men from among the Muslims, then two men from the People of the Book."

1294 6- al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah narrated to me, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding "O you who have believed, the testimony between you" up to His saying, "persons of justice among you" (﴿ذَوَا عَدْلٍ مِنْكُمْ﴾): "This is for one who dies while Muslims are with him, so God commanded him to have two just Muslims witness his bequest. Then He said: 'or two others from among other than yourselves, if you strike in the land and the calamity of death befalls you' (﴿أَوْ آخَرَانِ مِنْ غَيْرِكُمْ إِنْ أَنْتُمْ ضَرَبْتُمْ فِي الأَرْضِ فَأَصَابَتْكُمْ مُصِيبَةُ الْمَوْتِ﴾). This is for one who dies while no one from among the Muslims is with him, so God, may He be remembered, commanded him to have two men from among non-Muslims witness."

* *

Others interpreted it to mean choice, and they said: What is intended by testimony in this passage is the oaths concerning the bequest to which they were entrusted, and the deceased's entrusting them with what he entrusted them with of property, so that they would deliver it to his heirs after his death, if suspicion arose about them. They said: A man may entrust his property to whoever he considers a place of trust, whether a believer or a disbeliever, in travel or at home. [[In the printed edition: "a man may entrust his property," but in the manuscript it reads "sammā al-rajul," unpointed, and the correct reading is what I have given: "a man was entrusted with such-and-such, and he entrusted him (ʾamina al-rajul ʿalā kadhā, wa-ʾtamanahu; the latter with doubled tāʾ)." See what has passed, 5:298, note 4.]] We have mentioned the report from some of those who said this earlier, and we will mention the rest of it later, God willing.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: "You detain them both after the prayer, and they swear by God, if you doubt, that we will not sell it for any price, even if it were a near relative" (﴿تَحْبِسُونَهُمَا مِنْ بَعْدِ الصَّلاةِ فَيُقْسِمَانِ بِاللَّهِ إِنِ ارْتَبْتُمْ لا نَشْتَرِي بِهِ ثَمَنًا وَلَوْ كَانَ ذَا قُرْبَى﴾)

Abu Ja'far said: God, may He be exalted, says to the believers in Him and His Messenger: "The testimony between you, when death approaches one of you, when making a bequest, is two men of justice from among you, or two others from outside your own (community), if you are traveling in the land and the calamity of death strikes you" — that is, if you are on a journey, death comes upon you, you make a bequest to the two of them, and you hand over to them the property and estate you have with you for your heirs. So when you have made a bequest to them and handed over to them the property you have with you, and the calamity of death befalls you, then they shall deliver to your heirs what you entrusted to them. If the heirs claim that they committed treachery, a betrayal they committed regarding what was entrusted to them, then the ruling concerning them at that point is that you detain them — meaning: you make them stop after the prayer. In the speech there is an omitted element, which is understood from what is expressed of it, and it is: "when the calamity of death befalls you, and you have entrusted your bequest to them and handed over to them the property you have with you," then you detain them after the prayer. "They swear by God if you doubt": meaning, they swear by God if you suspect them of treachery regarding what was entrusted to them, such as altering or changing a bequest entrusted to them. "Doubt" (al-irtiyab) means accusation (al-ittiham). "We will not sell it for any price": meaning, they swear by God that we will not exchange our oaths by God for any price; that is, we will not swear falsely for a compensation we would take for it, or for property we would carry off, or for a right we would deny, to these people for whom their guardian and deceased appointed us as executors.

* *

The pronoun in His words "by it" (bihi) refers to God, and what is meant by it is the oath and the swearing; but since mention of swearing by Him had already occurred before, the meaning of the statement was understood, so it was sufficient not to repeat the mention of the swearing and the oath. "Even if it were a near relative": meaning, they swear by God that we will not seek, by our swearing by God, any compensation, so that we would lie in them for anyone, even if the one by whom we swear were a relative of ours.

* *

Similar to what we have said on this matter has been related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Mention of those who said this:

12947 – Al-Muthanna told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih told me, on the authority of 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: "Or two others from outside your own (community), if you travel in the land and the calamity of death strikes you." This is for one who dies while no Muslim is with him, so God commanded him (to take) the testimony of two men from outside the Muslims. If their testimony is doubted, they are made to swear after the prayer by God: "We did not exchange our testimony for a small price."

* *

His words "you detain them after the prayer" refer to the prayer of the others. The meaning of the statement is: "or two others from outside your own (community), whom you detain after the prayer if you doubt them; they swear by God that we will not sell it for any price, even if it were a near relative."

* *

They differed concerning the "prayer" mentioned by God in this verse, when He said: "you detain them after the prayer."

Some of them said: it is the afternoon prayer (al-'asr).

Mention of those who said this:

12948 – Ya'qub told me, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Zakariyya informed us, on the authority of al-Sha'bi: that a man of the Muslims was overtaken by death at Daquqa, and he found no Muslim to witness his bequest, so he called upon two men of the People of the Book. He said: they came to Kufa, and went to al-Ash'ari and informed him, and they brought his estate and his bequest. Al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that did not occur in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ!" He said: so he made them swear after the afternoon prayer: "By God, they did not betray, nor lie, nor alter, nor conceal, nor change; and indeed it is the bequest and estate of the man." He said: so he upheld their testimony.

12949 – Ibn Bashshar and 'Amr ibn 'Ali told us, both saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Shu'bah told us, on the authority of Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding "or two others from outside your own (community)": he said: if a man is in the land of polytheism and bequeaths to two men of the People of the Book, they swear after the afternoon prayer.

12950 – Ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Shu'bah told us, on the authority of Mughirah, from Ibrahim, with the like of it.

12951 – Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, on the authority of Qatadah regarding His words: "O you who believe, the testimony between you..." up to "the calamity of death strikes you": this is a man who died in a foreign land, leaving his estate and making his bequest, and two men witnessed his bequest. If their testimony is doubted, they are made to swear after the afternoon prayer. It used to be said: "then the oaths take effect."

12952 – Al-Qasim told us, saying: Al-Husayn told us, saying: Hushaym told me, saying: Mughirah informed us, on the authority of Ibrahim and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: that they both said regarding this verse, "O you who believe, the testimony between you": they said: when a man is overtaken by death while traveling, let him call two men of the Muslims as witnesses; if he does not find them, then two men of the People of the Book. When they come with his estate, if the heirs confirm them, their word is accepted; but if they suspect them, they are made to swear after the afternoon prayer: "By God, we did not lie, nor conceal, nor betray, nor alter."

12953 – 'Amr ibn 'Ali told us, saying: Yahya ibn al-Qattan told us, saying: Zakariyya told us, saying: 'Amir told us: that a man died at Daquqa, and he found no one to witness his bequest except two Christian men from its people. Abu Musa made them swear after the afternoon prayer in the mosque of Kufa: "By God, they did not conceal nor alter, and that this is the bequest." So he upheld it.

* *

Others said: rather, they are made to swear after the prayer of their own religion and community.

Mention of those who said this:

12954 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn told me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal told us, saying: Asbat told us, on the authority of al-Suddi regarding: "O you who believe, the testimony between you..." up to His words "two men of justice from among you": he said: this is concerning a bequest at the time of death; one makes a bequest and calls two men of the Muslims to witness regarding what he has and what he owes; he said: this is in the case of residence; "or two others from outside your own (community)" in travel, "if you travel in the land and the calamity of death strikes you": this is the man whom death overtakes during his journey while no one from the Muslims is present; so he calls two men from the Jews, Christians, and Magians, makes a bequest to them, and hands over his inheritance to them; they accept it. If the family of the deceased approves the bequest and knows the property of their companion, they leave the two men alone. But if they doubt, they bring them before the ruler. That is His words: "you detain them after the prayer if you doubt." 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas said: "It is as if I am looking at the two foreigners when they were brought to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari in his house," and he opened the document; the family of the deceased denied it and accused them of betrayal. Abu Musa wanted to make them swear after the afternoon prayer, so I said to him: "They do not care about the afternoon prayer; rather, make them swear after their own prayer in their religion." So the two men are made to stand after their prayer in their religion, and they swear by God: "We will not sell it for a small price, even if it were a near relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of God; indeed, we would then be among the sinners," that "their companion bequeathed this, and that this is his estate." Then the ruler says to them before they swear: "If you have concealed or betrayed, I will expose you among your people, your testimony will not be accepted, and I will punish you!" When he says that to them, that is more likely to bring them to give the testimony in its proper form.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two opinions regarding this, in our view, is the saying of the one who said: "you detain them after the afternoon prayer." Because God, may He be exalted, made the "prayer" definite in this place by the addition of the "alif and lam," and the Arabs do not use these except for something known, either as a genus or as a specific, known one among those being addressed. Given that this is so, and since it is agreed that "the prayer" in this place does not refer to all prayers, it cannot be that the prayer intended is the prayer of the Jews and Christians who are made to swear, because they have prayers that are not one; so it is known that the intended prayer is a specific one of the prayers of the Muslims. Given that, and since it is authentically reported that the Prophet ﷺ, when he made the li'an between the 'Ajlani spouses, made it between them after the afternoon prayer and not after other prayers [see the report of the 'Ajlanis in al-Bayhaqi's al-Sunan al-Kubra 7: 398 and following], it is known that the prayer meant by His words "you detain them after the prayer" is the prayer which the Messenger of God ﷺ chose for making those swear who wished to intensify the oath upon them. This is in addition to the esteem in which the people of disbelief in God hold that time, because of its proximity to sunset.

* *

Ibn Zayd used to say regarding His words "we will not sell it for any price":

12955 – Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la told me this, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words "we will not sell it for any price": "we take it as a bribe."

* *

On the interpretation of His words: "And we will not conceal the testimony of God; indeed, we would then be among the sinners" (106).

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed in reading this.

The majority of the readers of the cities read: "wa la naktumu shahadata Allah" (and we will not conceal the testimony of God), with "shahada" annexed to "Allah" and the name of God in the genitive — meaning: we will not conceal a testimony belonging to God that is with us.

It is mentioned from al-Sha'bi that he used to read it like this:

12956 – Ibn Wakif told us, saying: Abu Usamah told us, on the authority of Ibn 'Awn, from 'Amir: that he used to read: "wa la naktumu shahadata Allahi inna idhan la-mina al-athimin" with the "alif" cut (i.e., "inna" instead of "a-inna"), and the name of God in the genitive — thus Ibn Wakif related it to us.

* *

It seems that al-Sha'bi directed the meaning of the statement to: they swear by God that we will not sell it for any price, nor conceal a testimony that is with us. Then he began a new oath with an interrogative: "By God, are they, if they exchange their oaths for a price or conceal the testimony that is with them, among the sinners?"

* *

A report from al-Sha'bi regarding the reading of this differing from this one has also been transmitted, namely:

12957 – Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Taghlabi told me, saying: al-Qasim ibn Sallam told us, saying: 'Abbad ibn 'Abbad told us, on the authority of Ibn 'Awn, from al-Sha'bi: that he read: "wa la naktumu shahadata Allahi inna idhan la-mina al-athimin" [In the printed edition: "shahadat Allah", which is an error; the correct form is in the manuscript. The readings of al-Sha'bi, or his readings transmitted from him, are mentioned in Abu Hayyan's Tafsir 4: 44 and Ibn Jinni's al-Muhtasab; consult them there.] He said: Ahmad said: Abu 'Ubayd said: "shahadatun" is read with tanwin and "Allahi" with kasra on the basis of connection (idafah). He said: some of them have related it with the "alif" cut, as an interrogative.

[The report: 12957 — "Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Taghlabi al-Ahwal" has passed under numbers 5919, 5954, 7664; in the printed edition here it was "al-Tha'labi," which is an error that I clarified there. "'Abbad ibn 'Abbad al-Ramli al-Arsufi," with the kunya "Abu 'Utbah al-Khawwas," narrated from Ibn 'Awn; he is biographed in al-Tahdhib.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: My own memorization of al-Sha'bi's reading is without the interrogative.

* *

Some of them read: "wa la naktumu shahadata Allah," with the "shahadah" nunated and the name "Allah" in the accusative, meaning: and we will not conceal from God a testimony that is with us.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the readings in our view is the reading of the one who read: "wa la naktumu shahadata Allah," with "shahadah" annexed to the name "Allah" and the name "Allah" in the genitive, because it is the widely transmitted reading among the readers of the cities, whose authenticity the community does not deny.

* *

Ibn Zayd used to say about the meaning of this: "wa la naktumu shahadata Allah," even if it is far-fetched. [In the printed edition: "even if its bearer is far," and I have kept what is in the manuscript; I am in doubt about it in any case, fearing that something may have dropped from the text. I did not find Ibn Zayd's statement in the books available to me.]

12958 – Yunus told me this, saying: Ibn Zayd informed us, on his authority.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 107 (part 1 of 4):

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And if it becomes known that the two have committed a sin, then two others shall take their place from among those who have a claim against them, the two nearest of kin⟩

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying "fa-in 'uthira" (And if it becomes known), He, may His mention be exalted, means: if it is discovered or becomes apparent from the two of them. [[In the printed edition: "fihima" (about them both); the correct reading is "minhuma" (from them both).]]

The root of "al-'athr" is to fall upon a thing and to stumble over it. From this is the expression "'atharat isba' fulan bi-kadha" (the toe of so-and-so struck against such-and-such), meaning that it struck it, hit it, and fell upon it. From this is the verse of al-A'sha, Maymun ibn Qays:

"With a strong, stubborn she-camel, when she stumbles, the fall is nearer to her than my saying 'la'a' (may she rise)."

[[From his Diwan, p. 83, from his ode concerning Hawdha ibn 'Ali al-Hanafi; its story has passed (2:94, note 1), and some of its verses have passed (1:106 / 2:540). The verse is said in describing a fearsome land of night, which is the "town" mentioned in the following verse: "And a town whose night-travellers dread its night-journey, until you see him seeking companions there. No man hears in it anything that would cheer him at night except the hooting of the owl and the cry of the 'du'a'. I burdened myself with its unknown [ways], and my resolve accompanied me upon it, whenever its mirages shone." "Al-dulja": travel by night. "Al-shiya'": companions. "Al-na'im": the cry of the owl, or its faint voice. "Al-du'a'": a bird of the night which, when it senses dawn, sings out; it is said to be the "karawan" (curlew). "Al-al": mirage. "Al-lawth": strength; he describes his she-camel as having flesh and fat, strong for travel. His saying "bi-dhat lawth" is connected to "kallaftu" (I burdened myself). "'Afarnāt" (with fatha on the 'ayn and the fa') is an epithet of the camel, meaning that she is strong, as though mad from her vigour. "Al-ta's": decline and stumbling. His saying "la'an" is a word said to one who stumbles, wishing that he rise from his stumble; its meaning is elevation, "la'a li-fulan," meaning God raised him up from his stumble. When al-A'sha described his she-camel as strong and energetic, he denied that she could have a stumble in her speed; so if she does stumble, the curse upon her that God overturn her onto her nostrils is more fitting than a prayer for the raising of her stumble.]]

He means by "'athirat" that the hoof-tip of her foot struck a stone or something else. [[In the printed edition: "maysam khuffiha hajar aw ghayruh"; the correct reading is what is recorded here. "Al-mansam" (with fatha, then sukun, then kasra): the tip of a camel's hoof, and of an ostrich and an elephant. "Mansamā al-ba'ir" are the two claws on its forelegs, which for it are like nails for a human.]] Then this is used for anything that falls upon something that was hidden from it, as in the proverb: ﴿"She stumbled upon the spinning late, and left not a single tuft in Najd"﴾, meaning: she fell upon it. [[This is a proverb. See Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda 1:181; al-Amthal of al-Maydani 1:395; and al-Amthal of Abu Hilal al-'Askari, p. 142. His saying "bi-akhira" (with fatha on the alif, the kha' and the ra') means "at last." One says "ma 'arafathu illa bi-akhira," meaning "I did not know him except at last." "Najd" is the well-known land. "Qarada": its plural is "qard" (all with fatha), which is what has been combed out of fur and wool and matted, the refuse of wool. Its origin is that a woman leaves off spinning while she still finds what she can spin of cotton or flax, until when it escapes her, she searches the refuse-heaps for the "qard" (the refuse of wool), gathering it to spin. It is struck as a proverb for neglect when one has the means, and then seeking after loss. Abu Hilal said: "This is like the common saying: we seek refuge in God from the lazy one when he becomes energetic." The author of Lisan al-'Arab transmitted this proverb under (q-r-d), with the wording "'akkarat 'ala al-ghazl..." and explained it as "'akkarat, i.e. 'atafat" (turned). With this transmission there is no evidence in it.]]

* *

As for His saying "'ala annahuma istahaqqa ithman" (that they have committed a sin), He, may His mention be exalted, says: if it becomes known from the two witnesses whose matter God has mentioned in this verse, after their swearing by God, "We shall not sell our oath for any price, even if it be a near kinsman, nor shall we conceal the testimony of God," that "they have committed a sin," meaning: that they have made themselves liable to sin by their oaths with which they swore, namely that it becomes known that they were lying in their oaths by God that "we did not betray, nor alter, nor change." If it is found that they have betrayed something of the dead man's property, or changed his bequest, or altered it, then they have sinned in that regard, by their swearing by their Lord, [[His saying "fa-athima... bi-rabbihima": see what I said regarding "athima bi-rabbihi" earlier, 4:530 note 3, and again 6:92 note 2, and its explanation there.]] then "two others shall take their place," meaning: then there shall stand in their place, from among the heirs of the dead man, the two nearest, those to whom the bequest was made.

Those of the interpreters who hold the same view as we have stated in this have said the same.

Those who said this:

12959 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Shu'ba told us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding "or two others from outside your own people": If a man is in the land of polytheism and bequeaths to two men from the People of the Book, then they swear after the 'asr prayer. If it is discovered after their oath that they betrayed something, the heirs of the dead man swear that it was such-and-such, and then they are entitled to it.

12960 - Ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Shu'ba told us, from Mughira, from Ibrahim, with the like of it.

12961 - Al-Muthanna told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih told me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying "or two others from outside your own people," from other than the Muslims: "you detain them after the prayer." If doubt arises concerning their testimony, they are made to swear after the prayer by God: "We did not buy with our testimony any small price." If the guardians become aware that the two unbelievers lied in their testimony, two men from the guardians stand and swear by God: "The testimony of the two unbelievers is false, and we have not transgressed." That is His saying "if it becomes known that the two have committed a sin," meaning: if it is discovered that the two unbelievers lied, "then two others shall take their place," meaning: from the guardians, and they swear by God: "The testimony of the two unbelievers is false, and we have not transgressed," so the testimony of the two unbelievers is rejected and the testimony of the guardians is allowed.

12962 - Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada: "If it becomes known that the two have committed a sin," meaning: it is discovered from them, a betrayal, that they lied or concealed.

* *

The interpreters differed concerning the meaning in respect of which God, may His mention be exalted, imposed the oaths upon the two witnesses and transferred them to the other two, after it became known that the two had committed a sin.

Some of them said: He only imposed the oath upon them when doubt arose regarding their testimony about the deceased in his bequest, that he bequeathed other than what is permissible in the judgment of Islam.
