[[In the printed and manuscript editions: "li-ghayri alladhi yajuz"; the correct reading is what is recorded here.]] That is, if they testify that he bequeathed all his property, or that he bequeathed that some of his children be preferred over others with some of his property.

Those who said this:

12963 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "O you who believe, let there be witnessing between you when death approaches one of you" to His saying "two just men among you," from the people of Islam, "or two others from outside your own people," from outside the people of Islam, "if you travel in the land" to "they swear by God," meaning: they swear by God after the prayer. If the two swear to something that contradicts what God, may His mention be exalted, has revealed of the obligatory share, ["al-fara'id" means the inheritance shares.] meaning the two who are not of the people of Islam, "then two others shall take their place," from the guardians of the dead man, and they swear by God: "Our companion would not have bequeathed this," or: "They are both lying, and our testimony is more deserving than their testimony."

12964 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn told me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, who said: The two men are stopped after their prayer concerning their debt; they swear by God: "We shall not sell it for any price, even if it be a near kinsman, nor shall we conceal the testimony of God; indeed we would then be among the sinners." "Surely your companion bequeathed this, and this is indeed his estate." When they testify, and the ruler permits their testimony regarding what they testified, he says to the guardians of the man: "Go out, travel in the land, and inquire about them. If you find against them any betrayal, or anyone who slanders them, we will reject their testimony." The guardians set out to inquire. If they find anyone who slanders them, or they are not acceptable in their eyes, or it becomes known that they betrayed some of the property which they found in their possession, the guardians come and testify before the ruler, [[In the printed edition: "fa-aqbal al-awliya' fa-shahadu"; the manuscript: "fa-aqbal al-awliya' shahadu"; the context requires what is recorded here.]] and they swear by God: "Our testimony is that they are both treacherous and accused in their religion, slandered in it, and more deserving than their testimony regarding what they testified, and we have not transgressed." That is His saying: "if it becomes known that the two have committed a sin, then two others shall take their place from among those who have a claim against them, the two nearest of kin."

* *

Others said: Rather, the two witnesses were only made to swear because they claimed that he had bequeathed to them some of the property. And it is only transferred to the others for that reason, when they doubt their claim.

Those who said this:

12965 - 'Imran ibn Musa al-Qazzaz told us, saying: 'Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'd told us, saying: Ishaq ibn Suwayd told us, from Yahya ibn Ya'mar, regarding His saying "you detain them after the prayer, then they swear by God," he said: They claim that he bequeathed to them such-and-such. "If it becomes known that the two have committed a sin," that is, by their claim for themselves, "then two others shall take their place from among those who have a claim against them, the two nearest of kin," that our companion did not bequeath to you anything of what you say.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter in our opinion is that the two witnesses were made to swear in this regard because of the heirs' accusation against them concerning what the dead man had handed over to them of his property, and the heirs' prior claim of betrayal of property of known value, and the oath was transferred afterward to the heirs when the doubt that arose from the heirs against them became evident, and the accusation against them was confirmed by the testimony of a witness against them or against one of them. Then the heir swears, in that case, together with the testimony of the witness against them or against one of them, since his claim is only confirmed when his right is verified; or else there is an acknowledgment from the witnesses of some or all of what the heir claims against them; then their claim regarding what they acknowledged of the dead man's property is one for which their claim is not accepted except with evidence; then, if they have no evidence for their claim, the oath is then transferred to the guardians of the dead man.

We have said this is the most correct of the views on this matter, because we do not know of any ruling in the judgments of Islam in which an oath is imposed upon witnesses, whether their testimony was doubted or not, so that the ruling in this testimony would be parallel to it. And if we do not find it so, it is not established by a report from the Messenger ﷺ, nor by consensus of the community. For the swearing of the witnesses in this place is a ruling of God, may His mention be exalted, and so it is a settled foundation. And when a view ceases to be a foundation or a parallel to a foundation in a matter in which the community has disputed, its falsity is evident.

And when this view is invalidated by what we have mentioned, the view that the two witnesses were made to swear because they claimed for themselves a bequest of property from the dead man is invalidated, because the people of knowledge have no disagreement that it is a ruling of God, may His mention be exalted, that if a claimant claims in the property of a dead man a bequest, the word of the heirs of the one against whom the claim is made is accepted regarding the bequest in his property, together with their oaths, not the word of the claimant with his oath, when the claimant has no evidence. God, may He be exalted, has made the oath in this verse incumbent upon the witnesses if doubt arises about them, and the oaths are transferred from them to the guardians of the dead man when it becomes known that the witnesses have committed a sin in their oaths. Thus it is known by that the view of one who says "the witnesses swore because of their claim for themselves of a bequest the dead man made to them from his property" is false.

Moreover, what we have said on this matter from the interpreters is the interpretation with which reports have come down from some of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ: that the Messenger of God ﷺ judged by it when this verse was revealed, between those concerning whom it was revealed and on account of whom it was revealed.

Those who said this:

12966 - Ibn Wakî' told me, saying: Yahya ibn Adam told us, from Yahya ibn Abi Za'ida, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A man of the Banu Sahm went out with Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Baddaa, and the Sahmi died in a land where there was no Muslim. When they returned with his estate, they lost a cup of silver inlaid with gold, [["Al-jam": a vessel of silver, an authentic Arabic word. "Mukhawwas bi-al-dhahab": it has plates of gold upon it in the shape of palm fronds, and "al-takhwis" is to put plates of gold upon a thing in the width of palm fronds.] and the Messenger of God ﷺ made the two swear. Then the cup was found in Mecca, and they said: "We bought it from Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Baddaa!" Then two men of the Sahmi's guardians stood and swore: "Our testimony is more deserving than their testimony," and that the cup belonged to their companion. He said: And concerning them was revealed: "O you who believe, let there be witnessing between you."

[[Report 12966: "Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim", al-Tawil, al-Kufi. He narrated from his father, and from 'Abd Allah and 'Abd al-Malik, the sons of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and from 'Ikrima. Narrating from him were Yahya ibn Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'ida, Abu Usama, and Hammad ibn Usama. Ibn Ma'in and Abu Hatim declared him trustworthy. Al-Bujayri said: al-Bukhari said: "I do not know Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim as I would wish, and 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah used to regard this hadith (meaning the hadith of Tamim al-Dari) as excellent. It was said to him: has anyone other than Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim narrated it? He said: No." He said: Abu Usama narrated from him, but he is not well known. The hafiz Ibn Hajar, after mentioning Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim, said: "He has nothing in al-Bukhari, nor does his teacher 'Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id ibn Jubayr, except this one hadith. The men of the chain, between 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah al-Madini (the teacher of al-Bukhari) and Ibn 'Abbas, are all Kufans."

"'Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id ibn Jubayr al-Asadi", al-Kufi, rare in hadith, trustworthy. Passed under number 12776.

"Tamim al-Dari" is Tamim ibn Aws ibn Kharija al-Lakhmi, attributed to his grandfather "al-Dar ibn Hani ibn Habib ibn Nammara ibn Lakhm." He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ in the year nine and became Muslim. He had been a Christian, and he was the one who said to the Messenger of God: "Shall I make you a pulpit as I have seen made in Syria?" So he made the pulpit. He was a devout worshipper.

As for "'Adi ibn Baddaa" (with the shadda on the dal), he was a Christian. It is recorded that he became Muslim, but Ibn Hajar, in his biography in al-Isaba, affirmed that he died a Christian.

This hadith was related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (al-Fath 5:307-309), and in al-Tarikh al-Kabir 1/1/215; Abu Dawud in his Sunan 3:418, no. 3606; al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra 10:165; Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas in al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh, p. 133; al-Jassas in Ahkam al-Qur'an 2:490; and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (in the Book of Tafsir), who said: "This is a good, strange hadith, and it is the hadith of Ibn Abi Za'ida."

Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his Tafsir 3:266, citing al-Tabari, without mentioning its narration in the Sahih of al-Bukhari. al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 2:342, but was imprecise in attributing it to al-Bukhari's Sahih, and attributed it to his al-Tarikh; he then added attribution to Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh.]]

**[12967]** Al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Shu'ayb al-Harrani said: Muhammad ibn Salamah al-Harrani narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Abu al-Nadr, from Badhan, the client of Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Tamim al-Dari, concerning this verse: ﴿O you who believe, let there be a witness between you when death approaches one of you﴾. He said: "The people were free of it except me and 'Adi ibn Baddaa'. Both of us were Christians who used to travel to Syria before Islam. We went to Syria for our trade, and a client of the Banu Sahm named Buzayl ibn Abi Maryam came to them with merchandise, and with him was a silver goblet (jam) which he intended for the king. It was the bulk of his trade.[[In the manuscript: "wa-hiya 'azm" (and it is the bulk); I have adopted what is in the printed edition, for it agrees with the other sources. His words "'azm tijaratih" mean its majority, i.e., that the goblet was the most precious and expensive of what he had.]] He fell ill, so he made us his executors and instructed us to deliver what his family had left. Tamim said: When he died, we took that goblet and sold it for a thousand dirhams, and 'Adi ibn Baddaa' and I divided it. [When we came to his family, we handed over to them what we had with us, and they missed the goblet, so they asked about it.]^[This sentence between parentheses is not in the manuscript or the printed edition; it is established in other sources, and I have included it from the text of al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh (Abrogating and Abrogated).] We said: 'He left nothing other than this, and he gave us nothing else.' Tamim said: When I became Muslim after the arrival of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in Medina, I felt guilty about that.[["ta'ththama min al-shay'" means he felt scrupulous about it and considered it a sin, desiring to be free of it.]] So I went to his family and informed them of the matter, and I paid them five hundred dirhams, and I told them that my companion had an equal amount! They rushed to him[[His words "fawathabu ilayhi" (they rushed at him) were omitted by the editor of the printed edition, but they are present in the manuscript and in al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh.]] and brought him to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

He asked them for evidence, but they found none. So he ordered them to have him swear by whatever is held in high regard among his religion's adherents, and he swore. Then God, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿O you who believe, let there be a witness between you﴾ up to His words ﴿after their oaths﴾.[Note: The text reads "an tarudda aymanun ba'da aymanihim" in the source; rendered as above.] 'Amr ibn al-'As and another man from among them stood up and swore, [[In the manuscript: "halafa" without the fa' conjunction; I have adopted what is in the printed edition and the other sources.]] and so the five hundred was taken from 'Adi ibn Baddaa'.[[The report 12967: "al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Shu'ayb al-Harrani", Abu Muslim al-Harrani, a trustworthy and reliable transmitter, whose biography has passed under no. 10411. In the printed edition here it read "al-Hasan ibn Abi Shu'ayb", dropping "ibn Ahmad", although it is present in the manuscript. The excuse is that the editor saw the copyist write "al-Hasan ibn Yahya Ahmad qala Ibn Abi Shu'ayb" and crossed out "Yahya" and "qala", so he also crossed out "ibn Ahmad", deleting it! This is poor carelessness.
"Muhammad ibn Salamah al-Harrani al-Bahili" is trustworthy, his biography having passed under no. 175. He appears in the chain of Muhammad ibn Ishaq hundreds of times.
"Abu al-Nadr" is Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, extremely weak, accused of lying. al-Thawri narrated from al-Kalbi himself that he said: "Whatever you hear from me from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas is a lie, so do not narrate it." His biography has passed under nos. 72, 246, 248.
As for "Badhan, client of Umm Hani'," or "Badham," he is Abu Salih, trustworthy, mentioned under nos. 112, 168 and elsewhere. He is discussed in al-Tahdhib (The Refinement), al-Kabir (the larger historical work of al-Bukhari) 1/2/144, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/431.
In the printed edition, the manuscript and al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh alike, it read "Zadhan, client of Umm Hani'," a thing no one has said. So I changed it to the correct form on which they agree, and it appears to be a copyist's error.
As for "Tamim al-Dari" and "'Adi ibn Baddaa'," they have passed in the preceding report.
As for "Buzayl ibn Abi Maryam," client of the Banu Sahm or client of 'Amr ibn al-'As al-Sahmi, the owner of this trade, Ibn Hajar addressed him in al-Isaba under "Badil" with a dal, as did Ibn al-Athir in Usd al-Ghaba. Badil was a Muslim among the Emigrants.
It is said his name was "Badil ibn Abi Maryam" and "Badil ibn Abi Mariyya." Then there is disagreement over "Badil": it is narrated as with a dal, and narrated as "Buzayl" with a ra', and narrated as "Buzayl" with a zay, and narrated as "Burayr." Ibn al-Athir said: "What the imams have mentioned in their books is Yazil, with a damma on the ba' and a zay. We shall mention him in his proper place, God willing." He said this and promised, but I have found no mention of him in his book afterward, so I do not know whether Ibn al-Athir forgot, or whether his book has a gap or omission!!
Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari 5: 308, what he did not mention in al-Isaba: "Buzayl," with a single dot below the ba'... hm: with a ba' unpointed and a zay, diminutive. Ibn Makula also vowelled it so, and it occurred in the narration of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Tamim himself, reported by al-Tirmidhi and al-Tabari (meaning this report): "Badil," with a dal in place of the zay. I saw it in a copy of Tafsir al-Tabari as "Bariyl," with a ra' without dots. And in Ibn Manda's report by way of al-Suddi from al-Kalbi: "Badil ibn Abi Mariyya." Then he said: "Whoever said 'Badil ibn Waraqa' erred, for he was Khuza'i and this man was Sahmi; and likewise whoever vowelled it 'Badhil' with a dhal erred."
In the printed edition it was "Badil," but I have adopted what is in the manuscript, and I fear that our manuscript may be "the correct copy of the Tafsir of al-Tabari" that Ibn Hajar mentioned, or that it is copied from the copy he described and verified.
This report was also transmitted by Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas in al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh, p. 133, and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan, in the Book of Tafsir, with this very same chain. Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib (rare) hadith, and its chain is not sound. Abu al-Nadr, from whom Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated this hadith, is in my view Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, known as Abu al-Nadr, and the scholars of hadith have abandoned him, and he is the author of the tafsir. I heard Muhammad ibn Isma'il say: Muhammad ibn Sa'ib al-Kalbi, known as Abu al-Nadr. We do not know of a narration by Salim Abu al-Nadr al-Madini from Abu Salih (Badhan), client of Umm Hani'. Something of this has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas in brief, by a route other than this one." Then al-Tirmidhi cited the earlier report with its chain.
Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 341, adding its attribution to Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifa.]]

**[12968]** Al-Qasim narrated to us, al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada and Ibn Sirin and others. [He said:] And al-Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ikrima. [The report of some of them has merged with that of others:] ﴿O you who believe, let there be a witness between you﴾ — the verse. He said: "'Adi and Tamim al-Dari, both of Lakhm, were Christians who used to trade to Mecca in the pre-Islamic period. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) migrated, they moved their trade to Medina. Ibn Abi Maryam, client of 'Amr ibn al-'As, came to Medina, intending to go to Syria as a merchant, so they all set out together. When they were at some point on the road, Ibn Abi Maryam fell ill, so he wrote his will with his own hand and slipped it into his goods, then made them his executors. When he died, they opened his goods, took what they wanted, then came to his family and handed over what they wanted to hand over. His family opened his goods and found his letter, his contract, and what he had set out with, but they missed something, so they asked them about it. They said: 'This is what we took charge of and handed over to you.' His family said to them: 'Did he sell something or buy something?' They said: 'No!' They said: 'Did he spend any of his goods?'[["fa-hal istahlaka min mata'ihi shay'an" (Did he waste any of his goods?) means: he lost it and failed to find it. This is a word the lexicons have not defined, and I have deduced its meaning from the context. It occurs in the hadith of 'A'isha (Sahih Muslim 2: 59, and Tafsir al-Tabari no. 9640) that she "borrowed a necklace from Asma' and it was lost," meaning it was lost, as I explained earlier at 8: 404, no. 2. So his words "istahlaka" here derive from the sense of this word, which the lexicons have not clearly explained; it is "istaf'ala," meaning: he found it lost. This is sound and good analogical usage, and this is its witness, God willing.]] They said: 'No!' They said: 'Did he trade in merchandise?'[["tajara yatjuru tajran wa-tijaratan" (on the pattern nasara yansuru) means he sold and bought. They meant here the sense of buying in exchange for a price, as far as I can judge, since they had already asked him about selling and buying.]] They said: 'No!' They said: 'Indeed we have lost some of it!' They were accused, so they brought them up before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, let there be a witness between you when death approaches one of you﴾ up to His words ﴿then we would surely be among the sinners﴾." He said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered that they be made to swear after the afternoon prayer: 'By God, other than whom there is no god, we did not receive anything for him other than this, and we did not conceal it.'" He said: "We remained as long as God willed that we remain,[[In the printed edition: "fa-makathna ma sha'a Allah an namkuth" (we remained as long as God willed that we remain). The editor changed what was in the manuscript and spoiled it.]] then a silver vessel, engraved and overlaid with gold, was found with them."[["zahara" (in the passive) means it was found with them: a vessel was found with them.]] Their family said: "This is from his goods?" They said: "Yes, but we bought it from him, and we forgot to mention it when we swore, so we disliked to call ourselves liars!"[[In the manuscript: "nafsa" without dots; if you wish, you may read it "nafsayna" (ourselves, in the dual) instead of "anfusana" (ourselves, in the plural); both are correct.]] So they brought the matter before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the other verse was revealed: ﴿Then if it is discovered that the two had become liable for a sin, two others shall stand in their place from among those who have a claim against them, the two first ones﴾. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered two men from the family of the deceased to swear to what the two had concealed and hidden, and that they deserved it. Then Tamim al-Dari became Muslim and pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he used to say: 'God and His Messenger spoke the truth: I took the vessel!'"[[The report 12968: "Abu Sufyan" is al-Mu'ammari, Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Yashkuri, passed under nos. 1787, 8829.
"al-Husayn," who narrates from him, is Sunayd ibn Dawud, who has passed many times.
"Ibn Abi Maryam" is Buzayl ibn Abi Maryam; I have explained this in the note on the preceding report.
This report was cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 342, adding its attribution to Ibn al-Mundhir.]]

**[12969]** Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words: ﴿O you who believe, let there be a witness between you when death approaches one of you, at the time of the bequest: two just men from among you﴾, the entire verse. He said: "This was a matter at a time when Islam existed only in Medina, and the whole earth was disbelief,[[In the printed edition: "kufr" (in the nominative); I fear the original may have been "wa-kanat al-ard kulluha dar kufr" (the whole earth was an abode of disbelief) or something similar. I have left what is in the printed edition as it is, and it is also correct.]] so God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, let there be a witness between you when death approaches one of you, at the time of the bequest: two just men from among you﴾ — from among the Muslims — ﴿or two others from outside your own﴾ — from outside the people of Islam — ﴿if you travel in the land and the calamity of death befalls you﴾." He said: "A man would go out traveling, and the Arabs were people of disbelief, so he might die during his journey, and so he would entrust his bequest to two men from among them," ﴿then the two shall swear by God if you doubt them﴾ — concerning their claim. If the heirs say: 'Our companion had such and such with him,' then the two swear by God that he had with him only what we said. ﴿Then if it is discovered that the two had become liable for a sin﴾ — that they had sworn to a falsehood and a lie — ﴿two others shall stand in their place from among those who have a claim against them, the two first ones﴾ — concerning the deceased — ﴿and they shall swear by God: our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; otherwise we would surely be among the wrongdoers﴾. We [heirs] said that our companion had such and such, and these two said: 'He did not have it!' He said: 'Then some of the goods were discovered with them.' When that was discovered, the oath was returned to the heir of the deceased,[["al-qasama" (with the qaf vowelled) here means: the oath.]] and they swore, and then these two were made to pay." God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿That is more suitable so that they bring the testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾,[[The words of God "ba'da aymanihim" (after their oaths) were not in the manuscript or the printed edition; the correct reading includes them.]] so that their oaths are invalidated. ﴿And fear God and listen. God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾ — the liars, those who swear falsely. Ibn Zayd also said: "Tamim al-Dari and a companion of his came, and they were polytheists at that time and had not yet become Muslim. They reported that a man had entrusted his bequest to them, and they brought his estate. The heirs of the deceased said: 'Our companion had such and such,' and he had a silver ewer!' The other two said: 'He had nothing but what we brought!' So the two swore after the prayer. Then, later, the ewer was discovered with them." When it was found with them, the oath was returned to the heirs of the deceased, based on what they had said their companion had; then these two were made to pay what the heirs had sworn to.

**[12970]** Al-Rabi' narrated to us, saying: al-Shafi'i narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'id Mu'adh ibn Musa al-Ja'fari informed us, from Bukayr ibn Ma'ruf, from Muqatil ibn Hayyan [Bukayr said: Muqatil said: "I took this tafsir from Mujahid, al-Hasan, and al-Dahhak"] concerning God's words: ﴿two just men from among you﴾, that two Christian men, one from Tamim and one from Yemen, from the people of Dara'in,[[Dara'in: a place name.]] accompanied a client of Quraysh on a trade mission. They sailed the sea, and the Qurayshi had property that was known, which his heirs knew about, consisting of vessels, cloth, and silver.[["al-Bazz" means garments, or types of them; the seller is called "al-bazzaz." "al-Riqqa" (with the ra' vowelled with a kasra and the qaf with a fatha) means silver; its origin is "al-warq" (with the waw vowelled with a fatha and the ra' with a kasra), then the waw was dropped and a ha' was placed at the end as a substitute for it.]] The Qurayshi fell ill, so he entrusted his bequest to the two from Dara'in, and he died. The two from Dara'in took possession of the property and the bequest, and they handed it to the heirs of the deceased. They also brought some of his property, but the people denied that the property was small. They said to the two from Dara'in: "Our companion set out with more property than what you brought us; did he sell or buy anything, so that some loss occurred in it?"[["yuqal: wada'a fi tijaratihi yudu'u du'atan, wa-wadi'ah, fa-huwa mawdu'un fiha" (it is said: he suffered a loss in his trade). It is also said: "awda'a" (both in the passive). It is also said: "wada'a fi tijaratihi wad'an" (like fariha farahan): he was cheated in it and lost from the capital."]] "Did his illness last long, so that he spent on himself?" They said: "No!" They said: "Indeed you have betrayed us!" So they took the property and brought their dispute before the Prophet (ﷺ), and God, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿O you who believe, let there be a witness between you﴾ up to the end of the verse. When it was revealed that they should be detained after the prayer, the Prophet (ﷺ) so ordered, and they stood after the prayer, and swore by God, Lord of the heavens: ﴿Your master's property was not left other than what we brought to you; and we do not take a paltry price for our oaths, even if it concerns a relative, and we do not conceal the testimony of God; otherwise we would surely be among the sinners﴾. When they had sworn, he released them. Then they later found a vessel among the deceased's vessels, so the two from Dara'in were seized, and they said: "We bought it from him during his lifetime!" They were lying, so they were required to produce evidence, but they could not. They brought this matter to the Prophet (ﷺ), and God, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿Then if it is discovered﴾, that is, if it is found out, ﴿that the two had become liable for a sin﴾ — meaning the two from Dara'in, if they concealed a right — ﴿two others﴾, from the heirs of the deceased, ﴿shall stand in their place from among those who have a claim against them, the two first ones﴾, so they shall swear by God: "Our companion's property was such and such, and what is sought from the two from Dara'in is a right, and we have not transgressed; otherwise we would surely be among the wrongdoers." This is the statement of the two witnesses, the heirs of the deceased. ﴿That is more suitable so that they bring the testimony in its proper form﴾ — meaning: the two from Dara'in and the people — so that they do not return to the like of that.[[The report 12970: "Mu'adh ibn Musa al-Ja'fari," "Abu Sa'id," I have found no biography for him except in Ta'jil al-Manfa'a (Speedy Benefit) p. 406, which says only: "Mu'adh ibn Musa, from Bukayr ibn Ma'ruf, and with al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him." In the printed edition it read "Sa'id ibn Mu'adh ibn Musa," which is an error, contrary to the manuscript.
"Bukayr ibn Ma'ruf al-Asadi," "Abu Mu'adh al-Nisaburi, al-Damghani," author of the tafsir, and a student of Muqatil. Ibn 'Adi said: "He is not a prolific narrator, and I hope he is not blameworthy, and his hadith is not extremely unacceptable." He is discussed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/2/117, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/406.
In the printed edition it read "Bakr," which is a clear error.
This report was transmitted by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra 10: 164 by way of Isma'il ibn Qutayba, from Abu Khalid Yazid ibn Salih, from Bukayr ibn Ma'ruf, from Muqatil ibn Hayyan. Then he transmitted it (10: 165) by way of Abu al-'Abbas al-Asamm, from al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman, from al-Shafi'i, then referred its wording to the preceding one.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The reports we have related show clear evidence for the soundness of what we have said: that God's ruling, exalted is His remembrance, concerning the oath imposed on the two witnesses in this place, comes only from a claim made by the heirs against those to whom the bequest was entrusted, alleging betrayal in what the deceased handed over to them of his property, or other matters in which the claimant cannot be cleared of the claim against them except by an oath. And the transfer of the oath to the heirs of the deceased is by what God, exalted is His remembrance, has made obligatory, after the two witnesses were found [to have incurred sin] in their oaths, [this addition between the brackets is necessary; I have inferred it from the text of the verse]. Then it became evident that they had lied in them, [namely] that the people claimed, regarding what was established, that the deceased had a claim of transfer of ownership from him to them by some of the means by which ownership is transferred, in which the oath falls upon the heirs of the deceased rather than the claimant, and the proof falls upon the claimant; and [that the one who differs in this verse from what we have said of the interpretation is in error]. [[In the printed edition: "مما قلنا من التأويل" ("of what we said of the interpretation"); in the manuscript: "ما قبلنا من التأويل" ("what preceded us of the interpretation"). The correct reading is what I have adopted.]]

And in it also, [[The phrase "وفيها أيضًا" refers back to the opening of the previous paragraph, "ففيما ذكرنا من هذه الأخبار التي روينا", and is coordinated with it.]] there is clear evidence that the meaning of "testimony" (shahada) mentioned by God at the beginning of this story is in fact the oath, as God says in other places: "And those who accuse their wives but have no witnesses except themselves, the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by God that he is surely of the truthful" (Surat an-Nur 24:6). So "testimony" in this place means an oath, from the speaker's words: "I bear witness by God that I am truthful." [[In the printed edition: "إنه لمن الصادقين"; I have adopted what is in the manuscript.]] Likewise the meaning of His words "testimony between you" is: an oath between you, "when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest," that two just men from among you swear, if the two who were entrusted with property are suspected, or two others from outside the believers are entrusted and then accused. [[See what he wrote on "اتمن" earlier, p. 172, notes 1 and 2.]] This is because God, exalted is His remembrance, when He mentioned the transfer of the oath from the two whose betrayal was discovered to the other two, said: "they will swear by God that our testimony is more worthy than their testimony." It is known that the heirs of the deceased who made the claims against those whose betrayal was discovered could not be witnesses in the sense of testimony by which a right is established in judgment for a claimant against a defendant. For there is no ruling of God, exalted is His remembrance, which decides in favor of someone by his claim and oath against a defendant without evidence, without an admission from the defendant, and without proof. Since it is established that His words, "our testimony is more worthy than their testimony," mean only: "our oath is more worthy than their oath," and the oath of the two found to have sinned is the testimony that God mentioned in His words "more worthy than their testimony," it is sound that the meaning of "testimony between you" is the same as "testimony" in "our testimony is more worthy than their testimony," and that it means oath.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The readers (qurra') differed concerning the reading of His words: "from among those upon whom the two [others] have an entitlement" (min alladhina istahagga 'alayhimu al-awlayan).

The readers of the Hijaz, Iraq and Syria read: مِنَ الَّذِينَ اسْتَحَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ الأَوْلَيَانِ, with a damma on the "ta'" [i.e., istaḥaqqa with the passive form, reading "al-awlayani" as the subject].

It is reported from 'Ali, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Hasan al-Basri that they read: مِنَ الَّذِينَ اسْتَحَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ, with a fatha on the "ta'" [i.e., istaḥqqa in the active form].

The readers differed also concerning His words "al-awlayan" (the two nearest).
The majority of the readers of Medina, Syria and Basra read: ﴿الأَوْلَيَانِ﴾.

The majority of the readers of Kufa read: ﴿الأَوَّلِينَ﴾.

It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to read: ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ اسْتَحَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ الأَوَّلانِ﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two readings in His words "from among those upon whom [the claim] is established" is the reading of the one who reads with a damma on the "ta'," due to the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it, together with the agreement of the majority of the interpreters on the soundness of its interpretation. This is because the majority of them agree that its meaning is: "two others from among the heirs of the deceased, upon whom the sin of the two entrusted with the deceased's property is established, stand in the place of those two whose sin is established, because of their betrayal of what they betrayed of the deceased's property."

We have already mentioned those who held this view, or most of them, earlier, and we will mention the rest, God willing:

12971 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of God, exalted is His remembrance: "testimony between you": that a believer dies and two Muslims or two unbelievers attend his death, and none other than two of them is present. If the heirs are content with what he hastened to give from his estate, that is well; and if the two witnesses are suspected, they swear that they are truthful. ["If it is found..." (fa-'athara) ... [[In the printed edition: "فإن عثر، وجد لطخ حلف الاثنان..." and the phrase "لطخ" here is strange. In the manuscript there is a blank space after "فإن عثر وجد" to the end of the line, with red marks after the words. It seems the copy from which the printer worked had the letter (ṭ) at this place as a sign of error, so he wrote what he wrote in its place. I have placed dots in the manuscript's blank space, and it appears the context was: "If it is found, it is discovered that they incurred sin," the two swear...; but I preferred to leave the blank as it is in the manuscript; the meaning is clear.]] the two heirs, the nearest of the heirs, swear, and so they deserve [the claim], and their oaths nullify the oaths of the two witnesses.

* *

I think that those who read it with a fatha on the "ta'" intended to direct its interpretation toward: "two others stand in their place," in place of the two entrusted persons whose betrayal was found in the oath, and "the entitlement upon them," meaning their claim against them, [is] from "those who are entitled" against the entrusted persons over their betrayal in standing in their place in the oath and the entitlement, the nearest to the deceased. [[In the printed edition: "في الأوليان" with an added "في"; I have adopted what is in the manuscript, which is correct.]] Such was the reading of the one from whom this reading is reported, who read: مِنَ الَّذِينَ اسْتَحَقَّ with a fatha on the "ta'," and "al-awlayan," [[In the printed edition the words "والأوليان" are omitted, and the sentence is run on in one continuous line. I have adopted what is in the manuscript.]] meaning: the nearest to the deceased and his property. This is a sound view and a reading whose soundness is not rejected; but we choose the other reading, due to the consensus of the authoritative readers upon it, together with its agreement with the interpretation we have mentioned from the Companions and the Successors.

12972 - Ibn Wakf' related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Adam related to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Kurayb, from 'Ali: that he used to read: ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ اسْتُحِقَّ عَلَيْهِمْ الأَوْلَيَانْ﴾. [[Report 12972: "Abu Ishaq" is al-Sabi'i. "Abu 'Abd al-Rahman" is "al-Sulami," the reader, "'Abd Allah ibn Habib," who has passed as No. 82. "Kurayb" is "Kurayb ibn Abi Kurayb," who related from 'Ali. Abu Ishaq related from him; he is listed in al-Kabir 4/1/231 and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/168, and neither mentions any criticism of him. He is listed in Lisan al-Mizan, which says: "He relates isolated reports (al-maqati'), and is among the trustworthy (thiqat) of Ibn Hibban."]]

12973 - Ibn Wakf' related to us, saying: Malik ibn Isma'il related to us, from Hammad ibn Zayd, from Wasil, freedman of Abu 'Uyayna, from Yahya ibn 'Aqil, from Yahya ibn Ya'mur, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: that he used to read: ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ اسْتُحِقَّ عَلَيْهِمْ الأَوْلَيَان﴾. [[Report 12973: "Malik ibn Isma'il ibn Dirham al-Nahdi," "Abu Ghassan," has passed as Nos. 2989, 4433, 4926, 8292. I fear the transmitter of this report is "Mu'ammal ibn Isma'il al-'Adawi," not "Malik ibn Isma'il," but this is how it is in the manuscript. "Hammad ibn Zayd ibn Dirham al-Azdi" has passed as Nos. 856, 1682, 5454. "Wasil, freedman of Abu 'Uyayna ibn al-Muhallab ibn Abi Safra," is trustworthy; he related from Yahya ibn 'Aqil al-Khuza'i, al-Hasan al-Basri, Raja' ibn Haywa and Abu al-Zubayr al-Makki. Hisham ibn Hassan, of his own generation, Mahdi ibn Maymun, Hammad ibn Zayd and others related from him. He is listed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/172 and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/30. In the printed edition and the manuscript it was "Wa'il ibn Abi 'Ubayda," which is an error beyond doubt, as clarified in al-Bukhari's al-Tarikh al-Kabir. "Yahya ibn 'Aqil al-Khuza'i al-Basri" related from Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Abi Awfa. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy, and Ibn Ma'in said: "There is nothing wrong with him." He is listed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/292 and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/176. As for "Yahya ibn Ya'mur al-Qays al-Judali," he is a trustworthy and great authority who related from the Companions and the Successors. He was a grammarian, a master of Arabic and the Qur'an, and he was the first to add dots to the mushafs. He is listed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/311 and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/196.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for the more correct of the readings in His words "al-awlayan" in my view, it is the reading of the one who reads: ﴿الأَوْلَيَانِ﴾, for the soundness of its meaning. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads "بصحة معناها" with a "ب"; the correct form is what I have written.]] This is because the meaning of "two others stand in their place from among those upon whom the two nearest [have an entitlement]" is: two others stand in their place from among those upon whom the sin is established, [[What I have put between the brackets is the true sense and meaning of the context, for the context requires that the verse be mentioned and then its interpretation be mentioned; and so I have done, and it is correct, God willing.]] Then "the sin" was omitted, and "al-awlayan" was put in its place, because they are the two who wronged and sinned in them, by the betrayal of the two whose sin was established and who were discovered to have betrayed what the deceased had entrusted to them. [[In the printed edition: "ائتمنهما" ("entrusted them"); see what I wrote earlier, p. 172, notes 1 and 2, and p. 193, note 4.]] As we have already shown earlier, this is the practice of the Arabs: they omit the verbal noun (fi'l) by relying on the noun, and omit the noun by relying on the verb. [["Al-fi'l" here means the verbal noun (masdar), as has passed many times; see the indexes of terms.]] See what has passed on p. 160. Among that is what we have mentioned in the interpretation of this story, namely His words: "testimony between you, when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest, two [witnesses]," and its meaning is: "that two bear witness." And as He said: "They will swear by God if you doubt: we will not exchange it for any price," where He said "by it" (bihi), referring with the pronoun to the name of God, while the meaning is: "we will not exchange by our oath by God," and the mention of the reference to the name of God was sufficient, meaning "we will not exchange by the oath by God," being content with the listener's understanding of its meaning without mentioning the name of the oath. Likewise, the mention of "the two nearest" is sufficient for the mention of "the sin" which the two betrayers deserved for their betrayal of them, since this was already mentioned in such a way as to make it unnecessary for the listener to hear it repeated, namely His words: "If it is found that they incurred sin..."

* *

As for those who read it as ﴿الأَوَّلِينَ﴾, they intended by it a translation of "those" (alladhina), and so they rendered it in the plural, since "alladhina" is plural, and in the genitive case, since "alladhina" is in the genitive. This is one aspect of interpretation. But a thing is only called "first" (awwal) if it has a last which is first to it, and for those upon whom the sin is established there is no last whom they precede. Rather, the oaths of those found to have incurred sin came before their oaths; so they are, since their oaths are the last, more properly called "the last" (akhirin) than "the first" (awwalin), and their oaths are the last to the first that preceded them.

* *

As for the reading reported from al-Hasan, it is a reading that is irregular (shadhdh) compared with the reading of the authoritative readers; and its irregularity compared with their reading is enough evidence of its remoteness from the correct reading.

* *

The grammarians differed concerning the element that makes "al-awlayan" nominative (raf') when it is read in this way.

One of the grammarians of Basra [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "فقال بعض نحويي..." ; the correct form is what I have adopted.]] claimed that it is nominative as an apposition (badal) to "two others" in His words "two others stand in their place." He said: "'Al-awlayan' may be an apposition to 'two others' even though it is definite and 'two others' is indefinite, because when He said 'stand in their place from among those upon whom [the claim] is established,' it was as if He had already defined them until they became definite in meaning, so He said 'al-awlayan,' and made the definite noun an apposition for them." He said: "Similar to this, which applies to meaning, is abundant." He cited as evidence for the soundness of his view the verse of the rajaz poet: [[I do not know who the poet is.]]

"Upon me, on the day that he rules the affairs, is a fast of months that became obligatory as vows,
And a fat, garlanded, slaughtered camel."

["Al-badin" means the large, fat, dense one. I have not found that they said "al-badin" meaning "al-badana" (with fatha on the "ba'" and "dal"), which is the camel they used to fatten and then sent as an offering to the House, and slaughtered there. Perhaps the poet used it as an adjective, but it is in my view a rare usage that needs qualification. "Al-muqallad" is the one on whom garlands are placed, as a sign that it is an offering led to the Ka'ba. The poet mentioned what he vowed if this man was put in charge of the affairs of the people.]] He said: "He made it: 'upon me is obligatory,' because in meaning he had obligated [himself]."

[I have left this sentence as it stands in the manuscript and the printed edition, although I incline to think that he cited the rajaz for its use of the accusative for "fast of months" and conjoined "and a fat, garlanded, slaughtered [camel]" to it, meaning: "I have obligated upon myself a fast of months, and a fat, garlanded, slaughtered [camel]." If this is correct, the proper wording of this statement would be: "He made it: 'upon me is obligatory,' because in meaning: 'I have obligated.'"]

* *

One of the grammarians of Kufa denied this and said: It is not permissible for "al-awlayan" to be an apposition to "two others," because "fa-yuqsimani" has been coordinated with "yaqumani" in His words "two others stand in their place," so the statement was not complete after "min [from among]." [In the printed edition: "فلم يتم الخبر عند من قال..." , which is different from the manuscript and is a plain error. The correct reading is what is in the manuscript, meaning: "after 'from among those upon whom the two nearest [have an entitlement]'."] He said: "An apposition is not permissible before the statement is completed." He said: It is not permissible to say: "I passed by a man who stood, Zayd and sat," with "Zayd" as an apposition to "man."

[[In the printed edition and the manuscript the word "قال" appears without the conjunction "و"; the correct form, as the context shows, includes the "و". Then in the printed edition, after that, it reads "كما قال: غير جائز..." with an added "كما"; it is in the manuscript attached to the letter "ر", and I preferred the reading "وقال" because it is what the context requires.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in this matter, in my opinion, is that "al-awlayan" is nominative by the passive verb (the verb whose agent is not named), which is His words: "is established upon them," and that the two [words] were placed in the position of the predicate about them, so that which was operating upon the predicate about them operated upon them. This is because the meaning of the statement is: "two others stand in their place from among those upon whom the sin is established through the betrayal," so "al-awlayan" was placed in the position of "the sin," as God, exalted is His remembrance, said in another place: "Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque like one who believes in God and the Last Day?" (Surat at-Tawba 9:19). Its meaning is: "Have you made the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque like the faith of one who believes in God and the Last Day?" And as He said: "And they were made to drink the calf in their hearts" (Surat al-Baqara 2:93). And as one of the Hudhalis said: [[He is al-Mankhal al-Hudhali.]]

"Among us walks a wine-seller of wine
From the mute, the bold, the tall-thin ones."

[[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 2:21, and al-Ma'ani al-Kabir: 472. Also Lisan al-Arab (hant) (qatt) (khuras), from a long poem of his in which he mentions the days of his youth, then says after the verse, in describing wine:
"Still in the vessel, its heat...
the hands of the drinkers delight in taking it
Sparkling like the eye of a rooster, when it is tasted
it has a taste from the vinegar of the Khimat."]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 5, verse 107 (part 4 of 4):

His saying "al-khuras" (ﭐالخرس), the plural of "akhras" (ﭐأخرس), is one whose speech has gone away, either through incapacity to speak or by creation. He means by it servants from the non-Arabs who do not speak clearly, and for this reason they were named "khurs" (mute). Some transmitted it as "min al-khars" (from the guessing), but that is an error, and al-Azhari (rahimahu Allah) drew attention to it.

And "al-sarasira" (ﭐالصراصرة) are the Nabat of Syria. In my view they were named thus because of something in their voices when they spoke: in their voices there is shouting, height and extension, as if it were the screech of the falcon (sarsarat al-bazi). And "al-qitat" is the plural of "qatt" (with two fatha vowels) and "qitt" (with fatha and shaddah), which is a man intensely curly-haired. His saying "rukud fi al-ina'" (ﭐركود في الإناء) means that it is clear and still. And "hamya al-khamr" (ﭐحميا الخمر) is its strength and its effect on the body. And "al-aydi al-sawati" (ﭐالأيدي السواطي) are the hands that reach out to it, that is, that take hold of it hastily, being very eager for it. And "mushashi'a" (ﭐمشعشعة) means it has been thinned by mixing it with water. And "al-khammat" from wine (ﭐالخماط) is wine that has been struck by wind, so that it has not matured and has not reached sourness.

He means: the owner of a wine-shop, but he put "the wine-shop" in his place, because it is known that "the wine-shop" does not walk! But since it was known to him that the one addressed would not fail to grasp what he intended by its meaning, he omitted "the owner" and sufficed with mentioning "the wine-shop" from it. Likewise His saying "min alladhina ustuhigga 'alayhimu al-awlayan" (ﭐمن الذين استُحِقّ عليهم الأوليان) means only: "from those against whom the treachery of the two was deserved," so "the treachery" was omitted and "the two who betrayed" (al-mukhtanan) was put in its place. So what would be applied to the omitted word, were it present, is applied to them.

* *

As for His saying "alayhim" (ﭐعليهم) in this place, its meaning is "fihim" (concerning them), as Almighty God said: "wa-ttaba'u ma tatlu al-shayatin 'ala mulk Sulayman" (Surat al-Baqarah: 102), meaning: "in the kingdom of Sulayman," and as He said: "wa-la-usallibannakum fi judhu' al-nakhl" (Surat Ta-Ha: 71). So "fi" is placed in the position of "ala," and "ala" in the position of "fi," each of them substituting for the other in speech. [See what has preceded 1:299, 2:411, 412, and other places in the chapter on the interchange of particles.]

And from this is the saying of the poet: [He is Abu al-Muthalmam al-Hudhali.]
"Mata ma tunkiruha ta'rifuha ... 'ala aqtariha 'alaqun nafith"
[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 2:224; Mushkil al-Qur'an: 295, 430; al-Ma'ani al-Kabir: 969, 970; al-Iqtidab: 451; al-Jawaliqi: 373; al-Lisan (nafatha) and others. From verses in a dispute between him and Sakhr al-Ghayy, concerning the blood-wealth (ʿaql) of a slain man which Abu al-Muthalmam was seeking, that is, his diyya. Before the verse: "Laḥaqa Banu Shughara an yaqulu ... li-Sakhr al-Ghayy: madha tastabit?" That is: "What are you stirring up?" He meant war, and so he said to him afterwards: "Whenever you deny it..." meaning: when war comes you deny it, but you hardly deny it until you see blood dripping from its sides, meaning the battalions of the combatants. "Al-ʿalaq" is blood, and "al-aqtar" are the sides. "Al-nafith" is the blood that wounds and sores discharge.]
Al-Batlyawsi has confused the explanation of this poetry, claiming that the pronoun in "mata ma tunkiruha" refers to "the saying" (al-maqala), meaning this mutual satire between them, and he brought in this a speech with no good in it, intending obscurity as is his habit.

A group of the interpreters have explained the saying of God, dhikruhu: "fa-in 'uthira 'ala annahuma istahaqqa ithman fa-akharani yaqumani maqamahuma min alladhina istuhigga 'alayhimu al-awlayan," that they are two other men from among the Muslims, or two men more just than the first two swearers.

Mention of those who said that:

12974 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated to us, from ʿAmir, from Shurayh, concerning this verse: "O you who believe, the testimony between you when death approaches one of you at the time of bequest is two men of justice from among you, or two others from outside your own," he said: If a man is in a land of strangeness and does not find a Muslim to witness his bequest, he calls to witness a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian, and their testimony is permitted. But if two Muslim men come and testify contrary to their testimony, the testimony of the Muslims is accepted and the testimony of the others is nullified. [The report: 12974 - This report has passed as nos. 12909, 12943; see the note on no. 12909.]

12975 - Bishr ibn Muʿadh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah: "fa-in ʿuthira" means: it became known from the two of them of treachery, that they had lied or concealed, so if two men more just than them testified contrary to what they said, the testimony of the latter is accepted and the testimony of the former is nullified.

12976 - Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from ʿAta', who said: Ibn ʿAbbas used to recite: "min alladhina istuhigga ʿalayhimu al-awwalayn," and said: How can "al-awlayan" be? Do you see, if the two "awlayan" were young?

12977 - Hannad and Ibn Waki' narrated to us, both saying: ʿAbdah narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: he used to recite: "min alladhina istuhigga ʿalayhimu al-awwalayn," and said: Do you see, if the two "awlayan" were young, how would they stand in their place?

Abu Ja'far said: Ibn ʿAbbas, as I see it, went toward the view I have related from Shurayh and Qatadah, that these are two other men from among the Muslims, standing in place of the two Christians, or two just men from among the Muslims who are more upright and more fit to testify than the first two witnesses or swearers.

And the consensus of all the people of knowledge that there is no ruling of God, dhikruhu, that requires an oath on a witness for what he has testified to, is clear evidence that other than this interpretation, that which al-Hasan and those who say his saying said regarding the saying of God, dhikruhu: "fa-akharani yaqumani maqamahuma," is more fitting for it.

As for His saying "al-awlayan," its meaning, in our view, is: "those nearest to the deceased among the first swearers, then the nearest." [The context: "al-awla bi-l-mayyit ... fa-al-awla."] It may also be that its meaning is: "those nearer to the oath of the two, then the nearer," then "minhuma" was omitted. The Arabs do this, saying "fulan afdal" and they mean "afdal minka" (better than you), and this is when "af'al" is placed in the position of the predicate. If it occurs in the position of a noun and "al" is added to it, they also do this when it is a reply to a previous speech, saying "hadha al-afdal" and "hadha al-ashraf," meaning: he is the more noble than you.

* *

Qatadah... [Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of that is: "al-awlayan bi-l-mayyit."]
12978 - Yunus narrated to me, from Ibn Wahb, from him.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: "fa-yuqsimani billahi la-shahadatuna ahaqqu min shahadatihima wa-ma i'tadayna inna idhan la-mina al-zalimin" (5:107)

Abu Ja'far said: God, dhikruhu, says: "Then the two others who stand in place of those upon whom the treachery of the two was proven, the two nearest with the oath, and the deceased [being] of the treacherous ones," "our testimony is more deserving than their testimony": that is, our oaths are more deserving than the oaths of the two swearers who merit sin and their false oath, that they had betrayed in such-and-such from the wealth of our deceased, and likewise in their oaths by which they swore, "and we have not transgressed": that is, we have not overstepped the truth in our oaths.

* *

We have explained that the meaning of "i'tida'" is going beyond a thing's limit.

* *

"Inna idhan la-mina al-zalimin" means: "If we had transgressed in our oaths, swearing falsely and lying in them, then we would be among the wrongdoers," that is: among those who take what is not theirs to take, and who by their wicked oaths seize the wealth of people.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 5, Verse 108

**The interpretation of His saying: ﴿That is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form, or to their fearing that oaths will be repeated after their oaths﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His saying "That," may He be exalted, He means this matter I have told you about concerning the executors (al-awsiya'), if you doubt them and suspect them of betraying the property of the one who made them executors, by detaining them after the prayer and making them swear by God regarding what the heirs of the deceased claim against them. "Closer" for them "to giving testimony in its proper form," meaning: this action, if you do it to them, is closer to their being truthful in their oaths [see the explanation of "closer" in what has passed, 6:78 / 7:548], and not concealing, and admitting the truth and not betraying [see the explanation of "in its proper form" in what has passed, 2:511]. "Or to their fearing that oaths will be repeated after their oaths," meaning: or these executors will fear, if it is discovered, that they have incurred sin in their oaths by God, that their oaths will be repeated against the heirs of the deceased after their oaths, which have been found to be false, so that they would forfeit by them what they claimed against them of their rights. Thus they would then be truthful in their oaths and testimony, out of fear of disgrace upon themselves and caution lest there be imposed upon them what they betrayed concerning the heirs and the inheritors of the deceased.

* *

Exegetes have said what we have said on this. The report has already been transmitted from some of them, and we will mention the report from some of those who remain among them.

12979 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿If it is found that the two had incurred sin﴾: he means, if it is discovered that the two unbelievers lied. ﴿Then two others will stand in their place﴾: he means, from among the guardians. They swear by God that the testimony of the two unbelievers is false, and that we did not transgress. So the testimony of the two unbelievers is rejected, and the testimony of the guardians is accepted. He, may He be exalted, says: That is closer to the unbelievers giving testimony in its proper form, or to their fearing that oaths will be repeated after their oaths. There are no oaths on the testimony of Muslims; oaths are only required when they are unbelievers.

12980 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿That is closer to their giving testimony﴾, to the end of the verse: he says, that is more likely to make them truthful in their testimony, and that they fear the consequence. [In the printed edition: "and that they fear the punishment," and the correct reading is what is in the manuscript, "al-'aqib" (with a fatha on the first letter and a kasra on the second), meaning the outcome: the outcome of their matter in their oaths being nullified, and the outcome of the disgrace returning upon themselves.]

12981 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿Or to their fearing that oaths will be repeated after their oaths﴾: he said, their oaths will be nullified, and the oaths of these others will be taken.

* *

Others said: [The meaning of that is: you detain them after the prayer. "That is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form, that they have incurred sin," then "two others will stand in their place."] [This whole sentence is confused in meaning and does not match the following report. My opinion is that there is a lacuna in the text, that the copyist dropped a line or so. I have left it as it stands in the manuscript and the printed edition, but I have placed it between brackets, doubting its soundness.]

Mention of those who said that:

12982 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: The two men are detained after their prayer regarding their debt. They swear by God: ﴿We will not sell it for a small price, even if it were a relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of God, for then we would surely be among the sinners﴾, that "Indeed, your companion bequeathed this, and indeed this is his estate." The ruler says to them before they swear: "If you have concealed or betrayed, I will disgrace you among your people, I will not allow your testimony, and I will punish you." If he says this to them, then that is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form.

* *

**The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And fear God, and listen; and God does not guide the defiant people﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: God, may He be exalted, says: Fear God, O people, and be mindful of Him in your oaths, that you swear by them falsely, and that you destroy by them the property of one whose property is forbidden to you, and that you betray the one who entrusted you [see what I wrote on "entrusted" in what has passed, p. 197, note 3]. "And listen," meaning: listen to what is said to you and what you are admonished with, act upon it, and comply with it. "And God does not guide the defiant people," meaning: God does not grant success to those who transgress the command of their Lord, oppose Him, obey Satan, and disobey their Lord.

* *

Ibn Zayd used to say: "The defiant (al-fasiq)" in this place is the liar. [See the explanation of "defiant" with this meaning from the tafsir of Ibn Zayd, in what has passed, no. 12103, in Volume 10, p. 376. Then see the explanation of "defiance" (fisq) in what has passed in the lexical indexes, root f-s-q.]

12983 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding ﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾: the liars, who swear on falsehood.

* *

What Ibn Zayd said on this, in my view, is not to be rejected. However, God, may He be exalted, made the statement general, that He does not guide all the defiant, and He did not specify some of them over others by any report or reason. Therefore it applies to all the meanings of "defiance," until something among them is specified by what must be accepted, and then it is accepted.

* *

Then the people of knowledge differed regarding the ruling of these two verses: is it abrogated (mansukh), or is it firm and established (muhkam)?

Some of them said: It is abrogated (naskh: the replacement of one ruling by a later one).

Mention of those who said that:

12984 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from a man whom he named, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, who said: It is abrogated.

12985 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: It is abrogated, meaning this verse: ﴿O you who believe, the testimony among you﴾, to the end of the verse.

* *

Others said: It is firm and not abrogated. We have already mentioned the opinion of most of them earlier.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this is that the ruling of the verse is not abrogated [in the printed edition and the manuscript: "that the ruling of the verse is abrogated," which is a gross error, for Abu Ja'far says afterwards that it is not abrogated, as you will see, so what I have established is correct]. This is because, among the rulings of God, may He be exalted, that the people of Islam hold, from the time God sent His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) until today, is that whoever is sued for a claim concerning something that the children of Adam may own, the defendant does not clear himself of what is claimed against him except by an oath, when the claimant has no proof to establish his claim. And if he acknowledges that something in the hand of the claimant is his own, [in the printed edition: "and if he acknowledges, and in the hand of the claimant is a commodity," which differs from the manuscript; the manuscript has "and if he acknowledges, in the hand of the claimant, a commodity." I have followed that, which is correct, and I have added "upon him" between brackets, because the meaning requires it.

His saying "acknowledges" means: recognizes it and distinguishes it, as will come in the rest of the passage.] and then claims that it belongs to him and not to the one in whose hand it is, and the one in whose hand it is says: "No, it is mine. I bought it from this claimant," then the word of the one who says he bought it from him is the word of the one in whose hand it is, along with his oath, rather than the word of the one who claims it, when the one in whose hand it is has no proof to establish his claim of purchase from him.

Since this is the ruling of God, about which there is no disagreement among the people of knowledge, and since the two verses in which God, may He be exalted, mentions the matter of a testator's bequest to two just men from among the Muslims, or to two others from among non-Muslims, the Prophet (ﷺ) required, as is reported from him, the two executors to swear when the heirs sued them for what they claimed. Then he did not require the two defendants anything when they swore, until the heirs acknowledged what was in their hands of the bowl, the jug, or other property of theirs, and they claimed that the two had bought it from their deceased. At that point the Prophet (ﷺ) required the heirs of the deceased to swear, because the two executors had become claimants by their claim that what they found in their hands of the property of the deceased was theirs, which they had bought from him. Thus they became acknowledgers of the property belonging to the deceased while claiming to have purchased it from him, and so they then needed proof to establish their claim. The heirs of the deceased, as the owners of the commodity, were then more entitled to the oath than the two. This is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If it is found that the two had incurred sin, then two others will stand in their place from among those against whom the two first were entitled, and they will swear by God: our testimony is more truthful than theirs﴾, to the end of the verse.

Since the interpretation of that is as it is, there is no basis for the claim of one who asserts that this verse is abrogated, because it is not permissible to declare any of God's rulings, may He be exalted, abrogated, except by a report that cuts off excuses, either from God, or from His Messenger (ﷺ), or by the transmission of a widely attested report to that effect. As there is no such report, and no reason rejects its authenticity, it is not permissible to judge that it is abrogated.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ (5:109)

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is His remembrance, says: "And fear Allah, O people, and listen to His admonition to you and His reminder to you, and beware of the Day when Allah will gather the messengers." Then "and beware" was omitted, and He sufficed with His saying "fear Allah and listen" from stating it, as the rajiz (rajaz poet) said:

"I fed her chaff and cool water, until her eyes began to flow with tears" [[The verse's source and explanation were given earlier, 1:264. In the printed edition here it read "until she became…", which differs from the manuscript.]]

He means: "and I gave her cool water to drink." He dispensed with his saying "I fed her chaff" from stating "I gave her to drink," since the listener, upon hearing it, understands its meaning. Likewise in His saying "On the Day when Allah gathers the messengers," "and beware" is omitted, because the listener knows its meaning, being satisfied with His saying "fear Allah and listen," since that is a warning concerning the command of Allah, Exalted is His remembrance, to His creatures regarding His punishment for their disobedience.

* *

As for His saying "What was your response?", it means: what did your peoples respond to you when you called them to My monotheism, to affirming Me, to acting in obedience to Me, and to refraining from disobeying Me? "They will say, 'We have no knowledge.'"

* *

The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: The meaning of their saying "We have no knowledge" is that it was not from the messengers a denial that they had knowledge of what their peoples had done; rather, they were bewildered from answering because of the terror of that day, and then they answered after their minds returned to them, by bearing witness concerning their peoples.

Those who said this:

12986 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding "On the Day when Allah gathers the messengers, and says, 'What was your response?' They say, 'We have no knowledge'": He said: That is because they came to a station in which intellects were bewildered; so when they were asked, they said, "We have no knowledge," then they came to another station, and bore witness concerning their peoples. [[In the printed edition: "That is because when they came to…", whereas in the manuscript: "That is because when they came to"; I have kept the manuscript reading and removed "lamma," as it has no place here and seems to be an addition from the copyist's haste.]]

12987 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Anbasa……… He said: I heard al-Hasan say regarding His saying "On the Day when Allah gathers the messengers," the verse, he said: from the terror of that day. [[The narration 12987: this isnad is clearly incomplete between "'Utba" and "al-Hasan al-Basri"; I placed dots in its place, and I was unable to find its completion in what precedes, so I left it until I find its completion.]]

12988 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid regarding His saying "On the Day when Allah gathers the messengers, and says, 'What was your response?'": they will be terrified, and He will say, "What was your response?" and they will say, "We have no knowledge!"

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us."

Those who said this:

12989 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid regarding His saying "On the Day when Allah gathers the messengers, and says, 'What was your response?'": they will say, "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us; indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: they said, "We have no knowledge, except a knowledge You know better than us."

Those who said this:

12990 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying "On the Day when Allah gathers the messengers, and says, 'What was your response?' They say, 'We have no knowledge,'": except a knowledge You know better than us.

* *

Others said: The meaning of "What was your response?" is: what did they do after you, and what did they innovate?

Those who said this:

12991 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying "On the Day when Allah gathers the messengers, and says, 'What was your response?'": what did they do after you, and what did they innovate after you? "They say, 'We have no knowledge; indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.'"

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the opinions, in terms of truth, is the saying of the one who said: "Its meaning: We have no knowledge, except a knowledge You know better than us," because He, Exalted is His remembrance, informed concerning them that they said, "We have no knowledge; indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen," meaning: indeed, nothing of what we have of that knowledge, or of other hidden and manifest knowledge, is concealed from You. The people only denied that they had any knowledge of what they were asked about that the Exalted does not know; not that they denied knowing what they witnessed. How could that be so, when He, Exalted is His remembrance, informs that they will report what their peoples answered them with, and that they will be witnesses to their conveyance of the message? He, Exalted is His remembrance, said: "And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you" [Surah al-Baqarah: 143].

* *

As for what Ibn Jurayj said, that its meaning is: "What did the nations do after you, and what did they innovate?", this is an interpretation with no meaning. Because the prophets did not have knowledge of what would occur after them except what Allah informed them of; and if they were asked about what their nations did after them, while the matter stands thus, it would be said to them: "What did We inform you would happen among them after you?" The apparent sense of Allah's report, Exalted is His remembrance, concerning His questioning them, indicates otherwise.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿When God said: O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says to His servants: Beware of the Day when God gathers the messengers and says to them: "What response did your peoples give you in the world?" ﴿When God said: O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit.﴾

* *

The particle ﴿idh﴾ (when) is connected to "you answered," as if its meaning were: "What did the peoples to whom Jesus was sent answer Jesus?"

* *

If someone says: How were the messengers asked about the response of the peoples to them in the time of Jesus, when among the messengers in the time of Jesus there were only a few of them? [In the printed edition: "illa aqall min dhalik" with an added "min", which spoils the sentence; the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]

It is said: It is permissible that God, exalted is His remembrance, meant by His saying "What did you answer?" the messengers who were sent in the time of Jesus, and the report came in the form of a general address while the intended meaning was those who were in the time of Jesus, just as He, exalted is His remembrance, said: ﴿Those to whom the people said: Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾ [Surah Ali Imran: 173], while the intended meaning was one man from the people, even though the form of speech is addressed to all people. [See what preceded: 405–413.]

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of the statement "When God said" is: at the time He said, ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit.﴾ He says: O Jesus, remember My bounties upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit and aided you with it. [See the explanation of "favour" in the earlier lexical indices (n-‘-m). See the explanation of "ayyada" in what preceded: 2:319 / 5:379 / 6:242.]

* *

The scholars of Arabic have differed concerning ﴿ayyadtuka﴾, as to what verbal form it is derived from.

Some of them said: it is ﴿fa‘‘altuka﴾ ["from al-ayd"], just as your saying "qawwaytuka" (I strengthened you) is "fa‘‘ala" from "al-quwwa" (strength). [The insertion between the brackets is necessary. In the printed edition: "as in His saying" with an added "fi", and the correct reading is what is in the manuscript, without it.]

* *

Others said: rather, it is ﴿fa‘altuka﴾ from "al-ayd".

It is narrated from Mujahid that he recited: ﴿idh ayyadtuka﴾, meaning "af‘altuka," from strength and ayd. [See the Ma‘ani al-Qur’an of al-Farra’ 1:325. What he mentions here regarding "ayyadtuka" is a detail he omitted in his earlier explanation at 2:319, and this is among the forms of his abridgment in tafsir, and it also indicates his method in composing this tafsir.]

* *

His saying: ﴿with the Holy Spirit﴾ means: with Gabriel. He says: when I aided you with Gabriel.

* *

I have already explained the meaning of that, and the meaning of "al-Qudus," in what has passed, with what suffices from repeating it in this place. [See the explanation of "Holy Spirit" in what preceded: 2:320, 321 / 5:379.]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿You will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and when I taught you the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel, and when you create from clay as the form of a bird by My permission, then you breathe into it and it becomes a bird by My permission, and you heal the blind and the leper by My permission, and when you bring forth the dead by My permission, and when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs, and those who disbelieved among them said: This is nothing but clear magic.﴾ (5:110)

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is His remembrance, reporting His speech to Jesus: ﴿remember My favour upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾, at the time you spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity.

* *

This is only a report from God, exalted is His remembrance, that He strengthened him with the Holy Spirit as a child in the cradle, and as a mature man in adulthood. So "maturity" is joined to His saying "in the cradle," because the meaning of that is "as a child," as God, exalted is His remembrance, said: ﴿He calls Us for his side, or sitting, or standing﴾ [Surah Yunus: 12].

* *

His saying: ﴿And when I taught you the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel﴾ means: remember also My favour upon you, ﴿when I taught you the Book﴾, which is writing; ﴿and wisdom﴾, which is understanding of the meanings of the Book I sent down to you, namely the Gospel; ﴿and when you create from clay as the form of a bird﴾ means: as the image of a bird...... [A blank space in the manuscript at this point, and in its margin the letter (ṭ), indicating a place of error. I have written it as it stands.
